NATALINA SOTGIA

ANNE

In Search of a Face

Presentation by Marco Nobile

EDIZIONI DEHONIANE BOLOGNA

© 2004 Centro editoriale dehoniano, Bologna · EDB · ISBN 88-10-51020-8. English translation of the Italian original.

PRESENTATION

I have a clear memory of the time when Sr. Natalina Sotgia was a regular presence in the library of the Pontifical Athenaeum Antonianum, preparing the reflections that I now have the pleasure of introducing. The vigorous woman I had met several years earlier was bent over her books not only because of the painstaking attention that study demands, but also because of the weight of an intense life lived in the service of her mission and of her religious family. And I was moved...

Whoever reads these pages that Sr. Natalina has left us as a legacy receives a testimony to her strong and determined personality, rigorous in research, yet simple and clear in what she asserts. The theme she set herself years ago was to offer her institute, the Daughters of St. Anne, a contribution toward the rediscovery of its charism.

The foundress, Blessed Rosa Gattorno, wished to link the spirituality of the new foundation to the figure of the mother of Our Lady. Certainly, in Blessed Rosa’s choice there was also a cultural component of a devotional nature, in keeping with the spirit of the age; yet her choice was equally interesting and stimulating, because it entrusted the patronage of her family to a mysterious figure whose age-old renown in popular devotion stood in contrast with the “anonymity”, as Sr. Natalina puts it, of her historical existence.

Among its other fruits, the Second Vatican Council gave new impetus to religious life, inviting the various orders and institutes to rediscover their own roots. Thanks to her culture, her rich interior life and her fidelity to the institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, Sr. Natalina welcomed the Council’s invitation and undertook a systematic piece of research, into which she poured, besides her constant passion for the word of God written in the Bible, the intense experience of her ten years in the Holy Land, in the Haifa community that she directed. Thus she set out to “discover the face of the Mother”, that is, of St. Anne.

The method chosen for carrying out the work, and the results obtained, are of a unique originality. Far from wishing to offer a pious and groundless reflection on a saint about whom historically nothing is known, Sr. Natalina did much more: she reconstructed her theological profile in a biblically irreproachable way, on the basis of a meticulous, well-informed and personal study of the Old Testament. She traced the features of the “eternal feminine” present in the Scriptures, with a unique wisdom, distinguishing each time the ideal aura of the great figures, such as Esther, Judith and Deborah, from the characteristics of the ordinary women of the Bible, no less interesting for the reconstruction of a biblical feminine face. Both, however, the great figures and the anonymous ones, are the object of careful scrutiny, from which Sr. Natalina draws surprising pictures or sculptures with a feminine subject.

Her procedure is always vigilant and never indulges in moments of devotional or spiritualistic weakness: her familiarity with specialist texts on the subject is evident. And yet Sr. Natalina’s reflections are equally nourished by a great passion, first of all for the Jewish people, toward whom she always showed boundless love, because it is a people that has suffered continually and because it is the people from whom St. Anne, the Virgin Mary and Jesus came; and then a passion for her religious institute, which must be grateful to have received the precious gift of her effective presence.

As I reread these pages that Sr. Natalina has left us, I thought, on the one hand, of her mature interior life, so masterfully poured into them, and on the other of the good they will do if the Daughters of St. Anne make them the subject of their own meditation, but also of diffusion beyond the institute, because they are reflections of biblical spirituality of a high standard.

Marco Nobile, OFM

A LONG-HELD DESIRE

The author as remembered by her sisters

Sr. Natalina Sotgia’s study of Women in the Bible, published some years ago – from 1995 to 1998 – in the column “Seeking his face” of the official magazine of the Daughters of St. Anne, Virga Jesse, now sees the light, three years after her death, in a unified edition. This is in homage to the memory of the author and in response to the widespread and recurring wish of not a few readers who, appreciating that original and instructive work, love to rediscover the taste of that reading and the attraction of the inexhaustible fascination of the biblical feminine world.

Other deep and pertinent motivations accompany these, and it is the author herself who explains them in a letter to a sister: “I dare to think that it was the Lord himself who was prompting me to take the Bible in hand in this way, in my own manner and with my modest strength, but with the deep and sincere desire to awaken, I do not say in everyone (...) but at least in some, the desire to continue, in a more scientific way, the research and the identification of our charism in the most authentically complete manner.” Her work of seeking the face of St. Anne, mother of Mary, as patroness of the institute of the Daughters of St. Anne,1 was therefore directed by her toward a deeper knowledge (in the biblical sense) of this figure, in order to possess her spirit, to love her more and to make her better known and loved, as the Constitutions, old and renewed, of the Daughters of St. Anne propose.

Sr. Natalina worked toward this end with fidelity and tenacity. With the passion proper to the educator who, aware of the mission she is called to carry out, makes herself a gift of pure gratuitousness, pouring out on all sides the charity of intelligence. In various settings – beginning with the school – and at various levels, she gave her service as a Daughter of St. Anne the unmistakable pedagogical and educational stamp that was natural to her. Her historical awareness, grounded in a firm demand for truth and justice, was always the guiding parameter that led her to look at reality with a sense of concreteness and personal responsibility. Paying attention to events and facts, grasping them, interpreting them, understanding them was a constant practice for her, who, “doing the truth in charity”, sought to communicate to others – considering this a grateful and due response of justice – what she had received.

With this deep experience she had taken part in the beginning of the path of renewal that the institute, in obedience to the Church of the Second Vatican Council, pursued in its Special Chapter (1969-1971) and in the following years. Sr. Natalina had been among the most active sisters on that path, as a member of that historic assembly and vicar of the superior general, both through the study of the documents of the institute’s origins, which fostered the discovery of its charism and its genuine spirituality, and through the clear and faithful exposition of the contents of that discovery in the Basic Documents for the drafting of the new Constitutions of the Daughters of St. Anne.

That first milestone was followed by the time of dissemination, acceptance and assimilation of those contents; Sr. Natalina was considered the right person for the role of formator, which she fulfilled by becoming all things to all, as for several years she illustrated, with her clear intelligence and human richness, nova et vetera.

The trajectory we are following, as we go back to the original inspiration of the present work, leads us at this point to follow Sr. Natalina to other horizons: the Holy Land. She had gone there to visit the sisters of the communities of Sepphoris, Haifa and Nazareth and asked to return, drawn by an inexplicable nostalgia. Then she immersed herself in that reality, in the light of the word of God, which she felt resounding from every corner, loving it in its many aspects.

She also found a way to write for Virga Jesse the history of the presence of the Daughters of St. Anne in the Holy Land, and began her narrative with a universal motivation: “This is the land of all men who wish to feel themselves such, because in it the roots of the whole of humanity are sunk... ‘All my springs are in you’, sang an inspired poet. In you... every FSA cannot help repeating with a grateful heart, going back to the sources of her own being a woman, a Christian and a religious, because this is the land in which St. Anne gave life to Mary, the mother of Jesus” (from Haifa, July 1985).

And it was precisely during the ten years spent in the Holy Land that Sr. Natalina carried in her heart the insistent question: how can we know the face of Anne, the face of the holy Mother? How can we overcome the distance in time between us and her? That passionate desire of hers, cultivated lovingly like a beautiful dream, is now entrusted to everyone in these pages.

Maria Eletta Convertini, FSA

PREFACE

THE FACE WE SEEK

1. In the most complete anonymity

“My heart says to you: seek his face.” When we reflect on our identity as Daughters of St. Anne, when we think of her or pray to her, and are forced to admit that, although she is one of the best known, most loved and most venerated saints of the whole of Christendom, her life remains wrapped in the veil of the most impenetrable anonymity, the verse of Psalm 27 comes spontaneously to our lips: “Seek his face.”

This verse, which Christian liturgy has made its own but which originally expresses the longing of the Jewish soul in its anxious search for its God, acquires, one might say, a twofold meaning for the Daughter of St. Anne. For she, committed to living fully the charism of her family and the commitments that flow from it, finds before her the figure of St. Anne who, from the pages of the first Rule (1869), explains to her that one of her fundamental commitments consists in knowing, making known and venerating her, her mother by election and patroness of the institute.

To know in the biblical sense means to possess, if not in fact, then in the full knowledge of the object: to know the mother is to possess her spirit. But how, and what is there truly to know of St. Anne, apart from the axiomatic fact that Mary of Nazareth had a mother? Nothing about her emerges, in fact, from the canonical Scriptures, and the very name of Anne is attributed to her only by the apocrypha. What do we know, then, and what can we communicate to others about this woman, certainly chosen by God, in view of the role he entrusted to her, among the most exalted of her race and of her time; about this woman who, bursting some two thousand years later into the life of Rosa Gattorno and, through her, into the life of the daughters present and future, set herself forth as a “copy of Christ”, a model of spirituality to be followed as a foundational element of their vocation?

“Seek his face.”

The first Daughters of St. Anne followed the foundress with trust, without tormenting themselves in the search for a more specific historical identity of their heavenly patroness. They welcomed her with joy, loved her deeply, entrusted themselves to her, and worked with great zeal in her name and in her honor, as the path traveled from the beginning in Italy and abroad demonstrates.

But the orientations of the Second Vatican Council, the development of biblical studies in general and the impulse given by the Special Chapter of the Daughters of St. Anne to the rethinking of their specific charism kindled in them, from that time on, a lively desire to know her and to make her better known, in the role she had as mother of the Mother of the Redeemer in the history of salvation (cf. Constitutions FSA 2).

Thus, just as the attempt to reconstruct our own spirituality led us, through the pages of the Old Testament (the historical time of St. Anne), to the discovery of the spirituality of the “poor of the Lord”, the same intuition and the same desire lead us today to attempt an identikit of Anne through the wealth of data that the same Testament is able to offer.

2. A Jewish woman

Anne was Jewish; if there is a people that, even through the dramatic vicissitudes of its thousand-year history, has been able to preserve, with its own spirit, a good part of the specific characteristics of its stock, it is the Jewish people.

Drawing on the traditions that are still alive in this people, and at the same time wandering through the rich and varied gallery of female figures who populate the pages of the Bible, we shall therefore be able to grasp some of the essential features of the face of Anne, mother of Mary, and recognize her in the unfolding of her family, social and religious life.

It may reasonably be objected that none of the women recalled in the Bible tells her own story in the first person; and that, since the sacred books were written by a male hand, it is easy to infer that the feminine figures described in them express the positive or negative ideal cherished by the writer, rather than persons caught in their genuine reality.

This may be true or plausible with regard to the women who emerge in the history of their people as emblematic figures, protagonists of singular events. But it should certainly be easier to grasp the genuine data of Jewish femininity in the simple figures placed as complementary elements in a family setting, such as, for example, the wife of Job or that of Tobit.

It may further be objected that every human being is a unique and unrepeatable entity, but it does not seem out of place to hold that, amid the varied aspects and emotional expressions of individual persons, it is possible to grasp ways of acting and reacting, of expressing oneself and communicating, that are common to a large majority and charged with an immediacy that has the value of a document. The Bible itself provides data of the utmost importance on the living conditions of Jewish women and on their tasks within the family and society.

Along these lines, and starting from general considerations, we shall therefore try to picture St. Anne in the intimacy of her home, in the concreteness of family relationships, in the depth of her participation in social life, in order to draw from the many threads a fabric as homogeneous as possible, from which there may emerge, with reasonable approximation, the face of the woman who was the wife of Joachim, the mother of Mary, the grandmother of Jesus.

An intention that perhaps errs by presumption, but is determined solely by the desire already expressed: to know how she prayed, how she loved, how she worked; in a word, how Anne embodied the type of God-fearing Jewish woman in the time that was hers.

3. The context of the Jewish woman

We know for certain that the whole lived experience of the Jew, man or woman, was summed up, and – while taking into account the great variety of situations that has arisen over the centuries – is still for the most part summed up today, in the observance of the precepts of the Torah: daily prayer, the celebration of the Sabbath and the feasts, respect for family and social law, oaths and even commercial transactions – everything is determined by the Torah or subject to it.

But, quite unlike the pagan who is subject to the inscrutable dominion of Fate, the Israelite knows that his destiny is in his own hands: “See, I set before you today life and good, death and evil. If you obey the commandments of the Lord your God that I command you today, by loving the Lord your God, walking in his ways... I have set before you life and death, blessings and curses. Choose life...” (Deut 30:15-16, 19).

Along this path unfolds the life of the Israelite, whose normal destiny is marriage, bound to the divine command: “Be fruitful and multiply” (Gen 1:28).

Along the same path the life of the woman passes from the family and social condition of daughter to that of wife; from her original family to that of her husband, who in principle turns out to be her master, her baal. This does not, however, exclude the richness of a human relationship that can be beautiful and deep, as the significant examples we find in the Bible show.

It is also easy to see that, despite their official position, examples are not rare of women who, by bold and decisive interventions, gave new impetus to the history of their people or changed its course and saved their country from the gravest dangers.

We also know that the collective life of the Jewish people has its vital center not in the Temple nor in the synagogue, but in the family; and it is in the family that a role of the utmost importance is assigned to the woman: “The wisdom of women builds their house”, we read in chapter 14, verse 1 of the Book of Proverbs.

To man are reserved the tasks belonging to public life and in particular those concerning worship, as laid down by the Torah; but since these precepts are expressed in an undifferentiated way, it cannot be said that woman as such is dispensed from their observance. In reality, since she must preside over the ordinary running of family life, and is therefore continually engaged in domestic work, the fulfillment of these duties takes the place for her of the other precepts, as the Talmud makes clear: “While one is engaged in one observance, one is dispensed from the fulfillment of others.”

Wife and mother, the woman therefore devotes herself serenely to the sanctification of herself and of the whole family, promoting the holiness of its members through the fulfillment of the norms concerning their spiritual and material well-being.

The family table, especially that of the Sabbath, is like the domestic altar. The education of the children, the care of their health, the exercise of hospitality, the harmony of relationships by which the atmosphere is steeped in the divine Presence, and gradually every prescription that regulates the running of the home – everything is equally sacred, as an expression of the divine will, regardless of the greater or lesser intrinsic importance of the individual precept, which, fulfilled in a spirit of faith, is a foundation of dignity and a cause of joy, security and strength.

“In Judaism faith is nothing other than the living awareness of the Omnipresent, the sense of his revelation and of his creative power which is manifested in all things... The biblical word that denotes faith designates inner steadfastness and interior peace, the strength and constancy of the human soul.”2

Nor are there lacking tasks which, reserved to the woman, may be considered as belonging to worship, such as the lighting of the Sabbath lamp, accompanied by the recitation of the relevant prayer; the long and painstaking preparation of Passover, the lighting of the menorah at the feast of Hanukkah, and so on.

Less conspicuous tasks, certainly; a situation effectively subordinate to that of man, which would not please today’s feminist stance, but which has to be measured by its own yardstick, in relation to the time, the environment and the mentality.

In truth, an unprejudiced reading brings out from the pages of the Old Testament figures of women who are not frustrated but free and spontaneous, with ready tongues that are not infrequently sharp and effective; shrewd and practical women in whom “the heart of her husband trusts” (Prov 31:11), because the edifice of the family is sustained by their vigilant fidelity.

An essential aspect of Jewish identity is given by prayer, into which the whole life of the believer is poured, just as prayer itself becomes incarnate in daily life. We have a luminous example in the Psalms, in which every aspect of life stands out and every feeling is expressed with vivid effectiveness. And yet, on reflection, one senses in them an entirely masculine cut; even those that express most clearly trusting abandonment to God lack that unmistakable and indefinable quid characteristic of the eternal feminine, which can be grasped only in the prayers that flow from feminine lips.

And this explains the perspicuity of the daily morning prayer of the man, so different from that of the woman:

“Blessed are You, Lord – the man says – our God, king of the universe, who did not make me a pagan, who did not make me a woman, who did not make me a slave...” Caste pride, chauvinism, exasperated male superiority? Perhaps a little of all this, but beyond any attempt at sociological evaluation, this prayer is steeped in a profound religious sense. In his virile gratitude, the one who prays thanks God because, having caused him to be born a Jew, a male and a free man, he has removed from him all the impediments that could have hindered the full observance of all the divine laws.

But how much more intimately religious, in its trembling humility, is the prayer of the woman:

“Blessed are you, Lord, who made me according to your will.” In a few words the woman sums up and encompasses the profound meaning of her being and her existing: she accepts the gift of life, with humble joy becomes aware of her rich possibilities and places them at the disposal of her God. How can we not think of Mary’s fiat, knowing that her mother had prepared her for life with the recitation of this prayer?

But what, in general, is man’s judgment of the companion the Lord has given him?

Leaving aside for now the frequent expressions in the wisdom books, which deserve particular attention, the rabbis declare that in a house without a wife there is no blessing, no peace and no joy.

Peace and joy: a lively and profound aspiration of the Jewish soul and its great wealth; despite the dramatic events of its thousand-year history, the Israelite is a creature of joy. And the guardian and guarantor of domestic peace and joy is the woman, the true queen of the house.

Her principal care is to bring up her children and look after their early growth with a long period of breastfeeding, at the end of which a family banquet celebrates the weaning. And even when, having left infancy behind, the son follows in his father’s footsteps while the daughter remains in her mother’s shadow until marriage, the mother has the same right as the father to the respect of her children.

“My child, keep your father’s commandment, / and do not forsake your mother’s teaching” (Prov 6:20).

The domestic queenship of the Jewish woman stands out especially in the preparation and celebration of the feasts; her weekly care is the scrupulous preparation of the Sabbath.

* * *

Shall we, by the way, with loving daring, enter into the intimacy of the home of Anne and Joachim on the eve of a Sabbath?

It is late afternoon; Joachim is at the Temple3 or the synagogue for the evening prayer. In the sky over Jerusalem the cobalt is darkening as it awaits the first star, at whose appearance little Mary keeps watch, well instructed by her mother.

Anne looks around once more, anxious that nothing should be lacking: on the table, the two loaves one upon the other, covered by the embroidered cloth, and the lamp ready to be lit. In the father’s place the cup of the wine of blessing; all around, the freshness of the room, the gleam of the furniture and objects; in the air, the sense of expectation.

Suddenly Mary’s little voice rings out: “Mommy, it’s out!” The gold of the first star in fact dots the deep blue of the firmament.

Ready, Anne in her turn scans the sky and, shading her eyes with one hand, lights the “Sabbath light” and prays: “Blessed are you, Lord our God, who have sanctified us by your commandments and commanded us to light the Sabbath light.”

Mary is beside her, praying with her, yet ready to run to meet her father, who takes her in his arms, turning his pleased gaze to the interior of the room and then resting it, blessing, on his wife, to bless, together with her, their little daughter, whom they wish to become “like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah”.

The preliminary rites completed, they sit at table and all is peace, love and joy.

Surrealism? No: incontestable sources authorize us to believe that a scene like this was repeated for weeks, months and years in the house on which, from eternity, the eye of the Almighty was fixed, as time flowed toward its fullness.

“Fancy imagines, but the heart contemplates.”

CHAPTER I

FROM SARAH TO EDNA

1. Among the people of life

“It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper as his partner” (Gen 2:18).

“This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen 2:23).

“... and they become one flesh” (Gen 2:24).

No people, in truth, more than the people entrusted with God’s primordial word has felt itself invested with this message or has given the institution of the family a meaning and value more fitting to the divine command.

For it does not appear from Scripture that the Jewish people, though obliged to live for a long time among peoples who, by culture and tradition, practiced a marked discrimination of rights and duties between the two sexes, relegated their own women to a sphere of decided inferiority, nor that Jewish women, though engaged, for reasons of practical necessity, in socially subordinate roles, felt themselves afflicted by inferiority complexes in speech and action.

Among the different types of woman that emerge from the pages of the Old Testament, two seem fundamental: that of the national heroine, such as Deborah, Judith or Esther, celebrated in epic songs, or some other lesser figure, less solemnly exalted but whose intervention proves equally decisive at crucial moments in the history of Israel; and the domestic type, who has more room in scenes of daily life, not particularly celebrated but deeply rooted in the heart: that of the woman as the companion of man.

In the language of the prophets the biblical concept of “covenant” with the Lord is identified with a feminine image: beloved, praised for her fidelity, or harshly reproved as unfaithful, but never definitively repudiated, because loved by God “with an everlasting love” (Jer 31:3): “As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, / so shall your God rejoice over you” (Isa 62:5).

Poetic images that imply a high significance with regard to woman as such, but do not exclude, for the Jewish woman too, a certain condition of legal inferiority: it does not seem that she was granted the right to learn to read and thus to be able to read the Torah. Her exclusion from every function of public worship is fundamental, perhaps also because of the legal impurities to which she was subject; she was not admitted to the courts as a witness; she had no faculty to choose her husband but had to accept the one her father destined for her, nor was she permitted to interfere in the drawing up of the marriage contract which, in tone and substance, in a certain sense represented a contract of sale.

According to some rabbinic schools, the husband was recognized as having the right to repudiate his wife by a unilateral act and even for reasons of slight importance. And polygamy, if not officially approved, in favor of the man alone, was long tolerated.

A condition certainly unacceptable to our evolved civilization, but not different, in certain respects, from the condition of women prevailing until not long ago in regions very close to us, and which must nonetheless be understood according to its own intrinsic logic, as with every situation proper to different places, times and mentalities.

Nevertheless, taking account less of the written law than of the normal custom of life, it is easy to note that in practice women were assigned roles of great importance and considerable autonomy within the family and beyond, so that, from the patriarchal age onwards, we meet types of shrewd and strong-willed, active and practical women.

2. Sarah and Hagar: two mothers and one son

Sarah, Abraham’s wife, not only acts as an authoritarian mistress toward the slave Hagar, but also exercises considerable ascendancy over the heart and will of her husband, who shows himself all too compliant toward her. And it is not to be excluded that, jealous and possessive as she appears, she decides to throw the slave into his arms only out of sharing the torment that he shows because of his condition as a rich man destined to die without heirs.

It must be acknowledged that of the two women the more sympathetic is Hagar, the mother by proxy. She alone is a mother, the true mother of Ishmael; Sarah, although it was she who wanted him, shows no sign of loving the child; it would even seem that in Isaac himself she sees more a means of revenge on the young rival than a son to be loved for his own sake.

The contrast between the two women is truly strong; but while it is understandable that in her sorrowful pride as a humiliated slave Hagar should at some moment display a certain superiority over the barren mistress, it is less admissible that Sarah, having become a mother, instead of softening her heart and attitudes, should harden to the point of cruelly exercising her rights not only over the slave but also over the boy who after all is Abraham’s son.

And that is not all: Sarah has various faults: she is curious (“she was listening at the tent entrance”, Gen 18:10); she is mistrustful (“she laughed to herself”, Gen 18:12); she is a liar (“I did not laugh”, Gen 18:15).

But she can be excused: anyone, woman or man, would have felt a tremendous curiosity to know what business, certainly important, the mysterious visitors had come to transact with Abraham; moreover, it was humanly incredible that Sarah should become a mother at her age; and if she excused herself by denying it, the Bible itself excuses her, explaining: “for she was afraid.”

In conclusion, Sarah is a true woman, alive, natural, certainly not wholly good, but we know that she had not yet been enlightened by the Revelation that was only beginning to touch Abraham. And it is not impossible that today’s representatives of the “stronger” sex would be capable of commenting even now: she was a woman like all the rest.

3. An edifying story?

It seems appropriate at this point to insert a reflection that may hold for the whole remainder of our work: is the Bible an “edifying” book?

In the ordinary sense of the word, a life or a gesture of great moral worth is edifying, and so worthy of admiration and open to imitation. This adjective, therefore, should not be applied indiscriminately to all the characters or all the events we shall meet in the Bible, especially in the books of the Old Testament.

These books, an immense panorama of life, are not the planned and rationalized creation of a moralizing novelist, but the account of the true story of man, lived by humanity over the centuries; of men and women different from one another but all traceable to a single matrix: that of the human creature conceived and willed by the Creator as a free and responsible being, capable of understanding, willing and loving.

It matters little that not all the characters described can boast historical consistency, or that many of the events narrated did not really happen or happened differently.

What counts is that the Bible is the only book that recounts facts which, in the essentiality – not always immediately identifiable – of cause and effect, explain the “why” of things, helping us to trace back to the one original cause. And if not a few gestures and events appear strange, to say the least, and disconcerting by our standard of judgment, it is precisely because, as a faithful mirror of life, the Bible is peopled with good and not-so-good people, saints and sinners who act freely and responsibly and at the same time (something hard if not impossible to understand outside the perspective of faith) under the guidance of God, who works within history but in a way known to him alone.

We shall thus meet, along the pages of this book, the protagonists of a distant past who are nevertheless still alive and very close to us, in a complex dramatic performance in which we ourselves today are the protagonists and which will last until the divine director lowers the curtain.

Through this wonderful story our search, as has already been noted, is directed toward the figure of St. Anne, because of the altogether singular role that God wished to entrust to her in the unfolding of the history of salvation as mother of the Mother of Jesus.

4. Rebekah the enterprising

The easy spontaneity of Rebekah, the young girl “very fair to look upon” who offers a drink to a stranger, stops to talk with him, accepts his rich gifts naturally and invites him home (cf. Gen 24:15-25), denotes a very self-assured temperament and a clear awareness of her position in the family.

Indeed her brother Laban too, who will later show himself so grasping and authoritarian toward his daughters and son-in-law, shows a certain regard for his sister, for to Abraham’s servant, who presses for departure, he replies: “Let us call the girl and ask her” (Gen 24:57).

Rebekah is more than ready to leave, and her meeting with Isaac is described with a brevity in which a note of passion seems to vibrate: “Isaac brought her into the tent of his mother Sarah. He took Rebekah, and she became his wife; and he loved her. So Isaac was comforted after his mother’s death” (Gen 24:67).

Considering the sequel to the story of Rebekah, wife of Isaac and mother of Jacob and Esau, it may well be said that in the spontaneous and hospitable girl at the well of Nahor there was already present the seed of the shrewd and strong-willed woman who knows what she wants and finds the means of obtaining it. A faithful wife, but a questionable mother because of her partiality for one son against the other; and, in this respect, questionable also as a wife, who for love of her son does not hesitate to deceive even her husband.

Evidently Isaac’s old age and blindness gave her the opportunity to take entirely upon herself the running of the family, which she conducts with energy and effectiveness.

It will again be she who persuades her husband to let the favorite son depart in order to remove him from Esau’s vengeance. This episode is one of the many that are particularly problematic, but for that very reason one in which there flashes, mysterious yet more recognizable, the light of a non-human Presence guiding men where they themselves do not know.

5. Tamar, the shrewd widow

What are we to say of the disconcerting yet courageous and shrewd initiative of Tamar, who will in the end force her father-in-law Judah to acknowledge: “She is more in the right than I” (Gen 38:26)?

Tamar, widow of Er, Judah’s firstborn, had returned to her father’s house after her husband’s death, but with the promise from her father-in-law that she would marry his son Shelah as soon as he was grown.

But Judah disappointed Tamar’s expectation, and she played on him a trick of sure effectiveness, receiving him after luring him disguised as a prostitute, but demanding from him certain objects (the seal, the cord and the staff) by means of which she could one day make herself recognized. And afterwards it happened precisely so, and this gave Judah the occasion to confess with unexpected honesty, precisely: “She is more in the right than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah.”

Disconcerting but explicable is the stratagem of Tamar, the frustrated and disappointed widow, if we place it in its own time and place.

It is no accident that Tamar takes on the appearance of a Canaanite prostitute, as if to give a patina of sacredness to the bold act; hence she has not improperly been set beside the many notable biblical figures and placed even by the evangelist Matthew in the series of Jesus’ ancestors.

6. Hannah of Elkanah and others, objects of tenderness

Spontaneous, then, sensitive, lively and respected, the Jewish woman, and surely also loved. Expressions of delicate tenderness that the Bible puts on virile lips are not rare.

“Hannah, why do you weep? Why do you not eat? Why is your heart sad? Am I not more to you than ten sons?” Elkanah whispers caressingly to his humiliated and weeping wife (1 Sam 1:8).

And for Jacob, who serves the grasping Laban for the first seven years dreaming of the day of his wedding to his beloved Rachel, “they seemed to him but a few days because of the love he had for her” (Gen 29:20). Nor does his love diminish during the following seven years, which certainly proved harder for him in every respect: “So Jacob went in to Rachel also, and he loved Rachel more than Leah”; and he continues to love her more than any other even when “the Lord saw that Leah was unloved, he opened her womb; but Rachel was barren” (Gen 29:30-31).

No less sensitive is the heart of the young Tobias who, when he heard the praises Raphael wove of her, “loved her so much that he could not turn his heart away from her” (Tob 6:19).

Loved, and certainly loving in return, in the modest sweetness or the passionate ardor of conjugal intimacy, the biblical woman nevertheless has a need that seems to surpass even love for the companion of her life: motherhood.

Elkanah’s love, though so suffused with tenderness, is not enough for Hannah; her assured preeminence in Jacob’s heart is not enough for Rachel; Hannah pours out her anguish in prayer with the bearing of a “drunken woman”, and Rachel cries out to her husband in her anguish: “Give me children, or I shall die!” (Gen 30:1).

One wonders whether so tormenting a longing had its root in the simple instinct of the woman formed to be a mother, or whether, especially in the barren, there prevailed the sense of frustration arising from seeing themselves deprived of what for the Jewish woman was the highest requisite of dignity, as well as from the fact that barrenness was regarded as a sign of divine curse.

In the mother of Samuel this second motive would seem to prevail, since she shows herself willing to give up the son that the Lord may eventually grant her, destining him from the tenderest age to divine service. It would be further confirmed by a certain sense of detachment that can be detected in her way of parting from the child, were it not for the delicate detail of the “little robe” that his mother, though now consoled by the birth of other children, made for her firstborn and “brought him each year when she went up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice” (1 Sam 2:19).

7. Anna, wife of Tobit, the mother “all mother”

Of more marked exuberance is the love of another mother for her own son: Anna, wife of Tobit, mother of Tobias.

A practical and energetic woman, she does not lose herself in wailing over her husband’s sudden blindness but rolls up her sleeves and adapts to spinning and weaving for pay to support the family, flaring up, with the liveliness of her temperament, only when Tobit, in his touchy honesty, comes to suspect her of stealing a kid: “Where are your charities? Where are your righteous deeds? These things are known about you!” (Tob 2:14).

A rebuke that seems the softened echo of the more acid and resentful one of Job’s wife: “Do you still persist in your integrity? Curse God, and die!” (Job 2:9).

But Anna becomes fire and rails against her husband when she fears that her son, now departed, may be in danger: “Why did you send my child away? Is he not the staff of our hands, and the guide of our steps? Let the money go, in exchange for our son.”

And as the days pass the lament becomes querulous: “My child is lost! Alas, my child, why did I let you go, the light of my eyes?”

With what longing, her work done, “she went out every day and watched the road by which her son had gone, and would not be persuaded by anyone; and when the sun had set she went in and mourned and wept all night, getting no sleep.”

It will be she, naturally, who is first to catch sight of her son from afar and, having warned her husband, to run to meet him and throw herself on his neck: “Now I can die!”

It is in her, more than in Sarah’s jealous possessiveness, more than in the perhaps self-interested religiosity of the mother of Samuel, or even in Edna’s sorrowful sweetness, that we find the affirmation of the instinct that takes hold of the whole being and fills the whole of life: the type of the mother, a universal figure.

8. Sarah and her mother Edna, the God-fearing

Two other exceedingly interesting female figures adorn the pages of the Book of Tobit, a true jewel of religious density, psychological depth and literary skill: that of Sarah, the sorrowful and humiliated protagonist of a story that might appear grotesque were it not clothed in poetic lightness by the writer’s skill; and that of Edna, the strong and most gentle mother who shares her daughter’s drama and sustains her faith.

Sarah, the virgin widow of seven husbands, “had been given to seven husbands... and the wicked demon Asmodeus had killed them before they had been with her as husbands” (Tob 3:8).

To this frustrating experience are added the insult and the curse of the maidservant: overcome by despair, Sarah suffered greatly that day, wept, and went up to her father’s upper room intending to hang herself. But reason, and still more the fear of God and trust in him, take the upper hand; her humble prayer, which sounds like a delicate arpeggio within the leitmotiv of the eternal prayer of the humble and the poor of the Bible, rising to heaven joins that of another righteous man tried by misfortune, Tobit, and together the two prayers are heard “in the presence of the glory of the great God” (Tob 3:16). Thus the divine plan is set in motion: “Raphael was sent to heal both of them.”

The delicately romantic story moves toward its happy ending, and in it divine providence will be manifested in all its power and effectiveness.

Guiding Tobias’s steps toward the house of Raguel in Ecbatana, in Media, Raphael speaks to him of Sarah, “a girl who is serious, brave and very beautiful”, whom Tobias is to marry, since, “before anyone else”, she is his by right as “his nearest kin”.

But the fame of the strange adventure of Sarah’s seven husbands had reached Nineveh, and the young man objects, reluctantly: “I am my father’s only son; I am afraid that if I go in to her I may die, as the others did, and so bring my father’s and mother’s life down to the grave.”

Yet the heavenly messenger does not lack arguments: “She was set apart for you from eternity: you will be the one to save her.” But in the end, the decisive argument for every genuine Israelite: “You will have children by her who will be like brothers to you.” And Tobias: “Brother Azarias, take me straight to our brother Raguel” (Tob 7:1): he could not express with more transparent simplicity the anxious impatience to see her whom he now feels he loves “so much that he could not turn his heart away from her”.

8.1. The strange wedding of Sarah and Tobias

Equally simple and lively is the scene of the meeting with Raguel: the warmth of the embrace and the spontaneity of the tears express well the profound sense of the unity of race and religion, against which national misfortunes, deportations, time and distance can do nothing.

But while he is attending to the duties of hospitality, Raguel starts on hearing Tobias urge his traveling companion: “Brother Azarias, ask Raguel to give me my kinswoman Sarah as my wife.”

The poor father tries to put off the moment of painful explanations, but seeing the young man’s firm will he decides to reveal to him the bitter reality, which, however, does not move Tobias from his purpose: “I will not eat or drink anything here until you settle the matter.” And the answer, now no longer to be postponed, sounds like a trembling but sincere entrusting to the God of the fathers: “Take her according to the law... The Lord of heaven will prosper you.”

Called by her father and guided by him, Sarah joins her hand to Tobias’s and, with her mother Edna also present, the marriage contract is drawn up without delay. Only now, sitting down at table, does Tobias accept the sacred rite of hospitality.

And there comes the moment perhaps most dreaded by Edna, who weeps and prays as she prepares the room and the bridal bed, but manages to hold back her tears in order to comfort her daughter: “Take courage, my daughter; may the Lord of heaven grant you joy in place of your sorrow.”

The story now follows two parallel but intimately contrasting lines.

Raguel knows that he has nothing to reproach himself with, since in revealing to Tobias the sad story of Sarah, and implicitly warning him against the danger of a new tragedy that would strike him in particular and plunge both their families into mourning, he has done his duty; he believes, moreover, in God’s mercy and wishes to entrust himself to it, but he cannot turn his mind from past experiences and wants, in his own way, to hasten to possible remedies. For this reason, when the couple have withdrawn to their room, he calls the servants and goes with them to dig a grave in which to lay, in secret, Tobias’s body should the wicked demon strike again. “Perhaps he will die – he thinks and says – and we shall become an object of ridicule and contempt.”

8.2. The victory of prayer

Quite a different scene meanwhile unfolds in the bridal chamber: the text is silent about Sarah, perhaps because everything has been expressed eloquently by her mother’s tears and prayers and her state of mind is not hard to imagine; but Tobias is full of trust, knows he can rely fully on his guide’s counsels, and hastens to perform the actions Azarias has suggested to him; then he gently invites his bride: “Sister, rise, let us pray and ask the Lord to grant us grace and salvation.” And he pours himself out in a prayer that is a marvelous act of faith in the God of life and at the same time a hymn to the holiness of spousal love and a prophetic exaltation of the dignity of marriage according to God’s plan.

Sarah listens and is silent, but with the submissive sweetness of her amen she entrusts herself wholly to God and to her husband, opening herself to the sudden flow of a life swollen with promise.

“Amen,” the couple said together. And an ineffable peace descends upon them. “They slept through the night.”

But Raguel does not sleep, and over the scene, steeped in a sort of macabre involuntary humor, there hovers the smile provoked by the cautious exploratory rite of the maidservant sent to see whether he is alive: “so that, if he is dead, we may bury him without anyone knowing.”

The inquiry culminates in the joyful discovery: “She found them sleeping together, deep in sleep.” And while the due blessings rise to the God of the fathers, Raguel does not overlook the concern for the concrete detail: “Then he ordered the servants to fill in the grave before daybreak.”

The ritual banquets and festivities follow one another; the faithful Azarias goes to Rages to carry out the task entrusted to him by Tobit and then to return and take part in the wedding feasts.

And it is already time to return to Nineveh: Tobias’s heart is weighed down by the thought of his parents’ waiting, who perhaps already despair of seeing him again. Sarah does not make her voice heard even at the hour of parting, and once again the silence is broken by Edna, who, bidding her daughter farewell, makes the most generous renunciation: “Honor your father-in-law and your mother-in-law, for from now on they are your parents.” But the fullness of a mother’s heart bursts out in her farewell to Tobias: “I entrust my daughter to you... Do not cause her grief all the days of your life.”

8.3. Beyond Sarah’s silence

The couple’s arrival in Nineveh and Tobit’s healing give occasion for new festivities and mark the epilogue of the story.

Here the author clearly reveals the sapiential and consoling purpose of his work: to his contemporaries tried by the experience of exile or compelled by life’s vicissitudes to live far from their homeland, as well as to those who in the homeland experience the bitter weight of foreign domination, he wishes to recall that the God of the covenant is always and everywhere faithful and worthily rewards the fidelity of his chosen ones.

A truth known and proclaimed by the wisdom and prophetic writings, but which this little novel has the merit of presenting with the immediacy of lived experience. In the concreteness of a simple and pious setting there move, in fact, not abstract types but creatures vibrant with humanity who express their own characteristic form of fidelity, summing up together, with complete naturalness, the essential qualities of the genuine Hebrew, of the righteous man according to the Law.

But what are we to say of Sarah, the silent one, whose voice is heard only twice throughout the whole story? In the first, in the prayer dictated by an uncontainable anguish, we hear the universal echo of the cry of the “poor of God” of all times; broken and humble, yet so certain of his Lord’s fidelity that in his very lament he almost dares to ask him to account for the undeserved trial to which his innocence is subjected. Indeed, even in the words of Sarah who, exasperated, begs for death, there vibrates an unmistakable note (“if you do not wish me to die!”) of hope and expectation.

And in the second, in the soft, trembling amen with which she joins in her husband’s prayer of supplication, she expresses the pouring out of her whole being in total trust in the God of the fathers, whose promises are about to be fulfilled in the most joyful way.

A typically feminine prayer, Sarah’s, which accompanies Tobias’s well; a single praying voice that runs through the millennia of the history of their people, rising more humble and heartfelt in the darkest hours but always steeped in that faith which “compels” the God of the covenant to merciful intervention.

CHAPTER II

FROM REBEKAH TO MIRIAM

1. Jacob’s two wives, sisters and rivals (Gen 29–31)

“You shall not marry one of the Canaanite women. Go at once to Paddan-aram, to the house of Bethuel, your mother’s father; and take as wife from there one of the daughters of Laban, your mother’s brother” (Gen 28:1-2).

Advised certainly by Rebekah, Isaac thus achieves two aims: by sending Jacob away he shelters him from his brother’s vengeance and secures for him lawful offspring, since Esau, to his mother’s great annoyance, has already married two Hittite women.

Jacob obeys and sets out. Comforted on the journey by a dream of great prophetic significance (cf. Gen 28:10-15), he arrives in the countryside near Laban’s house and stops beside the well, where “love at first sight” awaits him: the arrival of the beautiful cousin Rachel with the flock to be watered.

The chivalrous eagerness with which Jacob hastens to roll the stone from the well’s mouth to water the sheep, and then the moved and affectionate greeting by which he makes himself known, are the first signs of a feeling born at first sight, which will have occasion to deepen during the month of hospitality that Laban grants his young kinsman.

The labor contract at first strengthens the bond of kinship; then comes, inevitably, the request for marriage, which the cunning father and uncle welcomes with satisfaction, since, while he gains the immediate advantage of his nephew’s seven years of service, he reserves the right to bend the matter of the marriage too to his own advantage.

The deception of which Jacob was the victim after the long seven years of work and waiting, which to the young man in love “seemed but a few days because of the love he had for Rachel”, is universally known. And Laban’s offhand justification in answer to the disappointed bridegroom’s protests is known: “It is not done in our country to give the younger before the firstborn.”

And he cannot even find, in the aridity of his heart, a word that would bring out, apart from the more or less legitimate reason of seniority, any virtue or good quality that in the bridegroom’s eyes would raise his daughter’s dignity and compensate for her lack of beauty. Less cold, perhaps, less detached, in dealing with the sale or barter of a head of cattle!

But times and traditions granted him this right over his daughter; polygamy, moreover, was then commonly practiced, and so to Laban’s accommodating morality the proposed solution seems not only unproblematic but convenient for both: “... I will give you this other one also (daughter) in return for the service you will render me for another seven years.” And Jacob is so much in love that he accepts the proposal.

But Leah? In what frame of mind could she lend herself to a deception that involved her in so personal and definitive a way?

One can imagine that, herself in love with Jacob, afflicted by the inferiority complex arising from comparing her own physical insignificance with her younger sister’s beauty, and brought up in unquestioning obedience to paternal authority, above all regarding the choice of a husband, she complied willingly with a stratagem that, for better or worse, gave her the chance to raise herself to a level of superiority over her sister. But not without, one is led to think, an inner sense of unease and fear.

In fact it was she who paid dearly for her complicity in the deception devised against Jacob, with the tormenting and never satisfied desire to please her husband and be loved by him, and with the bitter and angry dejection of feeling herself invariably “unloved” in favor of her rival.

A faded figure, Leah’s, of slight human prominence, and yet a presence by no means superfluous in the story. It is she who gives birth to six of Jacob’s twelve sons, destined to perpetuate Abraham’s descendants in the series of the twelve thousand sealed in the Apocalypse and to have their names written on the twelve gates that open in the high walls surrounding the heavenly Jerusalem.

But in the context of her setting Leah’s figure has little prominence; she gains relief, one might say, only at the moment when the birth of a new son allows her a gesture of proud defiance toward her sister. And although she lives longer than Rachel, nothing more is said of her, apart from an occasional mention by Jacob who, dying, indicates the place of her burial (cf. Gen 49:31). Having accomplished the mission of giving life to the most considerable part of the future twelve tribes, she simply disappears.

A complex situation, this of the two sisters, in which the most intimate and obscure recesses of femininity come into play. Laban and Jacob himself, with their male-chauvinist mentality, do not seem to realize it, but the writer certainly perceives it and describes it with subtle acuteness, not hesitating to bring in, at a certain point, as deus ex machina, the Lord of heaven himself, who “saw that Leah was unloved, he opened her womb; but Rachel was barren”. And it seems that the lawgiver understood it, who later, though without forbidding polygamy to men, forbade in Hebrew legislation the marriage of two sisters to the same man.

Both disappointed, in truth, the sisters, and both betrayed because forced to become rivals, when perhaps not even before had they been bound by true sisterly affection.

Beautiful and mistress in her husband’s heart, Rachel, but desolately barren. Fertile, but not loved, indeed “unloved” by Jacob, Leah. The birth of each son is welcomed by her with joy, but almost exclusively in view of a gesture of pleasure, desired and hoped for, on her husband’s part. “This time – she says after the birth of her third son – my husband will be attached to me.” But in reality she only succeeds in exasperating Rachel’s jealousy still more, and Rachel turns to Jacob in the spasm of her cry: “Give me children, or I shall die!”, provoking in her turn the unexpected reaction of her patient husband: “Am I in the place of God, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?”

And Rachel resorts to compromise: following the example of Sarah, Abraham’s wife, she offers Jacob the slave Bilhah, by whom two sons are born: Dan and Naphtali. But her anguish is not appeased by this, all the more so since, out of evident spite, her gesture is imitated by Leah, who obtains two more sons through the slave Zilpah.

A disconcerting but most human contest, which lays bare one of the less happy aspects of the condition of the Jewish woman of the time, but also brings out the quality of her mettle: not favored by laws or traditions, legally subject to the prevailing male superiority, she does not withdraw into herself, does not yield to easy victimhood, but defends herself attentive and vigilant, holding with a firm hand her central position in the family. It will be seen how in not a few difficult moments in the history of her people, when proclaimed male superiority will seem to fail, it will be she, the woman, who finds the moral strength, the wisdom and the courage that will allow her to take the initiative and resolve dramatic situations.

Leah can boast of having six sons, four of her own and two of the slave, while Rachel has only the two born of Bilhah, and her spirit is more than ever in turmoil.

Illuminating in this regard is the amusing episode of the mandrakes, to which the people attributed aphrodisiac properties: “In the days of wheat harvest Reuben (Leah’s eldest son) went and found mandrakes in the field, and brought them to his mother Leah.” That is enough for Rachel, overcoming her pride, to humble herself so far as to beg her sister: “Please give me some of your son’s mandrakes!”

But Leah too has her grudge and does not fail to seize the favorable occasion: “Is it a small matter that you have taken away my husband? Would you take away my son’s mandrakes also?” To reach even a compromise, Rachel must feel truly crushed: “Jacob may lie with you tonight.” And she obtains the mandrakes, hoping for the miracle.

By irony of fate it is Leah who obtains the miracle: a good while has passed since the birth of her fourth son, and behold the Lord intervenes again: Leah conceives and bears a fifth and then also a sixth son. “God has endowed me with a good dowry – she exults – this time my husband will honor me, because I have borne him six sons!” And afterwards she will also have a daughter, Dinah, who will be the involuntary cause of a real tragedy (cf. Gen 34).

But God finally remembered Rachel, who conceived and bore a son and said: “God has taken away my reproach.” And she named him Joseph, saying: “May the Lord add to me another son!”

Rachel does not know, cannot know, what a gift of heaven this son truly is for the destiny of the people whom he will guide to a decisive turning point in its history; nor does she know that her wish for a second son will be granted, but at the price of the mother’s life.

Pathetic, truly, and in the end tragic, the fate of this woman to whom neither physical beauty nor her husband’s unquenchable love brings happiness, and who will pay with her life, on the road to Ephrath, for the birth of the longed-for second son, the “Benjamin” for Jacob, but the “Ben-oni”, the “son of my sorrow”, for his dying mother.

All this makes it easy to understand, reading further on, the story of Joseph and his brothers, and the reason for the preferential love that Jacob lavishes first on Joseph and then again on Benjamin; a sign of the feeling that still binds him to his dead wife, the only one he chose, the only one he loved.

The conflict of interests between Laban and Jacob is incessant and almost obsessive. The one a brother, the other the son of Rebekah, both endowed with the cunning enterprise of their respective sister and mother, each pursues his own interests in his own way; of the two, however, Jacob proves the more honest, and it will be he, in the end, who is the victor.

Now master of considerable wealth and rightly weary of twenty years of ill-paid servitude, he claims the right to return to his aged father, taking with him his numerous family and his possessions. But his father-in-law’s ill will forces him into a kind of flight, although the number of persons and the amount of goods he takes with him do not allow a truly secret one.

This time the attitude of the two sisters is united, and they show that they have nothing to regret in leaving a father who has regarded them as foreigners.

Strange is Rachel’s theft of the household idols, a theft which without her skillful stratagem (blood will tell!) could even have cost her her life. Given the nature of her relations with her sister, her act, however reprehensible, might be explained as a deliberate claim of inherited rights for her own son against the children of her rival. But it is certainly an indication of an uncertain and nebulous religiosity, not well centered on faith in the one God and in need of material signs and concrete guarantees. The delicate religious sensibility of Tobit’s family is centuries away!

But nothing slows or in any way deflects God’s preordained plan. It is during this journey back toward the land of Canaan, the land promised to Abraham, that the Lord renews the bond that, through the dream of the ladder reaching from earth to heaven, he had already established with Jacob as he set out for the land of Paddan-aram. “How awesome is this place!”, Jacob had exclaimed then, setting up the stone as a pillar in memory of the event. Far more awesome is the struggle he must now undergo on the banks of the Jabbok (cf. Gen 32:25-33), with the Unknown One who leaves a mark on his flesh, as if to indicate the deeper and definitive mark that God will indelibly imprint upon the people who will be born of Jacob’s twelve sons: the mark of the covenant.

Made more mature by the wearing experience in Mesopotamia, Jacob is now ready for the decisive struggle: he fights and wins. But it is above all the victory over himself that establishes him in faith and prepares him for the meeting with Esau. He wins because he has understood that from now on he must entrust himself solely to the God of Abraham and of Isaac, and not to the cunning and calculation to which he had so easily entrusted himself in the past.

The meeting with his brother, approached with deep humility, indeed ends in full reconciliation. And brothers in spirit more than in flesh they will meet again at the bedside of their dying father.

But the goal is still far off, and first Jacob will experience another, the sharpest of sorrows: Rachel, exhausted by the fatigue and hardships of the long journey, seized by the pains of childbirth, dies on the road to Ephrath giving birth to her second son. And it will not be granted to her, as it will later to Leah, to have the privilege of resting in the ground bought by Abraham for the burial of Sarah, and where with Sarah Abraham, Isaac and Rebekah will later find rest (cf. Gen 49:31).

The Bible says nothing of Jacob’s grief and is laconic also about Rachel’s burial: “Jacob set up a pillar at her grave... it is the pillar of Rachel’s tomb, which is there to this day” (Gen 35:20). But the pilgrim to whom, on the road from Jerusalem to Bethlehem, Rachel’s tomb is pointed out feels deep in his heart, across the millennia, the prophetic voice of Jeremiah who, raising the woman loved by Jacob to a symbol of the grief of all the mothers of the world, has erected to her the most lasting of monuments.

“A voice is heard in Ramah, / lamentation and bitter weeping: / Rachel is weeping for her children; / she refuses to be consoled for her children, / because they are no more” (Jer 31:15).

The story of Jacob and his two wives, with the chiaroscuro that characterizes it, shows how even the path of the patriarchs was marked by errors, uncertainties and weaknesses. But beyond the self-interested cunning and the bitter quarrels that overshadow the actions of creatures, there shines the patient pedagogy of a divine Father who, while appearing to adapt himself to the slow, halting walk of his children, in reality sustains it, preparing, even within their most ambiguous intentions and most distorted feelings, the generation of the twelve tribes that will give life to the people with whom he will make an everlasting covenant.

2. Shiphrah and Puah disobey Pharaoh (Exod 1)

“Now a new king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph” (Exod 1:8).

About four centuries have passed since the time when Jacob moved to Egypt with all his family, and now the country was ruled by a king perhaps belonging to a new dynasty, hostile or indifferent toward the previous one.

And the memory of the wise, powerful and beneficent Hebrew who during the great famine had saved the Egyptian people, and the neighboring peoples as well, from hunger had faded in the minds of the new generations.

But if Joseph could be forgotten, it was impossible to ignore the presence of his descendants and those of Jacob, from whom had arisen an ethnic group so numerous as to worry Pharaoh.

“Look, the Israelite people are more numerous and more powerful than we.” A probably exaggerated assessment, but in any case a reality to be borne in mind, in his view, especially in view of the danger that, in a possible war against Egypt, the Hebrews might ally themselves with the enemy.

“Come – says Pharaoh – let us deal shrewdly with them.” And “the Egyptians made their lives bitter with hard service in mortar and brick and in every kind of work in the field; in all their work they made them serve with harshness.”

But “the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and spread”.

They must be undermined at the root, Pharaoh therefore thinks; and he does not hesitate, he, the divine one, to stoop to two humble Hebrew women, the midwives, to impose on them his command: “When you act as midwives to the Hebrew women, and see them on the birthstool, if it is a boy, kill him; but if it is a girl, she shall live.”

The king’s orders are peremptory and disobedience is punished with death, but Shiphrah and Puah fear God more than the king and do not follow his command. Zealous, the informers hasten to denounce them to the king, and he, angry, summons them: “Why have you done this, and allowed the boys to live?”

Good Hebrew women that they are, the midwives have nimble minds and ready tongues: their answer drips with cunning and irony: “Hebrew women are not like Egyptian women; they are vigorous. Before the midwife comes to them, they have already given birth.”

They risk death, but have understood that the survival of their people is at stake, and divine protection saves them: “God dealt well with the midwives,” the Bible states. And the first benefit was certainly their deliverance from the death penalty. The king, moreover, has understood that if he wants to be obeyed he must resort to a command whose execution can be checked with certainty and directly. And he orders: “Every boy that is born to the Hebrews you shall throw into the Nile, but you shall let every girl live.”

Why not the girls too? Cruel but not stupid, the king protects his own interests; let the males die, potential enemies in case of war, but let the females live, who do not make war and, sturdy and tempered as the midwives themselves describe them, will be able to work like men. All the toil will fall on them and the number of births will obviously decline, thus setting a limit to the worrying numerical increase of the Hebrew population, without however compromising Pharaoh’s material interests.

Different, however, are God’s plans. And the names of the two Hebrew midwives, humble and unwitting pioneers of civil disobedience, are rightly remembered by the Bible.

Pharaoh’s emissaries now keep watch, rigorously checking the execution of his orders, and the poor Hebrew mothers are forced to throw their newborns into the Nile. But one rebels and keeps her little one hidden with her. There comes a time, however, when it is impossible to keep him hidden any longer, and she resorts to an expedient that at first sight would seem as absurd as it is useless: she entrusts him to the river, but shut in a basket coated with pitch and bitumen so that it will not sink; let the Lord provide now.

Hope and trust well placed. The “One who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord has them in derision” (Ps 2:4) – the iniquitous plots of the mighty – as the matchless humorist that he is, chooses, for the salvation of this child upon whom the divine eye has rested from eternity, precisely a woman who belongs to the family of the Hebrews’ implacable enemy, perhaps a natural daughter of Pharaoh.

The Egyptian princess cannot fail to realize that this is one of the Hebrews’ children; but while her eyes are drawn to the beauty of the child, God “moves to compassion” her heart and prompts the little sister, placed by her mother among the reeds and rushes to watch over the basket, to step boldly forward: “Shall I go and get you a nurse from the Hebrew women to nurse the child for you?”

It is done! Not only will the little one be nursed by his own mother, but moreover at the expense of the Egyptian treasury, from which the princess can draw freely. When the Lord decides to enjoy himself... he does it in style! And he entrusts the life of the future leader of the Hebrew people to just three women; of Moses’ father, the only male involved in the affair, the Bible says merely that he was “a man from the house of Levi”; enough to attribute to Moses and his brother Aaron, by right, membership of the priestly caste.

Of the women, instead, we shall hear again.

3. Miriam, the sister of Moses (Exod 15:19-21)

Indeed we hear again of Miriam, Moses’ quick and bold little sister who had proposed to the princess to call a nurse from among the Hebrew women, and had called her mother.

She has grown up and occupies a role of some authority in the train of her great brother; prophetess and inspired poet, she leads the dance and the chorus of the Hebrew women who celebrate the miraculous crossing of the Red Sea and the defeat of the Egyptians: “Then the prophet Miriam, Aaron’s sister, took a tambourine in her hand; and all the women went out after her with tambourines and with dancing.”

Miriam had them sing the refrain: “Sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously; / horse and rider he has thrown into the sea.”

The object of her song is evidently not the glory of her great brother Moses but exclusively the glory of the Lord who has guided his people and triumphed gloriously; she is therefore rightly entitled to the title of prophetess as well.

She will later be punished with leprosy, not for having claimed this title, but for having presumed, as indeed Aaron too, to put herself on a par with Moses, the one chosen by God above all (“they said, ‘Has the Lord spoken only through Moses? Has he not spoken through us also?’”); and perhaps also for some sin of jealousy toward the Cushite wife whom (Moses) had married (sisters-in-law!).

In the tent, in fact (cf. Num 12), the Lord contrasts the person of Moses and the importance of his mission (“entrusted with all my house; / with him I speak face to face”) with the relative importance, though without denying it, of the prophetic function which he attributes, time by time, to whom he wishes, as precisely also to Miriam and to Aaron.

What is astonishing, rather, is the fact that while the divine rebuke is clearly addressed to Aaron as well as to Miriam, only Miriam is punished with leprosy. An improbable male-chauvinist partiality on the Lord’s part, or a calculated elimination from the text wished by the priestly caste, which could not admit that the priest Aaron had been defiled by leprosy?

In the end, the episode does not seem to dim the figure of Miriam or take away her privileged position.

A lively, sensitive and bold woman, not free of faults and evidently dear to God, Miriam might even be thought of (an exception, in this case not without significance, among Hebrew women) as a virgin, since one notes the absence, beside her name, of that of a husband, which the Bible ordinarily puts beside the name of every woman, important or not. The author does not fail to note that “the people did not set out on the march until Miriam (healed) was readmitted” and takes care, moreover, to specify in due course the time and place of her death and burial (cf. Num 20:1).

CHAPTER III

SMALL GREAT STORIES OF WOMEN

1. The five daughters of Zelophehad (Num 27:1-11)

Zelophehad, a descendant of Manasseh, son of Joseph, had died leaving five daughters and no son: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah; more names of Hebrew women who stand out in the history of their people for clarity of ideas and determined will.

Among the peoples of the ancient Near East, Israel included, it was normal practice that only sons had a right to the father’s inheritance. But the five sisters, their father Zelophehad being dead, “approached and stood before Moses, before the leaders and all the congregation, at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and said: ‘Our father died in the wilderness without sons. Why should the name of our father be taken away from his clan because he had no son? Give to us a possession among our father’s brothers.’”

Concreteness and a sense of justice shine through their reasoning; and Moses, perhaps torn between the women’s good reasons and the force of the tradition that favors males, goes to the Tent to consult the Lord, who replies: “The daughters of Zelophehad are right; you shall give them possession of an inheritance among their father’s brothers and transfer the inheritance of their father to them.”

Thus, thanks to the daughters of Zelophehad, the rule is introduced into Israelite legislation: “If a man dies, and has no son, then you shall pass his inheritance on to his daughter.”

The men of the assembly, however, temporize; behind the legal question, already thorny for them, the economic question peeps out: if an heiress – they say – marries a man of another tribe she will bring him the inherited goods as her dowry, and the tribe of origin will be impoverished (cf. Num 36).

A new appeal to the Lord by the patient Moses and a new response from the eternally patient Father in heaven: the daughters of Zelophehad “may marry whomever they think best; only they must marry within a clan of their father’s tribe... no inheritance shall be transferred from one tribe to another” (Num 36:6-9).

Conditional freedom, then, in matters of marriage, even for heiresses; but in the final analysis the episode shows that the female presence, in the ancient Hebrew world, carried weight, and no small weight.

2. Awake, awake, Deborah! (Judg 4–5)

Deborah, wife of Lappidoth: another Hebrew woman whom God trusted.

For twenty years now Jabin, king of Canaan, had been oppressing the Israelites, for God had abandoned them into his hands. It was the dark period in which the twelve tribes were struggling to settle, each in the territory that Joshua had assigned to it, and whose inhabitants, all pagan peoples, forced them into ceaseless wars. In the brief periods of truce, moreover, the forced coexistence made it hard for the sons of Jacob to escape the contagion of pagan customs. Consciences were depressed, the moral sense weakened, strength sapped.

Without a leader when the danger loomed most menacingly, the Israelites would remember and “cry out to the Lord”, and the Lord would send them a deliverer in the person of a judge, who generally solved their problems by force of arms. But the judges did not always prove equal to the situation; even in the best of cases, when the judge died, the people, left to themselves, would go back to “doing evil in the sight of the Lord”. So the author sadly denounces time and again, adding in the same repetitive manner, like a monotonous refrain, the explanation: “In those days there was no king in Israel; all the people did what was right in their own eyes”, clearly giving to understand that this “right” was the worst of the worst.

In reality, among the various judges recalled, there are not many personalities who emerge in a positive sense. Resplendent among them all appears the figure of one woman; unique also in the sense that she alone seems to exercise the office of judge in the proper sense and full time, sitting “under the palm of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel”, when “the Israelites came up to her for judgment”.

Endowed with wisdom and invested with the spirit of prophecy, Deborah is the true guide of the people along the Lord’s paths, and it does not seem accidental that the prose text, essential and laconic, neglects any reference to her physical gifts, as is generally found, by contrast, regarding the other women of the Bible.

Seized by the Spirit of the Lord, Deborah sends for Barak, the army’s general, to communicate to him the divine message: “Go, take position at Mount Tabor... I will draw out Sisera to meet you, and I will give him into your hand.”

But Barak distrusts himself and perhaps a little God also, and answers Deborah: “If you will go with me, I will go; but if you will not go with me, I will not go.” He may want her beside him to learn from her, moment by moment, the Lord’s will, but Deborah certainly senses some hesitation in him, as her answer shows, curt and to the point: “The road on which you are going will not lead to your glory, for the Lord will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman.”

She goes with Barak and they encamp on Mount Tabor, according to the Lord’s command, with an army of ten thousand men; the victory is swift and a foregone conclusion. Sisera, the Canaanite commander, defeated and alone, flees on foot and goes in search of safety exactly where he will find death.

In the song that celebrates the victory, one of the loftiest poetic compositions of the Bible, composed perhaps shortly after the events, there vibrates and bursts forth not only the warrior instinct but above all Israel’s rediscovered religious consciousness. Two female figures stand out in it.

Deborah:

“The peasantry prospered in Israel,

they grew fat on plunder,

until you arose, Deborah,

arose as a mother in Israel.”

And Jael:

“Most blessed of women be Jael,

the wife of Heber the Kenite,

of tent-dwelling women most blessed.”

And at the end the praise of the Lord rises in chorus: “So perish all your enemies, O Lord! But may your friends be like the sun as it rises in its might.”

Thus, with the people’s consciousness awakened through Deborah’s work, the sense of unity re-emerged and the pride of the race strengthened, Israel was able to enjoy forty years of peace.

3. Jael: hospitality betrayed (Judg 4:17-23)

Both in Deborah’s song and in the prose account, Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, is regarded and exalted as the architect of the definitive victory of Deborah and Barak over Israel’s enemies. The episode poses, however, a real problem for every sensitive conscience, regardless of times and customs.

“For there was peace between King Jabin of Hazor and the clan of Heber the Kenite”, Sisera flees toward Jael’s tent; he is making for a refuge he believes hospitable and safe, and it is Jael herself who goes out to meet him and invites him: “Turn aside, my lord, turn aside to me; have no fear.”

Sisera is therefore a guest, and hospitality is sacred and inviolable for all Oriental peoples. Nor is Jael a Hebrew, so that her act might be regarded as a, however questionable, act of war against an enemy of the people.

Exhausted, Sisera asks her for water and protection. Jael gives him milk to drink “in a lordly bowl” and covers him with a rug. But when the man is fast asleep she takes a tent peg and with a hammer drives it into his temple, piercing it through “until it went down into the ground”.
