And, proud, to Barak, who arrives at her tent in pursuit of the enemy, she extends the invitation: “Come, and I will show you the man whom you are seeking.”

Millennia have passed since the days of Jael and Sisera, during which, alongside the worldwide expansion of Christianity, humanity’s moral and civil conscience has matured; but there have never lacked, and there still do not lack today, the upholders, in theory and in practice, of the principle that “the end justifies the means”.

An upright conscience rejects such a theory, but in the face of episodes like that of Jael, when the salvation of a people comes to be in opposition to principles held inviolable, it prefers to refrain from judgment and entrust itself, with a simple act of faith, to the well-known axiom that the wisdom of peoples has enshrined in the proverb: “God writes straight on the crooked lines of men.”

The Bible, the book that tells the history of humanity, teaches us on every page that, for good and ill, humanity walks along a way of salvation whose mysterious meaning is known only to God.

4. A woman punishes Abimelech (Judg 9:50-57)

Equally disconcerting in its crudity, yet bearing a clear message, is the episode of Abimelech, son of Gideon, the punctilious judge who boldly put the Lord’s patient condescension to the test.

After he had defeated the Midianites with his skillful stratagems, the Israelites said to Gideon: “Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson also.” But Gideon said: “I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the Lord will rule over you” (Judg 8:22-23). A gleam of light on a gloomy horizon, soon darkened again by Gideon’s own fall into idolatry.

At his death, besides the seventy sons he had by various wives, he left a son, Abimelech, born of a concubine he had at Shechem. This man, seized by lust for power, turned to his mother’s brothers at Shechem and asked them whether they preferred to be governed by seventy persons or by one (cf. Judg 9:2). Sure then of his uncles’ support, he hired a number of bold and violent idlers and went to his father’s house at Ophrah, where he killed his seventy brothers. Of them only one escaped, the youngest, Jotham, who, from the summit of Mount Gerizim, to dissuade Israel from following Abimelech, will proclaim the famous fable of the trees (cf. Judg 9:7-15).

Abimelech nevertheless manages to rule for three years over the Shechemites, who, however, grow weary of his haughty and violent ways and react.

Brutal and violent, like all his actions, is Abimelech’s response: having destroyed Shechem, he heads for Thebez and lays siege to it, preparing to treat it in the same way. He then approaches the “strong tower” in the middle of the city, “to which all the people of the city, men and women, had fled”, in order to set fire to it.

“But a certain woman threw an upper millstone on Abimelech’s head, and crushed his skull. Immediately he called to the young man, his armor-bearer, and said to him: ‘Draw your sword and kill me, so that people will not say about me, “A woman killed him.”’”

“So the young man ran him through, and he died.”

The story, which turns out somewhat tangled owing to the concurrence of clumsily interwoven details, nevertheless develops in the end a clear inner logic: God’s justice, it tells us, falling on all sinners, makes the one become the instrument of the other’s punishment: “Thus God repaid Abimelech for the crime he committed against his father in killing his seventy brothers; and God made all the wickedness of the people of Shechem fall back upon their heads.”

Moreover the last avenging act – supreme outrage for the proud Abimelech – is placed in the hands of a woman, anonymous like so many others, but wonderfully sculpted in the brevity of the words and in the determination of the act.

And the recognition of the value, or in any case of the decisive importance for the salvation of the people, of this woman’s act, in an entirely male context, gives the episode a characteristic note of naturalness, like a seal of truth.

CHAPTER IV

SACRIFICED WOMEN AND WISE WOMEN

1. The weeping of Jephthah’s daughter (Judg 11)

“The Israelites said to the Lord: ‘We have sinned; do to us whatever seems good to you; but deliver us this day!’” (Judg 10:15).

The Israelites are living through one of the many difficult moments of their history. But since, as the sacred author notes, “the people did not cease to do what is evil in the sight of the Lord”, it is easy to think that their troubles derived not so much from divine punishments as from the inevitable consequences of their own sins and errors.

The scourges of the moment were the Ammonites who, across the Jordan, had been afflicting the inhabitants of Gilead for a full eighteen years; and they were now about to cross the river and “fight against Judah and against Benjamin and against the house of Ephraim”.

Faced with danger, once again Israel recognizes its errors, repents, promises the Lord to remove the foreign gods, and meanwhile asks itself in anguish: “Who is the man who will begin the fight against the Ammonites?”

There is a man, but he is almost an enemy himself. He is Jephthah, illegitimate son of Gilead, whom his legitimate brothers drove from their father’s house and who, having taken refuge in the land of Tob, put himself at the head of a band of raiders and won a reputation as a strong and valiant man.

In dire straits, the inhabitants of Gilead turn to him and he, while restating the reasons for his indignation against his own city, agrees to undertake its defense, on condition, however, that “if the Lord gives the Ammonites into his hands, Israel must recognize him as head”. And the elders promise, in the name of all the people, calling the Lord as witness.

Jephthah shows himself at once cautious and shrewd; not at all with the intention of avoiding war but to gain the time needed to prepare the army, he resorts at first to diplomatic channels; the king of the Ammonites refuses to listen to him and it comes to arms.

“The spirit of the Lord – says the text – came upon Jephthah.”

He pursues the enemy through Mizpah of Gilead and catches up with them, making to God an ill-fated vow: “If you will give the Ammonites into my hands, then whoever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me... shall be the Lord’s, and I will offer that one up for a burnt offering.”

A foolish and wicked vow which shows how barbarous and rudimentary, steeped in idolatrous elements and contaminated by Canaanite cults, was the faith of this man, probably unaware of the Law of Sinai.

In any case, the Ammonites are defeated and Jephthah returns toward the house where the triumph will end in tragedy.

He has an only child, a daughter, whom he loves; and behold “his daughter came out to meet him with timbrels and with dancing”.

Sincerely in despair, the father tears his clothes: “Alas, my daughter! You have brought me very low; you have become the cause of great trouble to me. For I have opened my mouth to the Lord, and I cannot take back my vow.”

There vibrates undeniably deep in his soul, despite the error committed, a sense of honesty that imposes on him fidelity to the commitment made. And the agile little figure, already erect in the exultation of the dance, now bends, humble and submissive, before a mystery greater than herself, a mystery in which human folly and divine authority seem inextricably involved.

“My father, if you have opened your mouth to the Lord, do to me according to what has gone out of your mouth, now that the Lord has given you vengeance against your enemies, the Ammonites.”

A dark sacrificial destiny to which the girl submits, without however being able to restrain the cry that rises irrepressibly from the depths of her being: “Let this thing be done for me: grant me two months, so that I may go and wander on the mountains, and bewail my virginity, I and my companions.”

“Bewail my virginity.” Not so much, in her request, is it the weeping for broken youth as the cry of the motherhood denied to her virgin body, to her deepest being. A claim of life to be given, to be perpetuated beyond her own, a vocation inscribed deeply in the being of woman, of the Hebrew woman in particular, which the girl, up in the mountains, will bewail in chorus with her understanding companions, without however thinking of escaping the painful destiny that for her is a filial duty of sacrifice to her father’s triumph.

So, “at the end of two months, she returned to her father, who did with her according to the vow he had made”.

In the sparse, hurried expression of the writer one senses the discomfort that makes him hasten to end the story, not without, however, a perhaps instinctive remark that sounds like a summary and comment on the implicit absurdity of the drama: “She had never slept with a man.”

Many centuries later, in an obscure village of Galilee, this same phrase will sound on the lips of a Hebrew virgin who will apply it to herself; and it will be the announcement and beginning of a new fullness of life.

2. The wise woman of Tekoa (2 Sam 13; 14:1-24)

King David has reached the height of his power and his palace is the clearest manifestation of it. But the tangle of vipers that inexorably nests in every center of power insinuates its coils and spreads its poisons also under the gilded vaults of that palace, in which too many brothers, sons of different mothers, are encamped.

And the drama matures: Amnon, the firstborn, seized by a morbid passion for his half-sister Tamar, first rapes her and then drives her out ignominiously.

“When King David heard of all these things, he was very angry, but he would not hurt the feelings of his son Amnon, because he loved him, for he was his firstborn.”

The king therefore keeps silent, and so does Absalom, Tamar’s brother, to whom the distraught young woman confided. He is silent but burns with anger, Absalom, and for two whole years nourishes within himself the thirst for revenge, if indeed it is not accompanied by a cold calculation regarding an inconvenient half-brother of whom it is expedient to be rid.

When the right time comes, Absalom organizes a banquet to which he invites all his father’s sons, including Amnon, who, at a sign from Absalom at the appointed moment, is seized by the servants and killed.

David is deeply grieved and mourns his son’s death for a long time, while Absalom flees far from his father’s anger.

But Joab, general of the army and David’s trusted counselor, when he sees that the king’s grief has subsided and that his mind is no longer turned against Absalom, thinks it advisable to have the latter readmitted to the palace. Realizing, however, that it will not be easy to induce the king to take this step, he resorts to a stratagem.

There is in Tekoa a woman whose reputation for wisdom is widespread throughout the territory, and Joab sends for her. “Put on mourning garments – he tells her – and behave like a woman who has been mourning for the dead for a long time; then go to the king and speak to him.”

No sooner said than done: the mediator’s speech follows the pattern used by the prophet Nathan to induce the king to acknowledge the sin committed against Uriah (cf. 2 Sam 12:1ff.): that is, to tell of an imaginary event so that the king is led to pronounce a judgment which, once the fiction becomes reality, he cannot retract.

Humble and grieving, the woman tells the story of two brothers, her sons; falling into a quarrel, one killed the other. And now the people would like to do justice on the killer; but what will become of her, when, deprived of both, she will have no other consolation than to mourn them both?

The speech unfolds so skillfully and movingly that the king bursts out with a phrase that has the force of an oath: “As the Lord lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground.”

“Then the woman said: ‘Let your servant speak a word to my lord the king.’”

He replied: “Speak.”

“The woman said: ‘Why then have you planned such a thing against the people of God? In giving this decision the king convicts himself, inasmuch as the king does not bring his banished one home again. We must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again... Let the king devise some plan so that the banished one may not remain an outcast from him.’”

The king’s heart is certainly inclined to yield, but he wants to know what lies behind it and asks her: “Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?”

Shrewdly winning, the woman replied: “As you live, my lord the king, one cannot turn right or left from anything that my lord the king has said! Your servant Joab is the one who commanded me; it was he who put all these words into the mouth of your servant... but my lord has wisdom like the wisdom of the angel of God, to know all things that are on the earth.”

Then the king said to Joab: “Very well, I grant this; go, bring back the young man Absalom.”

Now it is Joab who prostrates himself in thanks.

Thus, through Joab’s initiative and the wisdom of the woman of Tekoa, Absalom was able to return to court; but he was not admitted into his father’s presence. Only after two years and by a new intercession of Joab did father and son see each other again.

3. The still wiser woman of Abel-beth-maacah (2 Sam 20:14-22)

Still during David’s reign, another female figure stands out, even more shrewd and resolute than that of Tekoa; a figure worthy of standing, in some way, beside those of Deborah and Judith.

Sheba, son of Bichri, a Benjaminite, has raised the men of his tribe against David, and the king sends Amasa, who has replaced Joab in command of the army, to gather the men needed for the defense. But Amasa delays, and Joab, whose pride has ill accepted the replacement, taking advantage of this, goes to meet him and kills him treacherously. Joab then once more puts himself at the head of the army and moves against Sheba, pursuing him throughout the territory as far as the fortified city of Abel-beth-maacah, in the far north of the kingdom, where Sheba had taken refuge with all those of his father’s family.

Joab besieges the city and threatens to destroy it, when from the top of the walls a woman’s voice rises: “Listen! Listen! Tell Joab to come here, I want to speak to him.”

The man approaches and a rapid and agitated dialogue begins: the woman reminds the warrior that the fortified city of Abel-beth-maacah has always held, among the tribes of Israel, the reputation of “guardian of what the faithful in Israel established”; “and you – she rebukes him – are seeking to destroy a city that is a mother in Israel.”

“The matter is different – replies Joab –; a man called Sheba has lifted up his hand against King David; hand over him alone, and I will withdraw from the city.”

The woman’s voice does not tremble in her reply: “His head shall be thrown to you over the wall.” And, having returned to the city, she speaks to the people with wisdom, so that all agree and, “they cut off the head of Sheba son of Bichri, and threw it out to Joab”, who lifted the siege.

Swift, summary justice, without appeal; more blood shed. But who can, this time, blame the woman who, by deciding the death of a rebel, saves an entire people?

Hard, pitiless times, marked by the labored steps of humanity on a road that is anything but easy, and still far from its goal.

4. Women of the shadows, foreigners among the people (1 Kings; 2 Kings; 2 Chronicles)

The popular discontent that was already simmering toward the end of Solomon’s reign, because of excessive taxation, bursts out unstoppably after his death, provoked by the foolish effrontery of Rehoboam, his son and successor.

We are at the beginning of the last millennium (BC). The twelve tribes that David had laboriously united under a single kingdom, and which Solomon had brought to the highest splendor, divide: to Rehoboam remains the kingdom of Judah with the tribe of Benjamin; the other ten form the kingdom of Israel with its center in Samaria, under Jeroboam, whose father had been one of the officials of the kingdom of Judah under Solomon.

The political separation is followed, in a more or less pronounced form, by religious schism. Jeroboam himself, to prevent his subjects’ hearts from turning toward Rehoboam as they went to Jerusalem on their annual pilgrimages, set up two golden calves, one at Bethel and one at Dan: “You have gone up to Jerusalem long enough – he told the people –; here are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.”

But “this thing – the author does not fail to note – became a sin”. And with sin, disorder, violence, discord and endless wars. From here begins a phase of unstoppable political and moral decline which, despite the now pleading now threatening interventions of the prophets, will bring the two kingdoms, first one and then the other, to the end of independence and to the deportation of the people.

The chief cause of the moral decline is the bad conduct of the kings, with the exception of very few who strive, never fully succeeding, to keep or bring the people back on the path of fidelity to the God of the fathers.

Among the worst kings, then, there emerge two truly perfidious women, whose presence and work mark the culminating point of the attempt to extinguish faith definitively in the hearts of the Hebrews and bring them to the worship of Baal.

Around the year 875 BC Ahab, son and successor of Omri, king of Israel, marries Jezebel, daughter of the king of Tyre; a proud, authoritarian and cruel woman, she drags her husband into the worship of Baal, for whom she has a temple and altar built.

The three years of drought foretold by Elijah as punishment for their impiety do not convert Ahab and do not change Jezebel’s heart. She, in fact, more irritated than ever by the slaughter of the prophets of Baal carried out by Elijah, and followed by her weak husband, does not cease to push the people along the path of idolatry and shows the height of her perfidy in the episode of Naboth’s vineyard.

At this point Elijah intervenes again, threatening terrible punishments that will not be slow to come true: “You have killed, and also taken possession – says the prophet to Ahab –; in the place where dogs licked up the blood of Naboth, dogs will also lick up your blood... I will bring disaster upon you; I will consume you... Concerning Jezebel the Lord also says: the dogs shall eat Jezebel within the bounds of Jezreel.”

And that is not all: “Anyone belonging to Ahab who dies in the city the dogs will eat; and anyone of his who dies in the open country the birds of the air will eat.” The severity of the terrible prophet is no surprise, since the author stresses that “there was none like Ahab, who sold himself to do what was evil in the sight of the Lord, urged on by his wife Jezebel”.

In reality, at the prophet’s last threats Ahab repented, but he did not avoid dying a violent death; and after his death all the members of his family were also exterminated. And Jezebel died in the horrible way that Elijah had foretold.

But the plague of idolatry spread by Jezebel in the kingdom of Israel soon penetrates also into the kingdom of Judah through Athaliah, daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, who marries Joram, son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah.

Jehoshaphat had been a relatively good king, but his son Joram, firstborn and successor, “when Jehoram had ascended the throne of his father and was established, he put all his brothers to the sword” (seven); he did what is evil in the sight of the Lord; he built high places in the cities of Judah, led the inhabitants of Jerusalem into idolatry and made Judah go astray.

A degenerate son, then, of a relatively upright father; one of the reasons is supplied by the author: “His wife was a daughter of Ahab”; and therefore of Jezebel. That is enough.

Elijah intervenes again with reproaches and threats of punishments which are punctually fulfilled. In only eight years of reign Joram suffers the rebellion of his subjects and loses part of his kingdom; a band of Arab raiders penetrates the palace, carries off a large part of his riches and kills or deports all his sons except the youngest. And finally, afflicted with a horrible and repugnant disease, he departs “with no one’s regret”.

He is succeeded by Ahaziah, the only surviving son, who reigns for a single year, docilely following the disastrous counsels of his mother Athaliah, and is killed by Jehu whom – according to the author – “the Lord had anointed to destroy the house of Ahab”: which Jehu does scrupulously.

Athaliah’s perfidy bursts out fully at Ahaziah’s death: “When she saw that her son was dead, she set about to destroy all the royal family of the house of Judah”, and has them all killed. Only the youngest is saved, Joash, whom his aunt Jehosheba, sister of Ahaziah and wife of the priest Jehoiada, manages to hide in the rooms adjoining the Temple.

And for six years Athaliah reigns over the country, the only woman, and moreover a foreigner on her mother’s side, who has ever reigned over Jerusalem.

But when Joash reaches the age of six, his uncle Jehoiada, in agreement with the priests of the Temple and the soldiers, hatches a conspiracy against Athaliah: having had the people gathered in the courts of the Temple he presents to them the little Joash, the only true heir, wearing the diadem: “Here is the king’s son! Let him reign, as the Lord promised concerning the sons of David.”

Drawn by the acclamations of the people, Athaliah goes down to the Temple and, seeing the child consecrated king, tears her clothes, crying treason. Jehoiada orders that she be taken out of the Temple so that it is not profaned by her blood, and that she be killed as soon as she has reached the gate of the palace.

Thus the legitimacy of the Davidic line promised by God to David through Nathan is restored; Joash, having become king at seven, reigned over Jerusalem for forty years and did “what was right in the sight of the Lord all the days of the priest Jehoiada”. A remark that makes clear that, despite the passionate interventions of the prophets, the fatal descent toward the end was not halted.

5. Huldah the prophetess (2 Chron 34:19-33)

For a century (721 BC) the northern kingdom has fallen under the blows of the Assyrian Sennacherib, and its inhabitants are exiles in the cities of Media. A punishment from God, the author reflects, “because the Israelites had sinned against the Lord their God” (2 Kings 17:7).

Nor does it seem that the terrible example had made the kings of Judah reflect seriously, their conduct differing little from that of the kings of the North. A glimmer of light opens, however, in the 29 years of the reign of Hezekiah, son of Ahaz, who, having become king in 716, with the support and counsel of the prophet Isaiah removes the cult of idols and carries out some wise reforms.

A brief parenthesis; his son Manasseh quickly destroys the good done by his father and leaves behind him a worthy son, Amon, who is killed after barely two years of reign.

Amon is succeeded by his son Josiah, barely eight years old, who soon shows a good nature and religious spirit: “While he was still a boy, Josiah began to seek the God of his ancestor David.”

Indeed he soon begins “to purge Judah and Jerusalem”, removing the signs of idolatry and, after purifying the land, entrusts to his officials the task of restoring the Temple, left in unseemly neglect by his predecessors.

During the restoration work the priest Hilkiah “found the book of the law of the Lord” (2 Chron 34:14), the memory of which the general decline had caused to be lost.

Josiah’s reaction is sincere and immediate: “Go – he orders the officials – inquire of the Lord for me and for those who are left in Israel and in Judah, concerning the words of the book that has been found; for great is the wrath of the Lord that is poured out on us, because our ancestors did not keep the word of the Lord, to act in accordance with all that is written in this book.”

Here a woman enters the scene to whom the title of prophetess is attributed tout court. Strange that the king’s envoys should resort to her, a woman and a contemporary of Jeremiah; striking, moreover, is the precision of the prophetess’s personal data and even of her residence, which gives the episode almost a seal of historical truth.

In fact “Hilkiah and those whom the king had sent went to the prophetess Huldah, the wife of Shallum son of Tokhath, son of Hasrah, keeper of the wardrobe; she resided in Jerusalem in the Second Quarter”.

In full harmony with Jeremiah’s prophecies, the decided tone of Huldah’s reply makes clear that the decline of the kingdom is now unstoppable, but there is not lacking a nuance, one might say entirely feminine, of sincere esteem and of understanding toward the king, whose merits and good deeds are acknowledged.

“Tell the man who sent you to me: Thus says the Lord: ‘I will indeed bring disaster upon this place and upon its inhabitants, all the curses that are written in the book that was read before the king of Judah. Because they have forsaken me and have made offerings to other gods, so that they have provoked me to anger... But as to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the Lord, thus shall you say to him... because your heart was penitent and you humbled yourself before God when you heard his words against this place and its inhabitants, and you have humbled yourself before me, and have torn your clothes and wept before me, I also have heard you... Your eyes shall not see all the disaster that I will bring on this place and its inhabitants.’”

“They took the message back to the king.” And the king listens. He has the book read to all the people, begins a series of most important reforms, has all the objects and places connected with the worship of Baal destroyed and restores the celebration of the Passover.

He will die in battle but mourned by all, Jeremiah included, after an entirely positive reign. His death marks the real beginning of the end of Judah.

The figure of Huldah, apart from the decided prophetic tone, has no particular prominence. What remains, however, is the not unimportant fact of the attribution to a woman of the prophetic role and mission, in one of the darkest periods in the history of the Hebrew people.

CHAPTER V

THE MOABITE ANCESTRESS

1. A special story

An elderly one; the other two still young; on their faces the gravity of great, painful decisions.

Sunlit and deserted, the land of Moab stretches all around as far as the eye can see, furrowed by three paths that diverge, moving away from one another toward distant, invisible goals.

And behold, the elderly woman speaks, in the tone of voice of one resuming a conversation already punctuated by sobs within the walls of a poor house that they are about to leave. “Go back, each of you to your mother’s house. May the Lord deal kindly with you, as you have dealt with the dead and with me. The Lord grant that you may find security, each of you in the house of your husband.”

She embraces and kisses them affectionately; but the young women raise their weeping aloud in renewed refusal: “No, we will return with you to your people.”

“Turn back, insists Naomi, turn back, my daughters! Why will you go with me? I am too unhappy to be of use to you, for the hand of the Lord has turned against me.”

Other voices of weeping rise in the absorbed silence of nature; but suddenly one of the young women kisses her mother-in-law with a gesture of finality and leaves with small steps, still uncertain but little by little more resolute, until she fades from sight; she leaves the story and goes toward life, and perhaps, still secret, there is already sprouting in Orpah’s heart a shoot of hope.

Two are left, eye to eye; a flicker of tears is still in those of the young woman, while the elder’s gaze is steady: “Ruth, see, your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and to her gods; what are you waiting for? Go back after her!”

But now Ruth’s voice, too, is steady: “Do not press me to leave you or to turn back from following you! Where you go, I will go; where you lodge, I will lodge; your people shall be my people, and your God my God. Where you die, I will die — there will I be buried. May the Lord do thus and so to me, and more as well, if even death parts me from you!”

To the oath nature now reacts, as if foreboding: a puff of wind stirs the leaves of the trees, and a light chirping, like the announcement of new life, rises among the branches.

2. The return

“In the days when the judges ruled, there was a famine in the land, and a certain man of Bethlehem in Judah went to live in the country of Moab, he and his wife and two sons. The name of the man was Elimelech and the name of his wife Naomi, and the names of his two sons were Mahlon and Chilion; they were Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. They went into the country of Moab and remained there.”

A serene period of modest well-being; the sons married two young Moabite women, but the joy of children was denied them, and their good fortune was short too: soon after the father’s death the two sons died as well, and for the young widows the land of Moab became almost foreign.

Now Naomi has decided: she will return to her homeland, where she has heard that the Lord has visited his people and given them food; the daughters-in-law, on the other hand, will be able to make a new life among their own people.

But this decision will hold only for Orpah. Ruth has made her choice: Naomi’s God will be her God and Naomi’s people her people. What fascination issues from this foreign woman, an unfortunate wife and mother, and what call resounds in Ruth’s heart from a foreign God who has denied her a son and deprived her of her young husband? Ruth does not know, but her fate is sealed.

“So the two of them went on until they came to Bethlehem. When they came to Bethlehem, the whole town was stirred because of them. The women said, ‘Is this Naomi?’ She said to them, ‘Call me no longer Naomi, call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt bitterly with me. I went away full, but the Lord has brought me back empty.’”

An irrepressible lament, a sad summary of a period of life definitively closed, a dark foreboding of a beginning still uncertain. But the welcome of the women, Naomi’s companions of youth, sounds encouraging and opens the heart to hope.

3. In the harvest season

The two women arrive in Bethlehem at the time when the barley harvest was beginning. A time foreseen by Naomi from when she had learned that God had given food to his people.

Barley bread, the bread of the poor of Israel; and it is the harvest season, the time of the providence of the poor. Leviticus and Deuteronomy are precise: “When you reap the harvest of your land – prescribes Leviticus (19:9-10) – you shall not reap to the very edges of your field, or gather the gleanings of your harvest; you shall not strip your vineyard bare, or gather the fallen grapes of your vineyard; you shall leave them for the poor and the alien: I am the Lord your God.”

Ruth, young and vigorous, knows that it is now her turn to provide for herself and her mother-in-law. She therefore says to Naomi: “Let me go to the field and glean among the ears of grain, behind someone in whose sight I may find favor.” And Naomi answers her: “Go, my daughter.”

We now enter the central part of the story: shortly before, almost casually, the author let fall a sentence apparently unconnected with the context: “Now Naomi had a kinsman on her husband’s side, a prominent rich man, of the clan of Elimelech, whose name was Boaz.” But it is certainly not by chance that the same author now directs the unwitting Ruth to a field where “she set out and went and gleaned in the field behind the reapers”, and where, a little later, Boaz, the owner, arrives from Bethlehem and notices the foreign gleaner intent on her work.

“To whom does this young woman belong?”

The servant questioned answers favorably about Ruth; and one would say that something new stirs in Boaz’s inmost heart: it is clear that from now on Naomi and Ruth will not lack bread and protection from the rich man, who, without revealing himself as a kinsman, opens a dialogue from which lively interest in the young woman shines through: “Listen, my daughter, do not go to glean in another field...” and to the woman’s humble protest he makes his thought clear: “All that you have done for your mother-in-law has been fully told me.”

Ruth, then, is not a stranger to him; Bethlehem is a small village, everyone knows everyone, “rumors” fly fast, and Boaz is not so young as not to have known Elimelech personally before his exodus to the land of Moab.

Did a reference to the law of “levirate” perhaps flash through Boaz’s mind? The undoubted interest he shows in the foreigner even “at mealtime” goes beyond the narrow limits of the duty of hospitality; and when Boaz orders the reapers: “Let her glean even among the standing sheaves... and also pull out some handfuls for her from the bundles” he goes well beyond the due respect for the “rights of the poor”.

At home, in the evening, Ruth tells her mother-in-law everything, and the possible hidden meaning of Boaz’s attentions does not escape Naomi. And it is with a new, though slight, hope in her heart that she informs her daughter-in-law of their kinship; but, prudent, concerning Boaz’s invitation to remain with his young women until the end of the harvest, she merely comments: “It is better, my daughter, that you go out with his young women, otherwise you might be bothered in another field.”

So Ruth “stayed close to the young women of Boaz, gleaning until the end of the barley and wheat harvests”, while, unhurried, Naomi, a new deus ex machina, weaves her threads.

4. The time of the crop

The harvest is over and the days have come when the crop is winnowed. Naomi’s gaze often rests, tender and thoughtful, on her daughter-in-law, because her concern is constant to procure for the young woman, who for her sake has left her father’s house, her homeland and even the gods of her people, a serene and secure future.

Naomi has by now worked out her plan: concrete, bold, perhaps disconcerting, in the context of a story that flows along the thread of an essential religiosity, but typically Hebrew. It does not, in fact, depart from the patterns of the Hebrew tradition, which likes to underline with symbolic gestures important events even in private life, such as the passage of a young woman from her father’s authority to her husband’s (cf. Ezek 16:8).

And the direct simplicity of her language shows how pure and free of dishonest intentions her proposal is. “My daughter – she says to her daughter-in-law – I must seek some security for you, so that it may be well with you. Now here is our kinsman Boaz, with whose young women you were. See, he is winnowing barley tonight at the threshing floor. Now wash and anoint yourself, and put on your best clothes and go down to the threshing floor; but do not make yourself known to the man until he has finished eating and drinking. When he lies down, observe the place where he lies; then, go and uncover his feet and lie down; and he will tell you what to do.”

Just as simple is Ruth’s answer: “All that you tell me I will do.”

Her immediate agreement to such a proposal may seem strange; but she has become part of the Hebrew world, of its way of thinking and acting, and has unshakeable trust in Naomi. On the other hand, her heart cannot fail to have given at least an approximate meaning to Boaz’s attentions, and marriage, for a Hebrew woman as she had become, in her time and in her condition, was the only honest and possible solution.

Certainly her heart beats hard at the moment when she carries out Naomi’s advice, but, serene in the purity of her intentions, she performs the act with such delicacy that the sleeper notices nothing, and only later, “at midnight”, startles because a shiver runs through his body, perhaps caused by a breath of colder air.

He sees the woman and his reaction is simple, one might say normal: perhaps he has already understood.

“Who are you?”

“I am Ruth, your servant; spread your cloak over your servant, for you are next of kin.”

Because her feelings are pure, the man’s reply is also deeply religious: “May you be blessed by the Lord, my daughter; this last instance of your loyalty is better than the first.”

Ruth, still young, could indeed have aspired to a younger husband; but she would not have thus assured Naomi’s future as she did by placing herself and her in Boaz’s hands, both by reason of kinship and with a view to the consequent redemption of Elimelech’s property foreseen by the law in such cases. And a nuance of humility and gratitude is in Boaz’s words, as he feels himself chosen despite his no longer young age.

Honest, however, and observant of the Law, he knows that in Bethlehem there is a kinsman who has a greater right than he to the fulfillment of the “levirate”. He must consult him before deciding, but meanwhile reassures Ruth: “Remain this night.” And, humble, honest but also reasonably prudent, “she rose before one person could recognize another; for he said, ‘It must not be known that the woman came to the threshing floor.’”

And finally generous: he sends Ruth home with six measures of barley, which he pours into her cloak and sets on her shoulders.

Times and circumstances did not allow him, nor perhaps inspire in him, the chivalrous gesture of carrying the not light weight himself all the way to her home. But the shoulders of Hebrew women must have been strong indeed.

5. The hidden God

Even in the certainty that these wonderful stories are nothing but imaginative summaries of ancient traditions rooted in Israel’s historical consciousness, apt to provide the authors with a useful pretext for sapiential reflections or moral teachings, when one lingers over these pages, pervaded by a breath of poetry that makes them limpid and light, one cannot overcome the impression of glimpsing, like a sudden flash within a cloud, the smile of Someone who bends, with an almost human, certainly fatherly heart, over the meeting of Isaac and Rebekah in the territory of the Negeb, or of Jacob and Rachel at the watering place, or over the loving impatience of Tobias whose heart leaps toward Sarah, the predestined and still unknown wife, or over the bold and chaste gesture of Ruth intent on securing for herself, by it, definitive belonging to Naomi’s people and Naomi’s God.

The smile of the divine weaver who, while leaving his children freedom of initiative, in the inaccessible secret of his eternal designs weaves, within the warp of human events, what will be their true, definitive meaning.

Naomi, Ruth and Boaz do not know; the sacred writer himself, who with this delightful tale thinks he is providing a respectable ancestry for the Davidic genealogy, does not know that he is preparing a piece for the far more important genealogy in which the evangelist Matthew will assign a conspicuous place to Ruth “the Moabite”.

Yes, “the Moabite”; the insistence with which, in the frame of a typically Hebrew narrative, the protagonist’s foreign origin is underlined seems to want to bring out, and undoubtedly gives food for thought about, another intention of the author: to affirm the universality of God’s love and of his saving will for all people.

And the wealth of points for reflection that can be gathered within the brevity and simplicity of the story is not exhausted here: respect for the law, in this case the law of “levirate”, which here, however, appears set in discreet but clear contrast with the excessive rigor of the laws against mixed marriages, issued in the period of post-exilic reconstruction; the exaltation of the virtues typical of the Hebrew woman, remarked, as in harmonious counterpoint, in a Hebrew and in a foreigner; the abiding value of the family virtues proper to the Old Testament world, which shine also in Boaz; and finally the common and profound sense of faith that vibrates on the wave of the prayer of praise and blessing to the faithful God who infallibly rewards those who walk the paths he has marked out. All this is present and alive, while secretly and omnipresently the work of Providence unfolds which, without spectacular gestures but with small discreet interventions, guides the story to its predetermined fulfillment.

6. A happy ending for all

To Ruth who, as we have seen, returns to her mother-in-law anything but empty-handed and presumably with a great desire to tell, Naomi says: “Wait, my daughter... for the man will not rest, but will settle the matter today.”

In fact Boaz has hurried to the city gate to meet “the next of kin” and negotiate with him. And everything is smoothed out easily. Boaz has set out the terms of the matter clearly: “The day you acquire the field from the hand of Naomi, you are also acquiring Ruth the Moabite, the wife of the dead man, to maintain the dead man’s name on his inheritance”; that is, you will recognize the hereditary rights of the sons who are born.

But although that man would gladly take over Naomi’s field to enlarge his property, he does not agree to the second part: “I cannot – he declares – redeem it for myself”; and he validates his words with the ritual gesture of handing over the sandal, which was “the manner of attesting in Israel”.

And the matter is closed, since Boaz has already shown himself more than willing to marry Ruth: to the legal confirmation of the “testimony” the elders present add the blessing: “May the Lord make the woman who is coming into your house like Rachel and Leah.”

The author’s allusive intention is clear: as Rachel and Leah were the mothers of the twelve tribes of Israel, so may Ruth, Boaz’s wife, be remembered and celebrated as the founder of the Davidic dynasty.

“So Boaz took Ruth and she became his wife.”

Great was the celebration her women friends held for Naomi at the birth of Obed. Naomi “took the child and laid him in her bosom”, recognizing by this gesture the newborn’s descent from the family of Elimelech and consecrating its continuity.

“And the women of the neighborhood said, ‘A son has been born to Naomi.’ She named him Obed; he became the father of Jesse, the father of David.”

“Let us now sing the praises of famous men, our ancestors” (Sir 44:1). To the richness of content is joined the fresh simplicity of the clean and incisive style, certainly the work of a great writer.

It is no accident that even today the Hebrew world shows its appreciation for this story by reading it officially every year, at the feast of the Seasons.

Its composition, although set in the late period of the Judges, seems later than the destruction of the first Temple because of the delicacy of feeling that characterizes it and that foreshadows the emergence of that spirituality which was proper to the “poor”, who, recognizing in humility of heart the absoluteness of God, entrusted their lives to him in trusting abandonment.

A spirituality widely diffused in the time when Anne, Joachim and Mary lived. To them we are sent back by Naomi’s solid faith and human sagacity, Boaz’s frank honesty, Ruth’s simple generosity, letting us glimpse, as in a transparent and delicate watermark, some of the distinctive features of those faces which, with filial care, we are seeking.

CHAPTER VI

THE WOMEN OF DAVID – I

1. Israel wants a king (1 Sam 8)

“When Samuel became old, he made his sons judges over Israel... Yet his sons did not follow in his ways... Then all the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah, and said to him, ‘You are old and your sons do not follow in your ways; now appoint a king to govern us, like other nations.’”

The fruit of the maturing of the civic consciousness of a people intent on seeking its specific identity, or a childish craze for imitation that made the descendants of the patriarchs forget their peculiar identity as God’s chosen people with a unique covenant, not yet well understood and assimilated?

“But the thing displeased Samuel when they said, ‘Give us a king to govern us.’” Therefore “Samuel prayed to the Lord”.

From the whole story, particularly from the various apparent contradictions, fruit of different interpretations and traditions, it is easy to deduce to what long and tormented rethinking Israel’s critical conscience subjected this controversial page of its history, which represents a definitive turning point.

The Lord’s very “answer” to Samuel’s prayer sums up the different positions: could the monarchy reconcile, in relation to a people such as Israel, the essential religious aspect with the secular aspect, proper to and inseparable from an earthly kingdom?

So the Lord answers Samuel: “Listen to the voice of the people in all that they say to you; for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them... Now then, listen to their voice; only, you shall solemnly warn them, and show them the ways of the king who shall reign over them.”

“Samuel reported all the words of the Lord... These will be the ways of the king who will reign over you: he will take your sons... he will take your daughters... he will take the best of your fields... he will take your male and female slaves... he will take one-tenth of your flocks... And in that day you will cry out because of your king, whom you have chosen for yourselves; but the Lord will not answer you in that day.”

And the predictions did not fail to come true in the many dark moments of Israel’s history, until the final sunset, first of one and then of the other of the two kingdoms.

2. In the shadow of the throne

Not even the certainly most brilliant period of Israel’s human and religious history, that of David and Solomon, was exempt from black pages of sin and red pages of blood; the royal mantle did not eliminate but rather weighed down the burden of sorrowing and sinful humanity that bore on them and was reflected on the people, among whom it spread like an oil stain.

A dark reflection that fell evidently also on the female world, especially on those women who, by birth or social position, came to be closest to the throne.

Not that figures of notable women are entirely lacking, even in this period, but they are no longer the splendid figures of shrewd, strong-willed, passionate matriarchs.

Woman easily becomes passive, an inert commodity of exchange, an instrument of pleasure in the private life of the powerful or a symbol of wealth and power in public display; and in any case, absorbed into the glare of royal majesty, she shines less with her own light.

In Saul’s life, in truth, woman has no apparent space: she does not seem to occupy any place other than that of mother of his children. The Bible attributes to him a wife, Ahinoam, mother of three sons, among them Jonathan, and of two daughters; and a concubine, Rizpah, who bore him two more sons.

Except for Jonathan, the favorite son who has an important place beside his father and in his heart but will have to share his defeat and death, and the lackluster Ish-baal who will reign briefly after Saul, nothing is known of the other sons except that they too died in the battle of Gilboa.

Of the two daughters, on the other hand, enough is known to suggest that being daughters of a king, and of that king and father, did not bring them good fortune.

3. Merab (1 Sam 18:17-19)

Merab is Saul’s elder daughter; not a character, but a pawn in her father’s hands.

At the moment when, Goliath having been killed by David’s sling, the women of Israel come out to celebrate the victory and fête the hero, dancing and singing:

“Saul has killed his thousands, / and David his tens of thousands”,

Saul becomes angry “and from that day on Saul kept a jealous eye on David”. Indeed “an evil spirit from God rushed upon Saul”, whose heart is exacerbated by the rejection that the Lord communicated to him through Samuel (cf. 1 Sam 15:10). “And he raved within his house.” Several times he tries to pin David to the wall with his spear, but the young man escapes him because “the Lord was with David but had departed from Saul”.

In his mad fury Saul decides to set a trap to harm the enemy: he promises him as wife Merab, his elder daughter: “Here is my elder daughter Merab; I will give her to you as a wife; only be valiant for me and fight the Lord’s battles.” And meanwhile he thinks: “Let not my hand be against him, but let the hand of the Philistines be against him.”

David’s reply, humble in appearance, seems to conceal absolute indifference toward Merab: “Who am I and what is my life, or my father’s family in Israel, that I should be son-in-law to the king?” and he does not protest at all when Saul, instead of giving Merab to him, gives her as wife to Adriel of Meholah.

We know nothing of Merab’s feelings; the five sons she bore to Adriel would learn later what misfortune it entailed to be Saul’s nephews.

4. Michal (1 Sam 18-19)

Saul’s younger daughter is Michal. The girl has fallen in love with David, and is loved in return; they told Saul and the matter pleased him. “He said: I will give her to him, that she may be a snare for him and that the hand of the Philistines may be against him.”

He therefore tells his ministers to tell David that the king does not require the bride-price, but only the killing of a hundred Philistines. In his blindness he does not adequately assess the valor David has already shown. Indeed, spurred on as he was by his love for Michal, before the days fixed for the enterprise had passed, David showed the king that he had struck down two hundred Philistines.

Saul has to face two problems: David more alive than ever, and strengthened by his new success, and Michal in love and determined; in his reckless fury he tries once more to pierce David with his spear, but in the end he pretends to give way, preparing another “snare”.

Perhaps on the very first wedding night, “Saul sent messengers to David’s house to keep watch over him, planning to kill him in the morning”.

In the dark depths of his soul poisoned by jealous hatred, his daughter’s grief counts for nothing, nor does Jonathan’s sincere and affectionate admiration for David; indeed this is the reason that rekindles his murderous frenzy; at all costs he must get rid of his rival.

But he has miscalculated; Michal is a determined and energetic woman. She knows her father’s plans and says to David: “If you do not save your life tonight, tomorrow you will be killed.” And she helps him escape by letting him down through a window, in the dead of night. Then she cleverly places the teraphim on the edge of the bed and fits goats’ hair over them, so as to simulate the figure of a man asleep. And when the messengers arrive she tells them that he is ill and sends them away.

But Saul does not give in: “Bring him up to me in his bed – he orders – that I may kill him.”

The deception and David’s flight discovered, Michal defends herself by saying that her husband threatened her with death if she did not let him escape. And by now the fugitive is far away.

For the couple a long separation begins and a busy odyssey for David and Saul: ambushes and pursuits, stratagems devised by David in order to show the king his feelings of peace and even devotion, followed by brief and precarious reconciliations. But everything will end only with the inglorious death of Saul, defeated by the Philistines on the heights of Gilboa, and mourned with such sincere grief, together with Jonathan, by David.

Michal, meanwhile, had been given as wife to Paltiel, son of Laish.

5. Abigail (1 Sam 25)

Escaping Saul’s implacable pursuit, David has gathered around himself some hundreds of men and has taken up the life and ways of a true “man of the bush”, refraining, however, in keeping with the generosity of his nature, from unjustified acts of violence.

One day, in the desert, he and his men are hungry; they find themselves not far from the lands of a rich landowner who, according to pastoral traditions, is celebrating in those days the feast of the shearing of the sheep; David sends him ten of his young men to ask for what is needed to satisfy their hunger. It is no small request; it concerns hundreds of men, generally of good appetite and, on top of that, famished; the matter nevertheless fell within local customs, especially during the shearing, when it was usual to offer food and drink to anyone who happened by. David, moreover, could claim a sort of right since he had at times protected and guarded his flock without ever stealing a single sheep from him.

But Nabal, the master, is a coarse and extremely miserly man; less foolish, he might have reflected that it would have been easy for the chief of a band of outlaws to take from him by force what he instead had asked of him courteously. And not only does he refuse, but he does so arrogantly and offensively.

“Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse? There are many servants today who are breaking away from their masters”, he replies, putting David on the level of a runaway slave.

It is too much for the patience of the fiery warrior, who orders his men to gird on their swords and prepare to assault the arrogant man to take from him, along with his goods, his life as well.

Nabal, however, has a wife as beautiful and wise as he is coarse and foolish. Abigail, aware of the danger, prepares an abundant quantity of food with which she has the servants go ahead of her, while she herself, without her husband’s knowledge, sets off on a donkey to meet David.

Before him she prostrates herself and, a true Hebrew woman of the best stock, addresses him with elaborate eloquence. She blames her husband’s conduct, for which she asks pardon, and begs David to accept the gifts she has prepared.

This is the language best suited to soften the warrior’s heart and bend him to gentleness, while his eyes are certainly not insensible to the woman’s beauty. And she, insinuating, continues: “When the Lord has done to my lord according to all the good that he has promised concerning you, and has appointed you prince over Israel, my lord shall have no cause of grief or pangs of conscience for having shed blood without cause or for having saved himself by his own hand.” And, finally, the personal note: “When the Lord has dealt well with my lord, then remember your servant.”

The soul of the poet and musician that throbs in David’s breast lets itself be won: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, who sent you to meet me today! Blessed be your discretion, and blessed be you, who have kept me today from blood-guilt and from avenging myself by my own hand!”

Having accepted the gifts offered with great pleasure, David and his men withdraw, and Abigail returns home, where she finds her husband at a banquet with friends and already dead drunk. She waits for the morning, until he has slept off his drunkenness, and then makes him understand to what danger he exposed himself by his foolish avarice and how she ran to the rescue by making David a substantial offering. Whether from the sense of danger or from grief and anger at the squandering of his goods, the miser’s heart “died within him; he became like a stone”. Ten days later he was dead.

David, as soon as he knew it, lost no time: “David sent and wooed Abigail, to make her his wife.” And Abigail, who in her turn must not have remained insensible to the charm of the young, handsome and valiant man, hastened to join him taking with her five maids; and she became his second wife, because “David had also taken Ahinoam of Jezreel”.

6. David wants Michal back (2 Sam 3:12-16)

Saul being dead, the way to the throne seems clear before David. But the struggles of succession among Saul’s heirs last a full seven years.

A deeply religious spirit even amid the contradictions of his nature, and mindful of Samuel’s teachings, David turns to the Lord: “Shall I go up into any of the cities of Judah?”

The Lord answers him: “To Hebron.” David therefore “went up there with his two wives, Ahinoam and Abigail, the widow of Nabal”, and with him go his men, “every man with his household, and they settled in the towns of Hebron” (2 Sam 2:1-4). Thus David is anointed king of Judah.

Abner, instead, formerly commander of Saul’s army, takes Ish-baal, the only surviving son of Saul, to Mahanaim and makes him king over all the rest of Israel, since only the house of Judah followed David.

The struggle between the followers of the two sides is long and hard, until Abner, considering himself offended by Ish-baal, proposes to David the unification of the kingdom.

David answers: “Good; I will make a covenant with you. But one thing I require of you: you shall not see my face unless you first bring Michal, Saul’s daughter.” And he also sends messengers to Ish-baal, son of Saul, demanding that he return to him his wife Michal, whom he made his bride by killing two hundred Philistines.

A rekindled flame or proud revenge? Michal has for some time been Paltiel’s wife; but who cares about the feelings and will of a woman?

“Ish-baal sent and took her from her husband... But her husband went with her, weeping as he walked behind her all the way to Bahurim. Then Abner said to him, ‘Go back home!’ So he went back.”

A cruel abuse summed up in a few lines. There comes to mind Samuel’s warning to the elders who asked for a king: “These will be the ways of the king who will reign over you!”

But the writer who records with care and apparent understanding Paltiel’s weeping does not trouble to plumb the abyss of Michal’s silence, the woman twice betrayed: by a father who had torn her, a young girl, from the freshness of first love, and by a king, once loved as a man but now perhaps detested as a despot who, out of proud will to political self-assertion rather than love, tears her from the sweetness of a home where she has found true love.

Michal thus becomes David’s wife again, David who, for his part, in the seven years of his stay in Hebron had not been slow to acquire other wives and concubines: at least six sons by as many women, born in this period, are recorded: by Ahinoam, the first wife, was born Amnon, the absolute firstborn, whom Absalom would have killed to avenge the affront done to Tamar his sister; Chileab by Abigail;

Absalom by Maacah; Adonijah by Haggith; two others by other women.

Michal alone has no children.

7. A “political” interlude

Following the contradictory but often generous impulses proper to his nature, David shows himself mild and even respectful toward the rest of Saul’s family (cf. 2 Sam 4:1-12); he in fact punishes with death Rechab and Baanah, men of the house of Ish-baal who, on the news of Abner’s death, thinking to do something useful and pleasing to David, treacherously kill Ish-baal in his sleep and bring his head to the king at Hebron.

But David’s generous indignation bursts forth: “When someone told me, ‘See, Saul is dead,’ thinking he was bringing good news, I seized him and killed him at Ziklag; that was the reward I gave him for his news. How much more when wicked men have killed a righteous man on his bed in his own house! And now shall I not require his blood at your hand, and destroy you from the earth?” And he gave orders to his young men and they killed them.

Summary and pitiless sentences, an extreme devaluation of human life, but within a line of consistency with a principle of justice and, in this specific case, a generous excess, since in the final analysis the fact turned out wholly to David’s advantage, having removed the only possible rival to the throne over all Israel.

Of the house of Saul, in fact, there remained by now only a son of Jonathan, Merib-baal, lame in both feet from childhood because of a fall and unfit for the kingship; David will take particular care of him, restoring to him all the property of the house of Saul and keeping him at his own table for life (cf. 2 Sam 9:1-12).

David shows himself, however, strangely weak toward Joab, the commander of his army, who treacherously kills Abner, considering him a possible rival of his beside the king. And as if he did not take into account the merits Abner had earned toward him by laying the foundations that enabled him to unite all the tribes of Israel in his own hands, David leaves the murderer unpunished. Only at the end, dying, will he entrust to his son Solomon the task of doing justice (cf. 1 Kings 2:5-6).

All the elders of Israel now go to beg David to accept the kingship over all the tribes. And David, who desires nothing else, is ready to accept.

But a united kingdom needs a single capital; and David dreams of a capital worthy of the kingdom he intends to found.

He sets his eyes on the stronghold of the Jebusites, which, besides its excellent geographical and strategic position, offers the advantage of belonging to none of the tribes of Israel and so of being able to represent effectively the political unity finally achieved. Despite the ironic opposition of the occupants (cf. 2 Sam 5:6-8), the stronghold is easily taken and David settles in it. And his prestige is already such that the king of Tyre hastens to send him a large quantity of cedar wood and carpenters and skilled workmen to build a house worthy of the king.

The Philistines defeated once again, while he is concerned to give an initial structure to the government, David sees his political power grow every day, and in the sincere religiosity of his soul he does not forget that he owes everything to the blessing and help of the Lord.

He therefore decides to transport the Ark of the covenant, which was at Gath, in the house of Obed-edom, to Jerusalem; by this gesture he makes the city not only the political but also the religious capital of the whole nation.

8. Michal’s start (2 Sam 6)

The rite takes place with extraordinary solemnity. “As the ark of the Lord came into the city of David”, he, “having laid aside his royal garments and girded with a simple linen ephod, danced before the Lord”... But behold, “Michal daughter of Saul looked out of the window, and saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord; and she despised him in her heart”.

And she does not keep silent; she goes out to meet him and: “How the king of Israel honored himself today, uncovering himself today before the eyes of his servants’ maids, as any vulgar fellow might shamelessly uncover himself!” she throws in his face, as David “returned to bless his household”.

Poor Michal, betrayed by an untimely resurgence of pride just at the moment when David, the king, humbly places the one, absolute divine majesty before every earthly dignity and power!

These words of hers, together with David’s just but cutting reply, are the only ones that, unfortunately not to her honor, have reached us, remaining fixed in the collective memory.

“A common little woman who always remains outside the real situations in which she finds herself”, Nazareno Fabbretti defined her in his book Le donne nella Bibbia.1 But it is in the deepest feeling and the painful experience of this woman that we must try to understand the meaning of the “contempt” and the cause of the uncontrolled outburst. Because she is forced to live “outside the reality in which she finds herself”: a reality she did not want, which she cannot love, which she is obliged to endure as in the past she had had to endure the effects of her father’s obsessive madness.

Nor is there any sign that David did anything to mitigate the bitterness of losing the only man who had truly known how to love her. How many times must the figure of Paltiel, who followed her weeping as she returned to David, have come to her mind? Forced to share the questionable dignity of “woman of the king” among who knows how many other “women of the king” and to bear the comparison... And how not to think of the comparison with Abigail, whose wisdom and beauty must have made a special impression on the king’s heart and inspired respect and admiration in all, as well as, though later, with the disturbing beauty of Bathsheba, the future queen mother? And on top of that she alone, Michal, without children!

Others, less beautiful, less noble by birth, could display what for the Hebrew woman constituted the highest dignity: a son. She not even this.

“Michal daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death.” By placing, in epigrammatic form, right at the end of the episode, this sentence that seems to wish to imply a divine punishment, the author (a male, naturally!) did not realize that he was giving poor Michal another reason to scream out her frustration not only in the faces of men but to the Lord himself, who deprived her, through no fault of her own, of the greatest and most desired good. A male chauvinist too, perhaps, the Lord himself, while, in the sumptuous setting of royalty, the Hebrew woman was losing part of herself and of her past moral dignity?

Solomon’s harem was not far off.

CHAPTER VII

THE WOMEN OF DAVID – II

1. Bathsheba (2 Sam 11-12:25)

“In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, David sent Joab with his servants and all Israel; they ravaged the Ammonites.” He, however, remained in Jerusalem.

Strange: by despising the messengers whom David, with courteous intent, had sent to offer condolences to the Ammonites on the death of their king (cf. 2 Sam 10:2-5), they had personally offended him, the king; and yet he does not go to fight and is not even held back in Jerusalem by any grave problem of domestic politics, for, on the contrary, according to the story, “late one afternoon, David rose from his couch and walked about on the roof of the king’s house”.

This is not the heroic or religious atmosphere within which we are accustomed to contemplate the “holy king”; what sort of torpid aura envelops him, inclining him to idleness and relaxation?

On the other hand the king is no longer very young and has the right, like everyone, to be tired; but behold, while he is walking on the roof, from above he sees “a woman bathing. The woman was very beautiful”.

It is unthinkable that David was seeing her for the first time, since she must have lived there, beneath his house. But this is the hour of the noonday demon, of the silent enemy who without speaking dulls the brain and awakens the senses.

“David sent someone to inquire about the woman.” She is the wife of Uriah the Hittite, they report to him. Uriah is a faithful servant, a valiant soldier who at this very moment is engaged in fighting the king’s war. No matter: David “sent messengers to get her”.

It is the beginning of a series of sins that David will long lament.

But what woman is this Bathsheba? The Bible limits itself to noting her beauty; and judging by this and by the other episodes in which we shall later find her involved, we could say: she is a beautiful statue. How does she react to the king’s initiative? Summoned, she goes; sent back, she goes home. In due course, as laconic as she is impenetrable in her inner self, she lets him know: “I am pregnant.” That is all. It is true, however, that she is only a woman and her interlocutor is the king of Israel.

Bathsheba therefore lets things be done; David sees to the action and acts, unfortunately, like an Assyrian despot rather than like the Anointed of the God of Israel. A simple order to Joab, the army’s general: “Send me Uriah the Hittite.”

And when Uriah has come, David does everything to make him go and rest at his home. But the Hittite protests: “The ark and Israel and Judah remain in booths; and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are camping in the open field; shall I then go to my house, to eat and to drink, and to lie with my wife? As you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do such a thing.”

The only clear figure in the sordid episode, this simple mercenary soldier, not a Hebrew yet exemplarily observant of the Law of the God of Israel and in solidarity with those whose toils and dangers of war he shares. David, on the other hand, who through the force of an unresisted natural impulse has become an adulterer, through a bad conscience now descends to murder: let the honest stubborn man die, provided his own sin remains hidden!

He sends him back, entrusting to him, in writing, his own death sentence: “Set Uriah in the forefront of the hardest fighting, and then draw back from him, so that he may be struck down and die.”

And Joab, whose morality is inversely proportional to his military valor, does not hesitate to obey, adding his own cynicism to the king’s malice; he in fact suggests to the messenger charged with bringing David the announcement of the “mission accomplished” the most suitable way of communicating it to him.

And Bathsheba? “When the wife of Uriah heard that her husband was dead, she made lamentation for him.” A dutiful ritual gesture, but... nothing more? Does this beautiful doll really have a soul, whom, “when the mourning was over, David sent and brought to his house”, and made his wife?

But since, as the narrator warns, “the thing that David had done displeased the Lord”, the Lord does not leave David’s sin unnoticed and sends him the prophet Nathan, whose terrible indictment bursts out in the implacable accusation: “You are the man!”

David realizes the gravity of the double misdeed and confesses in terror: “I have sinned against the Lord!” His sincere repentance obtains forgiveness for him but not the revocation of the death sentence on the son of sin. “Nevertheless, because by this deed you have utterly scorned the Lord – Nathan tells him – the child that is born to you shall die.”

David does not resign himself; deeply grieved, he pleads, weeps, fasts, spends the nights lying on the ground. The ministers worry about his health, but he refuses all relief and comfort. Until, on the seventh day, having guessed from the secret whispering of the ministers that the child is dead, he gives proof of solid common sense and of frank and almost humorous nonconformism: the child is dead? Then... “David rose from the ground, washed, anointed himself, and changed his clothes; he went into the house of the Lord, and worshipped.” Returning home he asks for food and eats.

Amazement, bewilderment, perhaps even scandal on the part of the ministers, but David is candidly sincere: “While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept; for I said, ‘Who knows? The Lord may be gracious to me, and the child may live.’ But now he is dead; why should I fast? Can I bring him back again?”

Humanly concrete in his earthly affections, he is so also in his relationship with the Lord; since God did not hear his supplications and carried out his plan, David as a humble creature conforms to it and shows that he recognizes his absolute authority by going first of all “to the house of the Lord”. Leaving aside his weaknesses, he is truly the religious king that Samuel would have approved.

The silence that had enveloped Bathsheba-wife continues instead to envelop Bathsheba-mother. Not a gesture, not a word, in a situation that could have struck her no less painfully than it had struck David. But in the end it does not seem out of place to imagine that rather than passivity in Bathsheba’s temperament it is a matter of lack of interest in her on the part of the narrator, whose exclusive aim is to bring into full light the royal figure of David and, it must be admitted, with honest objectivity, Bathsheba... is only a woman.

At any rate David sets about consoling her by consoling himself; and Bathsheba “bore a son, and he named him Solomon”. Sometimes God’s straight ways cross the crooked ways of men.

2. Tamar (2 Sam 13:1-22)

Although she is a daughter and not a wife of David, we cannot exclude from this rapid survey of “his women” the figure of Tamar, whose story opens a chink onto one of the squalidest aspects of the Davidic court, in which, under the appearance of great power and wealth, there were taking shape not negligible signs of moral decay that would become more pronounced toward the end of Solomon’s brilliant reign.

Amnon, David’s firstborn, born at Hebron of his first wife Ahinoam, fell in love with Tamar, his half-sister, born of Maacah, who was also the mother of Absalom.

Tamar is “very beautiful” and Amnon pines for her to the point of falling ill or pretending to be, and gets the king himself, excessively indulgent toward his firstborn, to order the young woman to “prepare food” for him and bring it to him. The inevitable happens and Tamar, desolate, takes refuge with her brother Absalom who, though burning with anger, advises her to keep silent for the moment. Yet “when King David heard of all these things, he was very angry; but he would not punish his son Amnon, because he loved him”.

He was, in fact, says the text, his firstborn. But the daughter? Did being a woman make her so insignificant even to the heart of a father who showed himself so tender toward his sons? It is one of the many emblematic episodes that illuminate the time and the setting as well as another aspect of David’s personality, easily attracted by female beauty but not equally sensitive to the essential data of femininity. The feminine personality seems to have had quite another depth in the time of the patriarchs.

With time Absalom’s resentment is not appeased, probably reinforced by another, subtler and more personal interest: as the king’s second son, by avenging his sister with the elimination of the firstborn, he will be able to smooth his own way to the succession.

And during a banquet to which he had invited all his brothers and even his father, who however did not go, he gives vent to his rancor: at a signal agreed by him, the servants attack Amnon and kill him.

Very fierce is David’s anger and Absalom will have to flee and stay away from the court for years before his father is appeased and readmits him. Nothing more is known, instead, of poor Tamar, whom the narrator abandons to her destiny as an outraged and betrayed woman.

3. Abishag (1 Kings 1-2)

“King David was old and advanced in years; and although they covered him with clothes, he could not get warm.” His servants said to him: “Let a young virgin be sought for my lord the king, to wait on the king and be his attendant; let her lie in your bosom, so that my lord the king may be warm.”

“So they searched for a beautiful girl throughout all the territory of Israel, and found Abishag the Shunammite, and brought her to the king.”

This evanescent female figure moves us to tenderness, sweet in her defenseless youth, reduced to a thermotherapeutic instrument in the attempt to restore life and vigor to the king, perhaps tired and disillusioned even more than old.

Meanwhile Adonijah, who after the death of Amnon and Absalom had remained the eldest among David’s sons, has begun to weave intrigues to secure the succession to the throne; and many, among them Joab himself, side with him.

Evidently there were as yet no fixed laws on succession to the throne and it was therefore within the king’s power to designate his successor; by gaining time and weaving intrigues, Adonijah therefore intends to confront the king and the court with a fait accompli.

But the prophet Nathan is watching; he knows that the Lord has chosen as king, after David, Solomon, the son of forgiveness. From the child’s birth, in fact, he had intervened to give him a name different from the one his father had given him; David had called him Solomon; Jedidiah, which means beloved of God, was the name Nathan had given him (cf. 2 Sam 12:24-25).

And Nathan intervenes now, determined to crush Adonijah’s machinations; and he turns to Bathsheba: “Have you not heard that Adonijah son of Haggith has become king? Now therefore come, let me give you advice, so that you may save your own life and the life of your son Solomon.”

Perhaps love for her son, as well as her own interest, shakes Bathsheba’s placid inertia, and she is ready to join the little plot hatched by Nathan and which he himself, as director, prepares to put into effect. Bathsheba will go into the king’s chamber and, reminding him that he swore that the throne would be Solomon’s, will begin to complain of Adonijah’s behavior. While she is still speaking, Nathan will have himself brought in, as if by chance, and will reinforce the woman’s words by presenting Adonijah as a king already acclaimed by his partisans and will give reasons for the necessity of crushing his plans at once.

And the king’s reaction is immediate; turning to Bathsheba David swears: “As the Lord lives, who has redeemed my life from every adversity: as I swore to you by the Lord, the God of Israel, that your son Solomon shall reign after me, and that he shall sit on my throne in my place, so will I do this day.”

Everything takes place without delay: according to David’s orders, Solomon is made to mount the king’s mule and is led to Gihon where the priest Zadok “took the horn of oil from the tent and anointed Solomon; then they blew the trumpet”. Those present acclaim and the din of sounds and acclamations reaches Adonijah and his guests who are sitting at the banquet. The news frightens and makes them all flee; only Adonijah remains and goes to seize the horns of the altar, a gesture equivalent to claiming the right of asylum.

When Solomon is informed he guarantees his safety on condition that he behave “as a worthy man” and sends him home.

But the ambitious Adonijah finds no peace. And after David’s death he devises a new way of securing, by another pretext, an eventual right to the succession. He turns to Bathsheba, whose authority at court, on account of her position as queen mother, must have carried great weight: “Please ask King Solomon – he says to her – for he will not refuse you – to give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife.” A request that could seem plausible and legitimate to anyone ignorant of court customs but which must not have seemed so to Bathsheba who, living at court, was in a position to realize the true import of Adonijah’s request. In fact, although Abishag had been more nurse than wife to David, she unequivocally had the title and dignity of wife; and according to custom, marriage to or even the mere possession of one of the wives or concubines of the dead king constituted a claim to the succession. The request therefore aimed at establishing for Adonijah a right to the succession in the event of Solomon’s death.

Bathsheba nevertheless presents herself to the king, who comes to meet her and bows down before her and has a throne placed for her beside his own. But when he hears what is the “one small request” that his mother has come to ask of him he flies into a rage and bursts out: “Ask for him the kingdom as well!”

Adonijah’s fate, already compromised by his earlier machinations and conditioned by the commitment he had made not to attempt anything further against the throne, is now sealed: “May God do so to me and more also – swears the king – if Adonijah has not devised this scheme at the cost of his life... today Adonijah shall be put to death.”

And he gives the order to kill him to Benaiah son of Jehoiada. More brotherly blood stains the splendor of the throne and the descendants of David. We shall never know whether this time Bathsheba’s heart trembled, more or less guilty and willing accomplice of this new murder.

As nothing can be known of Abishag’s death, she probably remained, another evanescent female phantom projected against the dark background of court intrigue, among the many “women of Solomon”.

4. Rizpah (2 Sam 21)

More blood is destined to drip also from the unfortunate descendants of Saul.
