For three years a great famine has been oppressing David’s kingdom, and he, king and prophet, inquires of the Lord, who reveals to him the reason for his anger: a sin weighs on the house of Saul for having broken the oath of peace established between Israel and the Gibeonites.

It is a question with distant roots: one must go back to the time when Joshua was about to cross the Jordan and all the kings who were beyond the Jordan... had allied to make war together against Joshua and the Israelites (cf. Josh 9:1-26).

The inhabitants of Gibeon, however, had preferred to avoid war by a clever stratagem and had succeeded in concluding with Israel an alliance which, respected until the time of Saul, had been violated by him, who, arousing the Lord’s anger, had put some Gibeonites to death.

Since the famine now afflicting Israel is an effect of this anger, David understands the need for reparation and asks the Gibeonites what he can do to make amends for the wrong Saul did them and to avert the divine wrath.

They reply: “The man who consumed us and planned to destroy us... let seven of his sons be handed over to us, and we will impale them before the Lord at Gibeon.” David can only say: “I will hand them over.”

Given the times and the customs then in use, the Gibeonites’ request was not, deep down, excessive; we prefer to think, however, that David’s heart, never closed to feelings of humanity, found it heavy to have to become the arbiter of the choice of seven men to be put to death. Seven innocent persons, perhaps not even aware of the remote reasons for their own condemnation. Heavy for David, just as there arises in us an inner unease when it seems that certain grim episodes, determined by the sins or errors of men, find some pretext in the manifest or presumed will of God.

In reality, only by placing facts, otherwise uncertain and distant, in the context of their own times, places and situations do we manage to glimpse the meaning of certain... anthropomorphic divine interventions. It is precisely then, however, that we are best able to grasp the signs of the Lord’s infinite patience and the delicate pedagogy with which, considering in that distant dawn of Revelation the immaturity of his children, he guided them along the path of history; as, for that matter, he guides us, still incoherent and recalcitrant, to the understanding and fulfillment of the marvelous ends that he traces for us in his infinite love.

The choice, then, falls to David; of Saul’s sons only the two born of the concubine Rizpah survive, besides a grandson, son of Jonathan, Merib-baal, lame in his feet from having fallen, as a little child, from his nurse’s arms (cf. 2 Sam 4:4). David, however, has great affection for him and by virtue of the blood pact made with Jonathan considers him as his own son, so much so that, as we have seen, he gave back to him all the property of the house of Saul and has him eat at his own table. How could he destine him in particular to death?

On the other hand the men required are seven; five are missing. And behold, exactly five are the sons that Merab, Saul’s eldest daughter, bore to her husband, Adriel of Meholah. They will be, with the two sons of Saul and Rizpah, the seven victims demanded by the Gibeonites. And, once handed over to them, they were “impaled on the mountain before the Lord” as had been decided.

At this point one of the most beautiful female figures of Hebrew history emerges: Rizpah, the mother who, torn with grief and powerless, watched the killing of her sons and grandsons. She “took sackcloth and spread it for herself on the rock, from the beginning of harvest until rain fell on them from the heavens”, which, announcing the end of the drought and of the consequent famine, gave a sign that God had been reconciled with Israel. “She did not allow the birds of the air to come on them by day, or the wild animals by night.”

A new Antigone, but more fortunate than she, since, when “David was told what Rizpah daughter of Aiah, the concubine of Saul, had done”, not only did he praise her conduct but completed the pious work for the wretched remains of the house of Saul: “David went and took the bones of Saul and the bones of his son Jonathan, as well as the bones of those who had been impaled; and they were buried in the land of Benjamin in Zela, in the tomb of Kish, the father of Saul.”

And at last God showed himself “placated” toward the land.

5. A reflection

Two, among those here recalled as “women of David”, were not his wives; the figure of the unfortunate Tamar, his daughter, is nevertheless inseparable from the events involving David himself together with the two sons dearest to him; nor could Rizpah be neglected, whose figure of pious and courageous mother casts a ray of typically feminine light onto a gloomy scene of tribal vengeance.

Certainly they do not exhaust the number of women who occupied a greater or lesser space in David’s heart and life, but it can be affirmed that it was a considerably smaller band than the one that crowded the harem of Solomon his son and which, beginning with the politically most important wife, the daughter of the pharaoh of Egypt, with the multiplicity of cults that for love of them he allowed to be introduced and himself introduced, contributed in large part to the initial decline of a kingdom that had not only known the height of earthly glory but, with the building of the temple, had also reached the greatest splendor of the worship due to the one God of Israel.

“If you say – warned Deuteronomy (17:14-17) – I will set a king over me... he must not acquire many wives for himself, or else his heart will turn away...”

6. But, in the period of the kings, the Shunammite... (2 Kings 4; 8:1-6)

Behind Solomon’s straying heart a good part of his people strayed; and it was the beginning of the end.

The slow but real moral and religious decline, begun toward the end of Solomon’s reign, continues inexorably both in the by now isolated kingdom of Judah and under the rule of the successive kings of Israel where, already from Jeroboam on, the relaxation of customs and religious institutions becomes more marked.

It was inevitable that the luxury and worldly splendor of the courts should exercise their influence on woman too, drawing her away from the simple piety and austerity of customs characteristic of the time of the patriarchs.

Without wishing to involve the entire female world in Isaiah’s invectives (cf. 3:26; 32:9) and Amos’ bitter insult (cf. 4:1), we may think that vanity and frivolity were considerable among the women of the city, while in the countryside there must still have lived women of simple and pure life, not conditioned by ceremonial or corrupted by court intrigues nor contaminated by bad example.

Normal and wholesome women.

The figure of the Shunammite who generously hosts the prophet Elisha in fact closely recalls the type of the pious, frank and strong-willed woman of the time of the patriarchs.

A “wealthy” woman, animated by religious spirit and self-assured even toward her husband, she invites the prophet to her table every time he passes by her house and even has a room built for him on the roof so that he can withdraw and rest there when he is with her. And, free and disinterested, to the prophet who, wishing to repay her attentions, asks what favor he might obtain for her from the powerful (the king and the army commanders), she replies proudly: “I live among my own people”, implicitly revealing the distance between the still healthy part of the people faithful to the Law of the God of the fathers and the idolatrous and corrupt court of the kings of Israel.

Left alone with his servant, Elisha asks himself: “What then is to be done for her?” Perhaps out of pride, perhaps out of modesty, the woman has kept her real problem from him, but Gehazi, the servant, knows it: “Well, she has no son, and her husband is old.”

Elisha is ready to call her: “At this season, in due time – he promises her – you shall embrace a son.”

Perhaps an already long experience of bitter disappointments now closes her to faith and joy: “No, my lord, O man of God; do not deceive your servant!” But when the year has passed the son is born, and great is the joy and greater still the renewed faith.

But here is a new trial: the sudden death of the son, by now a boy.

The narrator, who conducts the story with a swift and essential hand, does not fail here to bring out the Shunammite’s faith, for she keeps the son’s death secret even from her husband, busy with the harvest, and hides the body, sure that he who obtained him for her from Heaven will also know how to give him back, from dead, alive. And she goes, saddled on the donkey, toward Mount Carmel in search of the prophet, to whom, proud even in her grief, in a tone almost more of accusation and command than of prayer, she says: “Did I ask my lord for a son? Did I not say, Do not mislead me?”

And, true to her style, after Elisha has obtained for her the son’s life, she does not pour herself out in speeches: she pays him homage with a prostration and, “taking her son, she went out”.

A fortunate woman, she receives from the narrator better treatment than that granted to daughters and wives of kings; while Tamar and Abishag are abandoned to their fate, the Shunammite’s story also has an epilogue: when a famine is about to fall on the country, Elisha advises her to go elsewhere and she, a true energetic matriarch, takes her family with her to the land of the Philistines.

Returning to her homeland at the end of the famine, she finds her house and her field usurped and does not hesitate to present herself to the king to claim the return of her property. And the king, who in the meantime has learned from Gehazi, among other tales, the story of the boy raised by Elisha, is ready to entrust the woman to one of his officials with the order to have restored to her all that belonged to her, including the relevant revenues.

We cannot say that the Shunammite is an isolated case; the golden thread of faith must never have broken entirely during the troubled fortunes of the people of Israel, if it later re-emerged clearer and more genuine from the trial of the exile.

And as for the Shunammite, since it is evident that the whole story aims rather at highlighting the efficacy of Elisha’s prayer and his prestige before the powerful than the story of an obscure woman of Shunem, we can say that for that very reason her figure emerges all the more credible and endowed with inner moral strength, the more widespread was the decay of customs.

CHAPTER VIII

JUDITH, HONOR OF THE PEOPLE

1. Provisionally heroic women

It is significant that the Hebrew writings belonging to the edifying narrative genre, so to speak, of the period before the common era have a woman as protagonist or co-protagonist.

A woman, however, who although placed, by the needs of the script, “above the lines”, is not truly a type apart, or in any case a type intentionally set in opposition to the type of the pious, humble, discreet woman who, in other pages, is found immersed in the daily busyness of the family sphere.

Only when the religious spirit has to be awakened in the people or grave national interests press does woman emerge, as a necessary and irreplaceable element, as provisionally heroic.

Rahab, the prostitute of Jericho; Deborah and Jael, the saviors; Huldah, the prophetess; Abigail, the wise; and, at two moments of particular danger for Israel’s survival, the heroines Judith and Esther. In reality, these last two can be considered symbolic women rather than historical characters; but precisely for that reason a genuine expression of Hebrew thought, tradition and religiosity, which places them in the history of its people not as exceptions but quite naturally. At bottom, for the Hebrews, the true sole actor and protagonist is the God of the fathers.

It seems, therefore, that the Hebrew woman, considered, as wife and mother, the complementary and irreplaceable companion of man, in principle is not subject, though subordinate to him, to that certain misogynistic spirit which surfaces at times in the wisdom literature. In the latter, on the other hand, the severest passages concern foreign, pagan women, and can be understood as a warning to the Hebrew woman to guard against whatever might make her fall from the level of moral and social dignity at which tradition places her and which, in other passages, is openly acknowledged to her.

The shadow of “Eve’s guilt”, which later will weigh as heavily on the Hebrew woman as on the Christian, does not loom over her in this period; on the contrary, in fact if not in law, a certain freedom of movement and initiative seems to be granted to her not only within the family but also in the social and economic sphere.

We thus find, among the pages of the Old Testament, women honored with the title of saviors of the homeland and, at the same time, wholesomely normal according to the type proper to the Hebrew woman.

2. Israel in danger

“In the twelfth year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, who ruled over the Assyrians in the great city of Nineveh...” As solemn as the opening tone is, so inexact and arbitrary are the historical and geographical details to which the author resorts to reinforce within an authoritative frame his theological and moral, homiletic and consoling lesson, beneath whose literary plot it is not however difficult to grasp the essential elements.

Not by chance does the author put into the mouth of a foreigner, Achior, leader of the Ammonites allied to Holofernes, a synthesis of saving acts accomplished by the God of Israel on behalf of his people, concluding the account with a suggestion inspired by honesty and common sense: “If there is any error in this people... let us go up and fight; but if there is no transgression... let my lord pass them by... lest their God defend them.”

But the ally’s wise and truthful speech does not please the proud Holofernes, who foolishly has Achior taken outside the camp so that, bound and abandoned near the gates of Bethulia, he may fall into the hands of the Israelites.

Bethulia is an imaginary city that an improbable geographical note says is “situated facing Esdraelon, at the entrance to the plain that stretches before Dothan”. Nebuchadnezzar has sent Holofernes there, the best of his generals, with a strong army and the order to destroy all the peoples who dared to refuse to follow him in his war against Arphaxad. Among these peoples is Israel.

Faced with the danger of invasion, the high priest of Jerusalem, Joakim, has ordered the inhabitants of Bethulia to “seize the passes up into the hill country, for by them the entrance into Judea is possible”; which would suggest Bethulia as a city on the border between Samaria and Judea and connected to it in the general plan of defense.

The Israelite sentinels have spotted the man abandoned near their gate. They take him, untie him and lead him before the city’s leaders. Achior, with the same honest frankness with which he spoke to Holofernes, reports to the assembled population Holofernes’ intentions and threats of extermination, as well as his impious and blasphemous expressions; the people prostrate themselves to worship God and beg his help.

When Holofernes is about to give battle, he heeds the Ammonite counselors who, shrewdly, suggest that he avoid the frontal clash but rather put the city under siege and seize “the spring of water that flows from the foot of the mountain, from which all the inhabitants of Bethulia draw their water; so that they may no longer be able to take it and be overcome by thirst and forced to surrender without any loss on the Assyrians’ side”.

The description of the forces deployed against the city is impressive: having seized “the aqueducts and the springs of the Israelites, the Edomites, Ammonites and part of the Assyrians posted on the mountains opposite, the bulk of the army camps in the plain and the number of warriors is such that it covers the whole extent of the ground”. It really seems that little escape remains for the inhabitants of Bethulia. It is evident, however, that the author intends to contrast the weakness of the besieged with the crushing strength of the enemy, so that in the end it may be clearly seen that the salvation of the city and of the whole of Judea is the exclusive effect of divine intervention, solicited by the great fervor with which the besieged turn to the Lord.

But the difficult moment arrives. After thirty-four days of siege, every reserve of water fails and women and children are the first to fall exhausted; with physical strength faith also fails and the people gather, raising loud cries against Uzziah, one of the leaders: “You have done us a great wrong in refusing to make peace with the Assyrians. Now there is no one to help us, for God has sold us into their hands, to be struck down by thirst.”

It is a clear stand also against the Lord, recalling the complaints of the Hebrews in the desert when they asked Moses for water or urged Aaron to cast the golden calf. Faced with the gravity of the blasphemous challenge Uzziah finds no refuge but to ask the people for a sort of truce: “Let us hold out five more days”, he proposes. This too is a challenge, softened however by a small remnant of faith and hope: “It is not possible that God will abandon us to the end.”

God, in fact, will answer in his own way.

3. Judith, a woman uncovered

In those days Judith, daughter of Merari, widow of Manasseh, a rich woman respected by the people, beautiful and attractive, of whom “no one spoke ill... for she feared God with great devotion...” learned “the exasperated words the people had spoken to the authorities” and also how Uzziah “had sworn to them to surrender the city to the Assyrians after five days”.

At once Judith sent a maidservant to call together with Uzziah “Chabris and Charmis, the elders of the city”, and as soon as they came she attacks them: “What you have said to the people today is not at all fitting... to hand the city over to our enemies if the Lord does not send help in the meantime. Who are you, then, who have put God to the test and set yourselves above him, though you are only men?”

It is truly worth highlighting the salient points of this strong and severe speech in which the deep religiosity of post-exilic Judaism vibrates: “Who are you, who have put God to the test... though you are only men?”

Unconditional faith, total abandonment to the Lord’s will even to the acceptance of a possible defeat, and at the same time unshakeable trust. Indeed: “If he does not wish to help us within these five days, he has full power to defend us on whatever days he pleases and also to have us destroyed...” But “let us wait in confidence for the salvation that comes from him... if it pleases him”.

And, strong in an argument that confirms and echoes what the narrator had previously stated (“they had only recently returned from captivity”), she proclaims with conviction: “In our generation there has never been... (anyone) who worshipped gods made by human hands, as happened in former days.” The return of the exiles had in fact been characterized by a religious attitude alien to any idolatrous deviation and indeed subject to severely restrictive norms concerning relations with non-Hebrews.

To the acknowledgment of the fathers’ faults succeeds the sense of responsibility that now weighs on the inhabitants of Bethulia: “If we are captured, all Judea will be captured and our sanctuary will be plundered, and God will demand an account of that profanation from our blood...”

At this point there bursts forth, unstoppable, the will to defend the race and the temple, sacred pledges of Jewish identity: “Let us show our brothers that their lives depend on us; that our sacred pledges, the temple and the altar, rest on us”, and the speech calms into a theological-moral reflection: “... besides all this, let us give thanks to the Lord who is putting us to the test as he did our ancestors...”

It is easy to imagine what fascination seized the elders who, in the woman’s majestic beauty and in her strong and wise words, contemplated the image and felt the inextinguishable vibration of the deep soul of the race. And it is Uzziah who, humble and defeated, explains how, to appease the exasperated mind of the people, he could not help asking for a truce. Now... nothing remains but to pray. And let her pray, Judith, “a devout woman”, that the Lord “may send rain to fill our cisterns”.

But the woman aims at something quite different and in a quite different tone replies to the man’s resigned words; without revealing the virile purpose she keeps shut in her breast, she assures him that “the deed I am about to do will go down through all generations of our descendants”. And she feels so sure, of God and of herself, that she promises: “Within the days after which you have promised to surrender the city to our enemies, the Lord will deliver Israel by my hand.”

At the hour when the evening incense was being offered in the temple of God in Jerusalem, Judith falls with her face to the ground and her head covered with ashes and cries aloud to the Lord: “O Lord God of my father Simeon... hear me, a widow. The Assyrians are proud of their horses... they do not know that you are the Lord who crushes wars. Shatter their strength by your might... give to me, a widow, the strong hand to do what I have planned... break their pride by the hand of a woman! Give to your whole people and to every tribe the proof that you are the Lord, the God of all power and might, and that there is no other who protects the people of Israel but you alone.”

Devout, chaste, penitent, she has entrusted herself to the Lord; magnanimous, she has asked the men for silence and full freedom of movement; with full determination she now sets about using the human means at her disposal: beauty, intelligence, cunning, courage.

4. On the way

The woman who at nightfall goes out through the gate of Bethulia, with only a maidservant for company who carries on her shoulders the bag filled with food that Hebrew law declares “clean”, has nothing in common with the austere widow given to prayer and penance. Having laid aside her mourning garments and the sackcloth with which she habitually girded her loins; having washed and perfumed her body and head and put on the festive clothes she used to wear when her husband was alive; having placed a diadem on her hair and on her neck, ears, arms and fingers the most splendid jewels, she has made herself “alluring to the eyes of all men”; the leaders and the sentinels and the guards follow her with astonished eyes until she disappears from their sight.

“Go in peace, Uzziah has said to her, and may the Lord be with you to take vengeance on our enemies.”

She walks swiftly and meanwhile asks herself what the enemy’s most vulnerable points might be. She knows him strong and extremely ruthless toward his adversaries but certainly, like all satraps, not insensible to female beauty and, in this respect, rather easy to seduce. But as she measures the reach of this weapon of hers, beauty, she sets against it the risk to which she exposes herself, her honor, her life.

Now close to the Assyrian gate she takes heart: she renews her trust in the God of Israel who sends her, a woman, a widow and alone, on so risky an undertaking. The “God be with you” of old Uzziah echoes in her ear. God saves! I shall conquer with him!

5. In the lion’s den

At the gate she is welcomed by the astonished faces of the sentinels, who do not believe their eyes and still less their ears when the beautiful stranger, in a harmonious voice, begins her tale: “I have come into the presence of Holofernes to speak to him words of truth and to set before him the road by which he can pass and take possession of all these hills without losing a single one of his men.”

From all over the camp soldiers come running and gather round her, eager to present her to their chief. And such is the charm of her beauty joined to the dignity of her bearing that a single phrase runs on the men’s lips: “Who can despise a people who have such women?”, while at the same time the resolve to annihilate it is also strengthened: “It will be well not to leave a single man alive, for, free, they could make the whole world lose its head.”

But here is Holofernes who “came out to the front of his tent, with silver lamps carried before him”, and toward him is stretched all Judith’s attention as she prostrates herself before him with her face to the ground. The servants, however, are ready to raise her up while Holofernes addresses her with kind and reassuring words.

Judith is, however, well aware of the need to bring forward more than valid arguments to make her words credible and her presence plausible before there can arise in the mind of Holofernes, who gazes at her spellbound, the doubt that she might be a contemptible opportunist ready to betray her country or a skillful decoy sent into the enemy camp to lead him into deception. But she is a woman with many strings to her lyre, and who knows how to make first one and then another vibrate with perfect mastery.

The wise speech she begins cloaks her intentions in the most scrupulous fidelity to the laws of her own religion, so that Holofernes can feel completely reassured of any possible suspicion, all the more on hearing the very same argument already put forward by Achior and foolishly despised by him. “If there is any error in this people – the Ammonite had said – because they have sinned against their God... let us go up and fight them.” “Death will fall upon them – Judith now says – because sin grips them, for which they will provoke the wrath of their God as soon as they commit a rash act.” And it seems they are really about to commit this act because, driven by hunger and thirst, they have decided “to lay hands on their cattle and consume whatever God, by laws, has forbidden them to eat. They will go so far – she adds – as to use up the first fruits of the wine and oil, things reserved for the priests and which no one of the people is allowed to touch with the hand.”

Lying words, these, but deceptions and stratagems of this kind were considered lawful, if used in war for purposes of defense or offense. And the rough man of war, intoxicated by the woman’s beauty and the refinement of her speech, listens and believes; and as he was already sure of having the enemy in hand, so he is certain that he will not be long in making his own the woman he now considers the most beautiful in the world. Nor does the pagan pleasure-seeker see an obstacle in the frank religious profession Judith has just made: “Your servant is devout and serves the God of heaven day and night.” Another skillful argument, this, to obtain, under the pretext of ritual prayer, permission to go out freely, at night, from the camp to “the valley”, where, she says, “I will pray to my God and he will tell me when they have committed their sin. Then I will come and tell you, and you shall go out with your whole army.”

Holofernes asks no more, for now. “Her words pleased him and all admired her wisdom.” And the chief’s promise matches his admiration: “You shall sit in the palace of King Nebuchadnezzar and be famous throughout the whole world.”

It is night now, and Holofernes orders that the food from his own table be prepared for her; but Judith says she can eat only what she has brought with her. And to him, who worries that the supplies may run out without possibility of replenishment, with thinly veiled irony she assures him that they will not give out “before the Lord has accomplished by my hand what he has determined”.

Now the servants lead her, together with the maid, to a tent where she will rest until midnight, then to rise, at the hour of the “morning watch”, to go and pray. She had in fact asked Holofernes: “Let my lord command that your servant be allowed to go out for prayer.” So in the three following days: “She went out at night into the valley of Bethulia and bathed at the spring; coming up from the bath, she prayed the Lord, the God of Israel, to direct her undertaking to the raising up of her people. Returning purified, she remained in her tent until, toward evening, her food was brought to her.”

But the evening of the fourth day has come and Holofernes is by now impatient to establish less conventional relations with the beautiful guest. Judith is no less impatient, but for quite different reasons.

Holofernes orders a banquet to be prepared, but does not invite any of his officers. To Bagoas, the official assigned to his personal service, he orders: “Persuade the Hebrew woman who is in your care to come and eat and drink with us.” And, revealing his thought more clearly, he comments: “It would be a disgrace for us if we let such a woman go without enjoying her company. If we do not seduce her she will laugh at us.”

Bagoas hastens to convey the invitation and finds Judith more yielding than, perhaps, he would have expected: “Who am I to refuse my lord? Whatever pleases him I will do at once, and it will be a joy to me until the day of my death.”

And she makes herself as beautiful as possible so that at her entrance into the tent Holofernes is enraptured, and “his passion, born from the moment he had seen her, grew greatly”.

“Drink, he says to her, and be merry with us.” And Judith is not to be outdone: “I will drink, my lord, because today my life means more to me than in all the days since I was born.” And with skillful pretense she shows herself eating and drinking much more than she really does, while she sees to it that the delighted Holofernes drinks “more wine than he had ever drunk in one day since he was born”.

Holofernes lies drunk on the couch and the guards, drunk too, hurry off to their tents.

Left alone, Judith makes sure of the man’s unconscious state and prays from the depths of her being: “O Lord God of all might, look in this hour upon the work of my hands... Now is the time to help your inheritance and to carry out my plan for the destruction of the enemies who have risen up against us.”

Around is silence: the maid, outside the tent, waits, according to the orders received, for her mistress to come out for prayer; the sentinels, as agreed, will be ready to open the gate; they do not know, however, that this will be a different and final exit.

“She went up to the post at the end of his bed... and took down his sword... then she took hold of the hair of his head: ‘Give me strength today, O Lord God of Israel!’” And “with all her might she struck his neck twice and severed his head from his body”.

Swiftly she rolls the headless body off the bed, takes down the canopy from its posts and uses it to wrap the head and goes out. She hands the bundle to the maid, who puts it in the food bag, and the two set off along the usual path; having passed the gate they go down toward the valley, but after a quick circuit they climb up toward Bethulia.

6. The triumphal return

“Open! Open the gate at once! God, our God, is with us!” It is the cry of exultation that shakes the sentinels and makes the men run, some to the gate, some to call the elders.

They let her in, light a fire to give light, and gather round her in amazement and exultation. “Praise God – says Judith – praise him, for he has not withdrawn his mercy from the house of Israel, but has destroyed our enemies by my hand.” And, taking the head out of the bag, she proclaims: “Here is the head of Holofernes, here is the canopy under which he lay in his drunkenness. The Lord has struck him down by the hand of a woman!”

Loud voices are raised in praise of God and louder than all the voice of Uzziah, who extols the power of God manifested by the hand of a daughter of Israel.

But there is no time for celebrations. “My friends – orders Judith – hang this head on the parapet of your wall. Then, as soon as morning comes, let every valiant man take his weapons and go out of the city as if you were going down to attack the Assyrians. But do not go down to the plain. The enemy, thinking you are about to attack them, will run to warn Holofernes and, finding him dead, will be seized with terror and flee. Then you must pursue them and strike them down. But now call Achior the Ammonite, that he may come and see and recognize the one... who sent him here among us as if to doom him to death.”

Achior hastens to come and, seeing Holofernes’ head held by a man, falls to the ground breathless. But, rising, he throws himself at Judith’s feet and joins the others who beg her to tell how the undertaking went.

While Judith tells it amid the admiring exclamations of those present, Achior feels himself so overwhelmed by a wave of faith in the God who works such marvels on behalf of his faithful that he suddenly asks to be circumcised and joined to Israel.

Meanwhile the first light has dawned and the warriors hasten to carry out Judith’s order. Down in the Assyrian camp, the headless corpse of Holofernes found and the deception discovered, most flee in terror crying: “One Hebrew woman has brought shame on the house of King Nebuchadnezzar.”

With the flight the pursuit begins, and while the news of the event spreads everywhere, trust and the will to fight are rekindled in the Israelites. To the warriors of Bethulia are joined those of all Judea as far as Jerusalem; those of Galilee, meanwhile, outflank the Assyrian ranks fleeing toward Damascus and strike them without mercy. Everywhere great booty is taken.

The high priest Joakim and the Israelites came from Jerusalem to Bethulia to pay homage to Judith.

“You are the glory of Jerusalem – they sang – you are the great pride of Israel, you are the great boast of our nation” and they raised a solemn prayer of thanksgiving to the God of Israel.

Thirty days the plundering of the Assyrian camp lasted, and three months the feast in Jerusalem, “before the sanctuary”. And Judith remained with her people throughout and consecrated to the Lord all the objects from Holofernes’ tent that had been assigned to her as part of the booty.

The women of Israel composed songs and performed dances in her honor and she herself, crowned with olive branches, led the dance and intoned a song.

“After those days... Judith returned to Bethulia and stayed on her estate, and was honored throughout the whole land...” But she did not change her former way of life; although many sought her in marriage, she remained faithful to the memory of Manasseh.

She gave her maid her freedom; in view of death she divided her property fairly among those entitled and prolonged her old age to one hundred and five years.

They buried her in the burial cave of her husband Manasseh and Israel “mourned her for seven days”.

7. Judith’s lesson

In this true little “novel with a thesis”, almost in contrast with the apparent carelessness with which times, places and situations are linked, the logical concatenation of events emerges remarkably.

The author masters the subject with true command, letting the hidden meaning, the one really most pursued, filter through clear and discreet, without harming the immediate interest inherent in the literal sense, proper to an invented narrative. He plays with a light hand also in the care of details, abundant but necessary to give life to the intrinsic poetic and moral truth of the story, which in the full verisimilitude of the setting appears easily traceable to events not foreign to history. And lively and true, though not historical, are the characters.

The true protagonist is the Hebrew spirit, of which the figure of Judith constitutes the highest and most significant expression; a living lesson that expresses the type of the Israelite in his purest, albeit ideal, identity.

Masculine in physical and moral energy, Judith does not forgo any of the devices suited to bring out her beauty, which she uses as a weapon and, conscious of the danger to which she exposes herself, she stands as a symbol of the most total and unconditional abandonment to the Lord, even to accepting from his hands defeat and death. “He has full power... also to have us destroyed”, she serenely told the elders, with a profession of faith so lofty that even a Christian fully advanced in the ways of the spirit could make it his own today.

She loves her country intensely, knows that it must be saved at all costs because it constitutes the Lord’s gift to his people and the pledge of his covenant with him. Intrepid in the face of danger, she is obedient and even scrupulous before the Law: from the use of foods to ritual prayer, she teaches how it is a duty, and possible, to observe it even in extraordinary situations.

And finally... she appears inclined even to a certain respect for legal forms. It may seem strange, for example, that Achior is not present when the whole people of Bethulia gather round Judith; a clever device of the author to give her the means to have him expressly summoned and thus bring out that only he, having known Holofernes alive, is in a position to carry out a sort of juridical “recognition of the corpse”; “let him come and see and recognize”, she says, sending for him, and thus to validate, with his testimony, the authenticity of the deed which, accomplished by a woman, might appear incredible.

Thus, a creature of art and a living lesson of fidelity to the God of her people and to the people of her God, among the many characters of the Bible Judith is among those who still teach us many things.

CHAPTER IX

ESTHER: FAIRY TALE, TRAGEDY, PROPHECY

1. The fairy tale

Protagonists? The king, first of all: “that Ahasuerus who reigned from India to Ethiopia, (who) in the third year of his reign gave a banquet for all his officials and ministers, the army of Persia and Media, the nobles and governors of the provinces... for one hundred and eighty days... at the completion of which he gave another banquet lasting seven days in the court of the garden of the king’s palace...” And here the author, with a wealth of detail, describes the pomp and luxury of the court, the beautiful and precious things the king showed his guests.

But he still had to display the priceless “piece” of his treasure; perhaps the second banquet had precisely the purpose of showing off to the eyes of a smaller circle of admirers the unique jewel: the resplendent beauty of Queen Vashti.

The queen, however, summoned, refuses to appear. Out of haughty awareness of her dignity, or jealous assurance of her merits and prerogatives, or absolute trust in her power over the king’s heart, so as to be able to disobey him publicly? At any rate, she was mistaken. The feminist era was millennia away. And the prologue whose protagonist is Vashti, the rebel queen, could only end with her exit from the scene.

All the more so since the leaders closest to the king, whom he asks for advice, express without mincing words their own masculine indignation and their concern about the very bad effect that Vashti’s bad example will have on all the women of the kingdom.

“What the queen has done... will be known to all the women and will induce them to despise their husbands. The princesses of Persia and Media will speak of it to all the king’s officials and there will be insolence and anger in excess. Let an edict therefore be issued (by the king)... by which Vashti shall never again come before the king. When the edict is known... all women will give honor to their husbands, high and low alike, and so... every man will be master in his own house (and able) to speak as he pleases.”

This interesting lesson in one-sided matrimonial law must be borne in mind to understand the situation in which Esther will find herself, the little Jewess still unaware of the destiny that is ripening for her. The royal edict has indeed already been sent out: “Let beautiful young virgins be sought out for the king... in all the provinces of his kingdom... The girl who pleases the king shall be queen instead of Vashti.”

Needless to say, to this particular “beauty contest” of four thousand years ago there is a flocking, spontaneous or compelled, of young girls who, according to the king’s order, “were gathered in the citadel of Susa, under the custody of Hegai, guardian of the women”. Thus enters the scene the little queen of the fairy tale, the beautiful, poor and obscure girl whom a shrewd uncle-guardian in the guise of a good fairy will bring to the steps of the throne.

Shrewd, but also an upright guardian of the faith and customs of his people, the Jew Mordecai has adopted as a daughter his niece Esther, left an orphan of father and mother at a tender age, and has brought her up in the faith of the fathers. And she has grown up simple, docile, candid, and moreover very beautiful.

“Indeed she pleased Hegai and won his favor”, and he reserved for her a regime of privilege for all the time – not less than a year – that Esther, like all the other candidates, had to spend, subjected to a meticulous treatment of aromatics and cosmetics, awaiting the king’s summons. Always docile to Hegai’s advice, when her turn came she presented herself to the king in the simple charm of her pure beauty, and succeeded. “The king loved Esther more than all the other women, and she won his favor and grace more than all the other virgins: he set the royal crown on her head and made her queen... then he gave a great banquet.”

The good Mordecai, in view of the possible fulfillment of a dream never dreamed, had kept watch throughout the year “walking every day in front of the court of the harem, to learn how Esther was and what was happening to her”.

Frequenting the court in this way, he came to discover a plot that some officers were hatching against the king and made it known to Ahasuerus. The report was confirmed, the guilty were punished, and Mordecai’s name “was recorded in the book of the annals in the king’s presence”.

Esther meanwhile, placed in the fairy-tale setting of the palace, enjoyed a royalty more nominal than real. Though she was first among all the concubines, she too, if the king did not summon her, was forced to live “in the second house of the women” under the supervision of Shaashgaz, the king’s eunuch and guardian of the concubines. And Mordecai continued to watch over his niece, staying every day at the entrance or in the vicinity of the palace.

Soon, however, he was able to experience how dangerous it is to linger within the spatial sphere of the powerful (and overbearing).

King Ahasuerus had in the meantime promoted Haman, son of Hammedatha, to the highest dignity in the kingdom and “set his seat above all the officials who were with him”. Which entailed for all the king’s subjects, beginning with the ministers, the obligation to “bow down and do obeisance” every time they found themselves before Haman. “But Mordecai did not bow down or do obeisance.”

The matter could not pass unnoticed. To the courtiers who reproached him for it, Mordecai explained – convinced that the reason was sufficient – that he was of the Hebrew religion. But this did not convince the others and still less Haman who, furious, asked who this man was, as obscure as he was insolent. And, learning that he belonged to the Jewish people, he decided to take vengeance not only on the offender but on the whole race to which he belonged.

2. The tragedy

His plan hatched, Haman “casts the lot”; that is, he entrusts to a lot the choice of the day favorable for carrying out the vengeance. And he presents himself to the king sure of obtaining, also by offering ten thousand talents of silver to the royal treasury, the signature of the edict of extermination for all the Jews living within the immense borders of the kingdom.

“There is – he denounces – a certain people scattered and dispersed among the peoples in all the provinces, whose laws are different from those of every other people and who do not keep the king’s laws. It is therefore not appropriate for the king to tolerate them.”

Credulous and easily yielding, the king not only consents to issue the edict but also exempts Haman from paying the sum offered. And, now free to act in his own way, Haman sees to the drafting of the decree. The tone of the narrative thus passes from the lightness of the fairy tale whose protagonist is a Hebrew girl to the dark drama whose protagonist is the whole Jewish people gathered within Ahasuerus’s kingdom.

“The nation of the Jews – says the edict – is the only one in continual opposition to every human being... differs by a strange tenor of laws from every other people... is ill-disposed against the interests of the kingdom... commits the worst evils... proves an obstacle to the stability of the kingdom. We have therefore ordered that those indicated in the written reports of Haman... all, with their wives and children, be utterly destroyed by the sword of their enemies, without pity or mercy, on the fourteenth day of the twelfth month, that is, Adar.”

And the tragedy takes on the flavor of prophecy. It seems in fact that the author, perhaps experiencing in his own flesh the burning of Antiochus Epiphanes’ cruel and arrogant persecution, foresees, marks out and sums up in a single act of accusation and condemnation all the accusations and condemnations that will be repeated down the centuries, marking with painful stages the age-old journey of Israel.

The common and almost sole cause of every accusation and pretext for every slaughter: Israel’s fidelity to the Law of the God of the covenant; fidelity which in the eyes of tyrants takes the guise of disobedience and rebellion and in the eyes of other peoples of an incomprehensible and intolerable “difference”.

Authenticated with the royal seal, the edict was dispatched “to all the king’s provinces, with orders to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate all Jews, young and old, women and children, in one day, and to plunder their goods”.

When Mordecai “learned all that had been done, he tore his clothes and put on sackcloth and ashes, and went out into the midst of the city, crying with a loud and bitter cry... up to the king’s gate”.

Esther sends Hathach, one of the eunuchs whom the king had appointed to attend her, to ask him why he is doing these things, and Mordecai informs Hathach in detail of the danger that hangs over the Jewish people. And between uncle and niece, with Hathach’s mediation, a dramatic dialogue opens.

“Remember the days of your lowly state, when you were nourished by my hand – has Mordecai say to Esther –, Haman has spoken against us to have us put to death. Call upon the Lord, speak to the king on our behalf and deliver us from death.”

But Esther is young and, unexpectedly caught up in an adventure greater than herself, is not yet tempered to difficulties. On the other hand her stay at court must have made her understand how drastic and ruthless, when need be, the king’s decisions are.

“All know – she has him answer her uncle – that if anyone, man or woman, goes to the king without being called, there is but one law: to be put to death.” And perhaps a trace of disappointment and fear trembles in her voice: “I have not been called to come to the king for thirty days.”

Mordecai, however, knows the enemy well, is aware of the danger that threatens, and insists, severe and peremptory: “Do not think that in the king’s palace you will escape any more than all the other Jews. For if you keep silence at this time, relief and deliverance will rise for the Jews from another quarter, but you and your father’s family will perish. Who knows? Perhaps you have come to royal dignity for just such a time as this.”

Irresistible, the call of blood overwhelms her. “Go – has Esther say to Mordecai – gather all the Jews, and fast on my behalf, neither eat nor drink for three days, night or day; I and my maids will fast as you do; after that I will go to the king, and if I perish... I perish.”

Humble, sincere and revealing is the prayer that Mordecai addresses to the Lord in the three days of fasting: “You know all things... you know that it was not in insolence or pride that I did this, in refusing to bow down to the proud Haman, for I would have been willing to kiss the soles of his feet for the salvation of Israel. But I did this so that I might not set the glory of man above the glory of God. I will not bow down to anyone but you, who are my Lord. And I will not do so out of pride. O Lord God and King, God of Abraham, spare your people. They plan to destroy us, they long to destroy the inheritance that has been yours from the beginning. O Lord, do not let the mouths of those who praise you be silenced!”

And while “all Israel cried out with all their might”, Queen Esther too sought refuge in the Lord: “I have heard from my earliest years that you, O Lord, took Israel out of all the nations as your inheritance, and did for them all that you promised. Now we have sinned before you, and you have handed us over to our enemies. You are righteous, O Lord! But now they are not satisfied that we are in bitter slavery. They have sworn to abolish the decree of your mouth, to destroy your inheritance, to stop the mouths of those who praise you and to quench the glory of your house and your altar.”

It is not Esther’s slender voice alone that vibrates in this prayer, but the cry of the collective conscience of all Israel which more than once in its long history, trembling for itself, has also feared for the end of its own mission. Who would any longer proclaim among the nations the glory of the one true God?

But in Esther’s heart trust in the God of the promise does not fail, and her prayer turns to more intimate and personal tones; a voice that confesses and pleads: “You know that I hate the emblem of my high position which is upon my head on the days when I must appear in public... Your servant has had no joy since the day that I was brought here until now except in you, O Lord God of Abraham... Hear the voice of the despairing, and save us from the hand of the wicked. And save me from my fear!”

3. Before the king

But when the awaited and dreaded day of the meeting with the king has come, Esther takes off the signs of mourning, puts on splendid royal robes and adorns herself so as to bring out her beauty to the utmost.

And it may be said that Esther, no less than Judith, the national heroine par excellence, possesses several strings to her lyre: the resplendent beauty whose charm is made sweet by languor – an effective and wholly feminine instrument of seduction – with which she leans softly on her maid as she advances toward the royal chambers; the changing of her face from rose to wax when, “her heart frozen with fear”, she addresses the king in a speech in which she nevertheless knows how to blend skillfully respect, fear and flattery. And finally the swoon that seals the scene and, awakening in the king anxiety and tenderness, consecrates her first victory and magisterially prepares the final act, in which audacity and cunning will come into play, in shrewd progressive sequence.

Indeed, when, comforted by her husband’s gentle manner, she hears him promise: “Even to half my kingdom, it shall be given you”, she is ready to reply: “If it pleases the king, let the king and Haman come today to the banquet that I have prepared for him.”

During the banquet the king renews his questions and promises, but Esther is in no hurry and, with great delicacy, reverses the situation: it is no longer she who pleads but the king who begs; and she can even afford to defer her answer: “Let the king and Haman come tomorrow also to the banquet that I will prepare for them, and I will do as the king has said.”

When he leaves the palace, Haman is on top of the world; invited again by the queen and, apart from the king, he alone! But at the sight of Mordecai who, at the gate, “neither rose nor trembled before him”, he has a new surge of rage and strengthens his resolves of vengeance. At home, with his wife and trusted friends, he recovers his stature and exalts himself recounting what honor the queen shows him, but does not hide his anger at Mordecai’s attitude. And then, worthy of him, wife and friends suggest: “Have a gallows built fifty cubits high, and in the morning tell the king to have Mordecai hanged on it.”

Needless to say, he finds the advice to his taste.

The invitation to the two banquets on two consecutive days serves the author to insert in the narrative the night episode of the king’s insomnia and the reading of the passage of the book of the annals that records the fact of the conspiracy against the king and Mordecai’s decisive intervention, thus preparing the immediate development of the plot.

4. Fortunes reversed

It is barely morning when the king, having ascertained that nothing had been done for the man who had saved him, asks Haman – first to arrive – point-blank: “What shall be done for the man whom the king wishes to honor?”

Haman does not doubt that he is the recipient of the honors the king would like to bestow, and so immediately advises the most sumptuous of ceremonies. Hatred has made him sleepless and impatient; in the king, on the other hand, a sudden attack of remunerative justice inspires haste to reward the benefactor hitherto neglected.

But what disappointment at finding himself forced to prepare for his most hated enemy the honors he had believed destined for himself, and with what insuperable humorous touch the author condemns him to accompany the honored man through the streets of the city, crying out: “Thus shall it be done for the man whom the king wishes to honor!”

To say that he goes home “scowling” is truly little. But although the family atmosphere is this time anything but euphoric, at the hour of the second banquet he sets off for the palace animated by a vague hope: who knows, perhaps the queen’s favor holds some reward in store for him!

“As they were drinking wine” the king renews the question and repeats the promises: “What is your petition, Queen Esther? What do you desire? Even to half my kingdom, it shall be done.”

Ready and explicit now is the queen’s answer: “If I have won your favor, O king, my petition is that my life be given me; my desire, that my people be spared.”

And once again in Esther’s voice is the cry of her people begging mercy from the tyrant of the day; we know that, for once at least, the victim’s cry will succeed in stifling that of the persecutor.

“I and my people – Esther continues undaunted – have been sold to be destroyed, killed, annihilated...”

“Who is he – asks the king – where is he who has presumed to do such a thing?”

The accusation is ready: “The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman.”

At this unexpected blow the king, perhaps at the moment more stunned by surprise than truly “enraged”, rises and goes into the garden. But, coming back in suddenly, he finds Haman who, terrified, has thrown himself before the couch on which the queen is seated “to beg for his life”.

The king misunderstands, and his anger overflows: “Will he even assault the queen – he cries – in my presence, in my own house?”

For Haman it is the end. “As soon as the word left the king’s mouth, (the servants present) covered Haman’s face”; a gesture which signified a death sentence by hanging. Swiftly there comes to the mind of the eunuch Harbona the image of the gallows that Haman had had erected for Mordecai. He mentions it, and the king pronounces: “Hang him on that.” “Then the king’s anger abated.”

On that same day he gave Esther the property of Haman’s house and she revealed to him the bond of kinship, until then kept hidden, that joined her to Mordecai; and on Mordecai’s finger the king placed the ring that had been on Haman’s finger.

But although somewhat reassured, uncle and niece cannot help thinking with anguish of the edict of extermination that is gradually reaching the distant provinces of the empire and of the day fixed for the slaughter, which inexorably draws near. And they are not unaware that according to Persian law every edict sealed with the king’s ring is “irrevocable”. Esther therefore hastens to throw herself at Ahasuerus’s feet to beg him to prevent the effects of Haman’s wickedness: “How can I bear to see the destruction of my kindred?”

5. Salvation for the people too

The secretaries are summoned at once and, in the king’s name but under Mordecai’s inspiration, a new edict is drawn up which grants the Jews the right to defend themselves by every means against anyone who, whether by virtue of Haman’s decree or for any other reason, might wish to attack them.

Founded on the principle of legitimate self-defense and alien to any vindictive intention, this edict represents a complete reversal of the situation, and because of the truly significant elements that characterize it can be considered an authentic document, if not of historical import, certainly of moral qualification.

Addressed officially to the governors of the provinces, but in reality directed to the Jews, it does not repeal the previous “irrevocable” edict, but with great diplomatic skill empties it of meaning and force; of meaning, in that it eludes the original persecutory intent by authorizing the Jews to defend themselves; of force, with the mild but clear expression: “You will do well not to put into effect the letter sent by Haman.”

Moreover, by declaring “false and crooked” the arguments adduced to justify the decree of extermination, it takes up the defense of the Jewish people, rehabilitates them, proclaims their total innocence. Not “evildoers”, but “children of the Most High God” and “chosen race”; not “different from all other peoples” because of “a strange tenor of laws”, but on the contrary governed “by most righteous laws”, which they must be allowed to “use in all security”.

The accusation of “non-observance of the laws of the nation in which they live” and on account of which they would be “an obstacle to the stability of the kingdom” is thus nullified; and the principle is affirmed of the Hebrews’ right freely to practice their own religion even among foreign peoples and under foreign dominations. A principle of evident universal value for the Hebrews of all times.

Furthermore, in perpetual remembrance of the deliverance from a most grave danger from which Israel emerged not only “saved” but even morally and materially victorious, the institution of a national feast to be celebrated every year on the 14th and 15th of the month of Adar was established, a decision considered the foundation of the feast of Purim, in which still today the cheerful dressing-up of children, the public reading of the book of Esther and the din and cries of execration that accompany the reading each time the name of Haman is pronounced bring back to life the atmosphere of fairy tale, of tragedy and of prophecy.

At this point one could almost consider it a story with a happy ending, if blood did not drip precisely from the last pages. In fact, “on the day when the enemies of the Jews hoped to gain power over them, the reverse occurred, for the Jews gained power over their enemies... (and) struck all their enemies with the sword, killing and destroying them...”

They were authorized to do so by virtue of their right and duty of legitimate self-defense and, given the times and circumstances, it was inevitable. It is right also to take into account, as a merit of the Jews, the fact that they refrained from the plunder which the king had authorized; nevertheless we cannot feel fully in tune with Mordecai when, peace having now returned, we hear him pronounce placidly and serenely: “These things have come from God.” Because every slaughter (and may we be forgiven the easy moralism) not only cannot be willed by God but is a wound inflicted on the heart of humanity.

But perhaps Esther...

6. Blood on the happy ending

By the way: what of Esther?

On the day of the massacre, while in the citadel of Susa the king was being told the number of enemies killed, he, more tender and caressing than ever, asked the queen: “What more do you ask? What else do you desire? It shall be done.”

And we are dismayed to hear that she, in a voice hard as that of an implacable executioner, asks that the fighting be prolonged for another day and “that the ten sons of Haman be hanged on the gallows”.

The compassion for Haman’s sons, perhaps all innocent of their father’s faults, is barely mitigated by the thought that of them, already killed, Esther asks only the public display of the corpses. A question of... measure and perhaps also of customs! But still more surprising is the request for another day of fighting, which amounts to a duplicate of the carnage, albeit hyperbolically quantified.

How are we to identify in this new, unknown Esther, who asks death for the enemies already defeated, the “little spring... the light that came, the sun and abundant water...” of Mordecai’s premonitory dream with which the Greek version of this story opens?

This is a new Esther, a female figure that we may call unprecedented even in comparison with the other female figures of the Bible hitherto reviewed.

We take comfort in the thought that it is not a true story. One or more writers, sharers in their people’s painful humiliation in a time of political and religious domination, wished to console it with the account of a gratifying maxi-victory and perhaps also to encourage it to defend itself by force against unjust persecutions. As a whole, in fact, the narrative has the evident aim of strengthening its faith and sustaining hope in the God who, with constant fidelity and infinite love and patience, saves his people from the gravest dangers.

And this is the new and not unusual, but always reassuring, moral that Mordecai draws at the end, recalling the initial dream: “I remember the sign I saw concerning this matter. God has remembered his people and has vindicated his inheritance.”

CHAPTER X

SUSANNA THE CHASTE

1. She was very beautiful

“...Susanna, daughter of Hilkiah, of rare beauty, who feared the Lord; her parents, who were righteous, had trained their daughter according to the Law of Moses.” With the addition of the marriage to the important and wealthy Joakim and of the description of the setting in which she lives, Susanna can almost be equated to the stereotyped portrait of the “daughter of a good family, well brought up and better married” who could easily be found in centuries of socially dominant Christianity.

There is nothing in her at the moment that, apart from physical beauty, confers on her any personal attribute or virtue that would place her in a category of persons worthy of particular mention. And yet, among the many female figures of the Old Testament worthy of remembrance, she is perhaps the best known and most widely cited at the level of popular culture.

Although it may seem so, Susanna is not the true protagonist of the story which, placed as an appendix to the book of Daniel, constitutes a sort of didactic or, better still, hagiographic sequel, since it is easy to infer that the author’s main intention is to celebrate the prophetic charism with which Daniel would have been endowed from childhood.

Nevertheless the edifying aim is also well present in the story, and the moral lesson that springs from it is clear. One may therefore think that the story formed part of an older popular tradition; in the Greek version, enriched with suitable adaptations and set in a context whose general lines are historically documentable, it acquires a character of remarkable verisimilitude.

By birth and marriage Susanna in fact belongs to that elite of Hebrews deported by Nebuchadnezzar in 587 from Jerusalem to Babylon who, precisely because they came from a high class, had readily accepted Jeremiah’s practical and realistic invitation (cf. 29:4-7): “Thus says the Lord of hosts: Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat what they produce. Take wives and have sons and daughters... But seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile... and pray to the Lord on its behalf...”

Thus there had been constituted and consolidated, in the land of exile, Hebrew communities with their own well-defined socio-economic and cultural-religious physiognomy which, while respecting local laws, had given themselves a particular status, with their own norms and their own leaders.

A touch of real historical consistency is given to the story also by the figure of the two elders, co-protagonists; by long tradition the “elders” had already constituted in Israel a sort of caste which, founded more on respect than on authority, had in time achieved a certain legal recognition; in a foreign land, moreover, deprived of place of worship and of priests, the deportees had spontaneously recognized in the elders among their fellow-deportees the true spiritual and juridical guides of the community.

Of this by now solidly constituted environment Joakim was a leading exponent: rich, owner of “a large garden adjoining his house”, which seems to have been a sort of status symbol for the owner, esteemed, moreover, “more than all others”, he had made his house a center of common gathering and, when necessary, the seat of a tribunal.

The two elders “appointed judges that year” are there, naturally, at home; but beneath the austere mantle of age and dignity they hide the vices that had furnished Ezekiel with matter for bitter invectives: “He said to me (the Lord): Have you seen what the elders of the house of Israel do in the dark?...” (Ezek 8:12). And again: “Certain of the elders of Israel came to me... and the word of the Lord came to me: these men have taken their idols into their hearts, and have put the stumbling block of their iniquity before their faces” (Ezek 14:1-3).

And the occasion of their iniquity shows itself every day to the two elders in the person of Susanna.

2. Under impure gazes

Nothing, however, appears in her that provokes, still less justifies, the “burning passion” that gradually leads them “to lose the light of reason”.

Susanna, we know, is beautiful, of “rare beauty”, but the author, extremely sparing with regard to her, adds no physical or psychic connotation that might constitute a means of seduction. If anything it is the reader’s fancy which, almost reading between the lines, draws from the text’s laconism an image of Susanna endowed with a particular charm, almost surrounded by an aura of graceful and easy modernity foreign to the women of her time but alien to those tones of sensuality that the writings of the Old Testament sometimes seem to consider almost inseparable from woman’s make-up, taken as an instrument of snares and a symbol of sin.

An exquisite specimen of woman, in her authenticity Susanna appears equal only to herself. Her very conspicuous gifts, psychic and moral, will manifest themselves only at the moment when they are put to the test.

Skillfully tinged with well-measured sarcasm, on the other hand, unfolds the account concerning the two old men, who, while trying to hide from each other their own guilty feeling, find themselves face to face, forced first to unmask themselves and then to become accomplices. A whole masterly psychological crescendo that culminates in the moment when the unwitting object of their desires offers the two suitors the occasion to surprise the woman.

Abject their language no less than their intentions; limpid, on the other hand, and strong, in the purity of her unconditional fidelity to God’s law and to the conjugal bond, is Susanna’s reply: “I am completely trapped. If I do this, it will mean death for me; if I do not, I cannot escape your hands. I would rather fall into your hands innocent than sin before the Lord.”

Alone and defenseless, the woman defends herself as she can: she cries out aloud. The two old men cry out as well; hardened in vice, they soon turn into mortal hatred the morbid passion that dominated them. Let the rebellious woman die provided their life and their false dignity are safe.

In the refusal of the fragile and strong Susanna a twofold message is contained which manifests resistance on two fronts: no to the violation of the Law of the God of the covenant, which has already cost Israel its freedom and homeland; no to adultery, a sin against which the voice of the prophets has hurled and hurls itself.

Pleasant reminiscences of literary classicism are stirred by the choral participation of the people in the epilogue; strangely superficial, however, is the ease (and Daniel himself reproaches them for it) with which “the assembly believed them (the elders) and condemned Susanna to death”, to whom no one seems to listen although she must have been generally esteemed since “nothing like this had ever been said about her”.

The author intervenes to reassure us: “The Lord heard her cry.”

3. The boy prophet

And the moment of Daniel has come, or rather of the “Spirit of truth” which invests the youth and sets face to face two innocences that, in different circumstances and under different forms, have been equally put to the test.

It might be observed that the probative argument chosen by Daniel to unmask the two guilty men appears ambiguous and of uncertain outcome. It would have sufficed, in fact, for one of them to declare that in the agitation of the moment – quite natural – he had not paid attention to the kind of tree under which the offense was being committed, and the charge of false witness would have fallen and with it the only proof on which, ultimately, Susanna’s innocence rested.

But since everything takes place in an atmosphere of prophetic inspiration, it is fitting to set aside every rationalizing pretension and leave room for divine initiative alone.

One could also point out the chronological inexactitude of the story, which makes Daniel present and active as still a “youth” within a community that, being solidly established in Babylon, must have settled there not a few decades earlier, having renounced the possibility of returning to Jerusalem granted by Cyrus in 538. A community that, in any case, reflects its own clear Hebrew identity also in the unappeased dissension between the kingdom of Judah and the kingdom of Israel. “This is how you have been dealing with the daughters of Israel – Daniel reproaches the elders – and in their fear they have been intimate with you. But a daughter of Judah would not tolerate your iniquity.”

4. The Lord saves!

Although born and raised in a foreign land, Susanna shows herself a true “daughter of Judah” by the solidity of her character and her boundless fidelity.

And yet, unlike Deborah, Ruth, Judith, Esther and so many other noteworthy Hebrew women, Susanna plays no role, performs no historically saving act. She fulfills, however, in herself, a task of singular witness: she is the only woman of the Old Testament whose memory has been handed down with the epithet “chaste”; chastity to be understood in the general sense of modesty, purity, reserve, discretion, self-respect, rectitude at every level and, in the more specific sense, unblemished conjugal fidelity, since the concept of virginity as a virtue in itself was foreign to the Hebrew mentality. Chastity understood, therefore, as a virtue in which are summed up all the virtues that can enhance a woman in an attitude of devotion equivalent to loving and total consecration to all that, in the plan of God’s will, is identified with her own personal destiny, and that of the family and the race.

In this respect Susanna the chaste, the innocent woman ensnared who prefers death to sin, can also be seen as a prophetic sign of the future restoration of Israel which, punished with exile and lashed by Ezekiel’s violent and realistic allegory, is reassured by the promise: “I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall know that I am the Lord, in order that you may remember and be ashamed, and never open your mouth again because of your shame, when I forgive you all that you have done” (Ezek 16:62-63).

“In that day innocent blood was saved”, the author concludes. Blood. How much of it still drips from the pages of the history of the Hebrew people which is then the presage, sign and history of the whole of humanity!

Blood shed unjustly, blood offered in sacrifice and witness, blood of victims and martyrs that flows today as yesterday on all the roads of the earth; here an impure stain, there a saving washing whose mystery we are not given to understand but on which, as the story of Susanna also confirms, the Lord’s gaze is constantly fixed.

Because the Lord is he who “saves those who hope in him”.

CHAPTER XI

A MOTHER COURAGE

1. The historical scene

“There was also the case of seven brothers arrested together with their mother.” This announcement, after the gloomy sequence of intrigues and betrayals, usurpations and vendettas that darken the pages of the two books of Maccabees, can only be the prelude to new atrocities. And yet, placed immediately after the account of Eleazar’s martyrdom, it seems at last to bring a breath of purer and more breathable air.

Israel is living through one of the darkest and most dramatic periods of its history, particularly of the post-exilic centuries. With the sudden end of the Babylonian empire swept away by the Persian armies (539 B.C.) the Lord “stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia” (Ezra 1:2-3) in favor of the deported Hebrews and opened the exiles’ hearts to the loveliest hopes: “Thus says Cyrus king of Persia: The Lord, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house at Jerusalem in Judah. Who is among you of all his people? May his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem in Judah, and rebuild the house of the Lord, the God of Israel... Then the heads of the families of Judah and Benjamin, and the priests and the Levites, everyone whose spirit God had stirred, got ready to go up and rebuild the house of the Lord in Jerusalem...” (Ezra 1:1ff).

Slow and wearisome is the journey home but useful and profitable for a deep rethinking of the whole experience.

And the returnees recall the times when “the Lord, the God of their ancestors, sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place; but they kept mocking the messengers of God, despising his words, and scoffing at his prophets... until the wrath of the Lord against his people became so great... and he brought up against them the king of the Chaldeans, who killed their young men with the sword, and had no compassion on young man or young woman, old man or aged; he burned the house of God and broke down the walls of Jerusalem...” (2 Chr 36:11ff).

And those “who had escaped from the sword”, become slaves of the conqueror, had been taken and deported; leaving buried among the ruins of the destroyed homeland the vain certainties and presumptuous illusions of a people many times unfaithful to its God.

But from the depths of abjection, from the bitterness of exile among foreign people, the enslaved people had raised its gaze to its God and, in the impossibility of performing the traditional rites, had recovered fidelity of heart and called upon its God. And God had remembered it and now called it back to its homeland.

Traveling, in small detached groups, the road of return, the returnees discover the true meaning of their journey: it is not so much a return to the homeland as the sincere and definitive return of the heart to the God of the fathers, once again faithful to his covenant, still and always Father of this people he has chosen as his exclusive possession.

Meanwhile there fade away in the distance the songs, hymns to their gods, of the Persian conquerors, unaware that they are nothing but a mere instrument in the hands of the one true God, lord of history.

In the hearts of the returnees good resolutions mature.

The arrival at Jerusalem was disappointing. The city in ruins, the surroundings devastated, misery and squalor everywhere. And, on the faces of those who had occupied the places abandoned by the deportees, distrust and hostility.

High, however, was the returnees’ morale, effective the leaders’ drive, favorable the conditions granted by the Persians; ready, therefore, and well disposed were the wills for the immense work of reconstruction.

Between 520 and 515 the temple is rebuilt. Far indeed from the splendor of the first, the work of Solomon, but still a reassuring sign of the Lord’s presence in the midst of his people.

Among the repatriates the more thoughtful minds and the more sensitive consciences feel the pressing need to know themselves truly: to seek their own origins, to rethink their own history, to discover their true identity as a people marked by the singular destiny of a particular and exclusive relationship with their God; and, insistent among all, the question that will torment man’s conscience until the end of the world: if God is goodness by essence, why evil? What is its origin?

With the clarifying of ideas the authentic spirit of Judaism is born, the numerous writings are composed or completed which, gathered in the sacred Book, will hand down to the whole of humanity for the millennia to come, together with the particular history of the Hebrew people, the marvelous history of God’s work, supreme coordinator of events, in view of the eternal salvation of the whole human race.

Amid so much fervor of thought and works, Israel cannot, however, recover its own autonomy as a nation.

After about two hundred years the Persian empire collapses and the astonished world witnesses the stormy rise of the star of Alexander the Great, which however sets rapidly, leaving in turmoil the regions on which his lightning impetus fell.

With Alexander’s successors, the Ptolemies first and then the Seleucids, Israel knows a rather favorable interlude, but then falls at the mercy of a series of despots who, to varying degrees, exercise power ruthlessly.

The great riches of the temple, plundered by Nebuchadnezzar but restored by Cyrus (cf. Ezra 1:7-11) and increased over time, excite the greed of the rulers of the day.

The episode of Heliodorus (cf. 2 Macc 3) is not enough to convince them of the inviolable sacredness of the goods consecrated to the Lord; nor does the anguished word of Onias, the holy high priest, who explains that the temple gold is the sacred deposit of widows and orphans, serve to curb the cupidity of rulers often burdened with debts because of their luxurious and dissolute life.

2. Under the reign of Antiochus IV Epiphanes

The situation becomes dramatic with the advent of the impious and ruthless king Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175-164), who finds, unfortunately, the apostate Jason acquiescent in his designs; Jason, on payment of a large sum of money, illegally obtains, ousting his righteous brother Onias, the office of high priest.

In a delirium of power Antiochus sets himself the total Hellenization of the Hebrew people and, with a decree extended to all the Hebrew cities occupied by the Greeks, forbids, on pain of death, any open profession of Judaism. Forbidden therefore the observance of the sabbath and the celebration of all the traditional religious feasts and imposed the religious and civil practices of the pagan Greeks, and above all the eating of the flesh of animals offered in sacrifice to the gods and of all the meats forbidden by Hebrew law (cf. 2 Macc 6).
