Not a few out of fear obey the decree, and soon the evil spreads everywhere. With the practice of every dissoluteness under its porticoes, the temple is profaned, and some of the priests themselves neglect its worship and let it fall into squalor.

Antiochus’s impious arrogance goes as far as total profanation: having entered the temple he carries off all its treasures: “the golden altar, the lampstand for the light, and all its utensils” and every other object as well as the silver and the gold (1 Macc 1:21ff).

From Modein meanwhile breaks out the revolt of Mattathias and his five sons (cf. 1 Macc 2) who, followed by many faithful, withdraw to the countryside and begin the guerrilla warfare that will issue in open war and end with the victory of the Maccabees and the ignominious death of Antiochus Epiphanes, which will be followed for the people by a period of autonomous government.

3. The fortitude of a mother of martyrs

The martyrdom of the seven brothers with their mother takes place precisely under the reign of Antiochus IV Epiphanes. Having refused to eat the flesh, sacrilegious to them, the seven young men are seized with their mother and brought before the tyrant.

Six of them have already been atrociously tortured and killed before their mother’s eyes, who “because of her hope in the Lord” bore with a serene face the torment and death of her sons. Tempering, indeed, “her woman’s reasoning with a man’s courage” she animated and encouraged them: “I do not know how you came into being in my womb; it was not I who gave you life and breath... doubtless the Creator of the world, who shaped the beginning of humankind... will in his mercy give life and breath back to you.”

The mother has spoken to her sons in the language of their fathers which the tyrant does not understand, so that, suspecting that the woman is mocking him, he is the more irritated and with a still more perfidious intent sets himself to draw from the last of the brothers a more malign satisfaction by killing his spirit rather than his body: he will try with flattery to make him unfaithful to his God. And he speaks to him calmly, almost affectionately, promising to make him very rich and to make him happy provided he adapts to live according to the customs of the Greeks.

But seeing that the youth remains firm in his refusal he turns to the mother. It may be that maternal tenderness will end by yielding before the sacrifice of the last of her sons and succeed in bending the young man’s spirit too. And it is here that the Jewish faith attains the summit of heroism: the mother is glad to be able to speak to her son but certainly not in the sense intended by Antiochus, and with renewed constancy she prepares to uproot from her own womb the last, tenderest and deepest fiber that binds her to the last of the brood, perhaps the most beloved of her sons. “Have pity on me”, she says to him almost fearing that any possible yielding on the boy’s part might not only offend God but strike her too, more painfully than physical death itself, by breaking the bond of spirit that unites them; and she speaks to him as if immersed in a heart-rending wave of sweet memories, of tender recollections, spurring him to the last act beyond which true life will be assured to him.

“I carried you nine months in my womb, nursed you for three years, reared you, fed you...” With this insistence on the gift of life the woman seems to assert a new fundamental right of hers to take the gift back, not for herself but to make of it a splendid offering of youth, strength and purity to the God of the fathers; it is she who wants to offer him, almost with priestly hands, on the altar of her heart, now that the temple is deserted and ritual sacrifices are forbidden on the altar profaned by the usurpers.

There well up from her lips words of innate depth, dense with a theological wisdom which, so clear and precise, has not yet found a parallel in the writings of the sages of her time: “I beg you, my child, to look at the heaven and the earth and see everything that is in them, and recognize that God did not make them out of things that existed. Thus also the human race came into being.”

As in a prophetic leap, from the existential anguish of Job and the pessimistic wisdom of Qoheleth one rises to the light of a fuller revelation up to the discovery of a God who created out of nothing. A profession of faith that issues in a cry of triumph: “Do not fear this butcher, but accept death, so that in God’s mercy I may get you back again along with your brothers.”

The youth needs no further exhortations; indeed, he himself forcefully proclaims the right to die and turns to the executioner with scornful words and threats to the tyrant. The latter, “enraged by the scorn”, vents his rage more cruelly than on the others on this young man who “passed away undefiled, putting his whole trust in the Lord”.

Worthy of the mother and the sons is the lapidary conclusion: “Last of all, after her sons, the mother died.”

A splendid figure of woman and mother who recalls another, that of Rizpah who, undaunted amid the dark glare of tribal vendettas, stays, day and night until the rainy season, to protect from wild beasts the wretched remains of her sons and grandsons, seven in number, they too (cf. 2 Sam 21:10).

Rizpah, however, guarded only the lifeless flesh of those whom she had not been able to snatch alive from a senseless vengeance. This mother, instead, offers to the executioners, with greater pain than her own, the living limbs of her sons. But in the gesture of the offering is already the exultation of victory over the tyrant’s impiety, who will not succeed in tearing from the consciousness of the Israelites faith in the one God, and the joyful certainty of the endless life to which she entrusts and consecrates the creatures of her womb.

An emblematic figure? It is well known how much national feeling or the will to revenge can lend wings to the imagination and pathetic accents to a writer’s style. The narrative, however, a typical sign of adherence to truth also in relation to the historical context in which it is set, unfolds in a plain and calm style that does not indulge in rhetoric and, in the end, seems rather to wish to draw a weary veil of silence after the inhuman torment: “Let this be enough about the eating of sacrifices and the extreme tortures” (2 Macc 7:42).

Without need of artificial typological comparisons, this female figure standing out clearly against a horizon that is already almost a meeting point between the old and the new covenant recalls and in some way anticipates the figure of the woman who, in the mystery of her virginal motherhood, sums up and expresses the mystery of femininity in its essence and in its mission: Mary of Nazareth. She, at the foot of the cross, in sharing in the Son’s sacrifice, brings with him to fulfillment and anticipates for the centuries to come the saving value of the life of every woman, virgin or mother, who in spousal adherence to Christ becomes a sharer in universal motherhood.

CHAPTER XII

WOMEN AND WOMAN IN THE WISDOM WRITINGS

Unlike the many figures of women who, sculpted in the round, leap from the pages of the Old Testament as protagonists or participants in great or small events of Israel’s history, the female figures outlined in the wisdom books appear barely lit – by light now limpid, now murky – by fleeting flashes; and yet not evanescent as mere abstractions but as real, living persons and often set in moments and situations of concrete life.

Like figurines worked in relief against a background of absolutely masculine valence, at times they brighten it with touches of gentle femininity, at times they tinge it with ambiguous veins and at times they darken it with maleficent and devastating intrusions. But, each placed with her characteristics in her own proper place, they appear as if evoked by an instance of vital concreteness whose balance neither the glaring contradictions nor the occasional outbursts of that misogyny, perhaps more of manner than of substance, connatural to the male of every time and place, succeed in altering.

In the final analysis, the passages concerning woman constitute a document of sincere humanity, mirror of a society founded on the indissoluble complementarity of the human being, male-female, and bound to the recurring phenomena of life in its fundamental demands and manifestations.

One would say that, even in the proud awareness of a preeminence consolidated in the age-old exercise of absolute supremacy in all fields, man, before woman, senses an aura of arcane religiosity connected with the mysterious origins of life and feels a mixture of reverence and fear to which, by instinct, he reacts with misogynistic outbursts either angry or streaked with humor or shaded with tenderness which, on the border of paradox, are pregnant with that incontrovertible truth that springs from all human experience.

And in the end it turns out that, for good and ill, no less than woman’s instinct toward her husband proves strong (cf. Gen 3:16), strong is the attraction that man feels toward woman. Hence, as sincere as are the authors of the wisdom books when they express the sense of restful sweetness that a gentle feminine presence communicates, they are equally sincere when, denouncing the maleficent influence of the “wicked” woman and affirming the necessity of fleeing her, they implicitly admit the power of her seduction.

If not quite contemporaneously, at no great distance in time another Hebrew writer placed on Adam’s lips the words: “This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen 2:23) and on the divine lips: “The two shall become one flesh” (Gen 2:24).

Indivisible as life.

1. Woman as mother

Significant is the deep respect for the woman-mother that the father instills in his son, expressed with frequent parallelisms that place her on the same level as the father.

“Hear, my child, your father’s instruction, and do not reject your mother’s teaching” (Prov 1:8), the author of Proverbs, and Sirach reinforces the concept: “The Lord honors a father above his children – and he confirms a mother’s right over her children” (Sir 3:2). And again (7:27): “With all your heart honor your father, and do not forget the birth pangs of your mother”; and 3:4: “Whoever honors his mother is like one who lays up treasure”; while the author of Proverbs pronounces (17:25): “A foolish son is a grief to his father and bitterness to her who bore him.”

And Sirach warns (3:16): “Whoever forsakes his father is like a blasphemer, / and whoever angers his mother is cursed by the Lord”, and confirms it in 3:9: “A father’s blessing strengthens the houses of the children – but a mother’s curse uproots their foundations.”

And the citations can be multiplied.

2. Woman as wife

Still more numerous are the references to woman as wife, but not always characterized by equal respect and esteem; always, however, strongly significant.

“Do not dismiss a wise and good wife” advises Sirach (7:19), “for her graciousness is worth more than gold”; and continues, reinforcing the concept: “Do you have a wife after your own heart? Do not reject her”; but at 7:26, almost fearful of excessive idealization, he specifies: “but do not trust yourself to one whom you hate”.

Strongly vexed appears the author of Proverbs (or one of the many authors or compilers of the text) when he grumbles (21:9): “It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a contentious wife” and, with the immediacy of an image drawn from living experience, he adds (27:15): “A continual dripping on a rainy day and a contentious wife are alike”, which brings to mind the petulant acrimony of Job’s wife (cf. Job 2:9-10).

But the grumbler does not miss the other side of the coin and shows he knows how to appreciate it. Indeed, after warning the “son” against the charm of the “other” woman and “the smooth words of the foreigner”, he advises him, in a tone of domestic, sweet intimacy (5:15-19): “Drink water from your own cistern, flowing water from your own well. Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth, a lovely deer, a graceful doe. May her breasts satisfy you at all times; may you be intoxicated always by her love.”

Quite different sounds the judgment on the “foreign” woman, to escape whose snares the “son” is exhorted to have recourse to wisdom. Her faults are many and grave: she is an adulteress, “forsakes the partner of her youth”, impious and idolatrous, “forgets the covenant of her God”; a deadly instrument of ruin, “her house sinks down to death... none who go to her come back” (Prov 2:16-19).

Worthy of note is the bringing together of the moral value of conjugal fidelity and the religious value of fidelity toward God, brought out still more clearly by Sirach (23:22): “... the woman who leaves her husband – first, she has disobeyed the law of the Most High.”

It is right, however, to note also the honest and impartial stand taken toward the adulterous husband (Sir 23:18ff): “A man who is unfaithful to his marriage bed says to himself: Who sees me? No one sees me, what do I have to fear? The Most High will not remember my sins. His fear is confined to human eyes... Such a man will be punished in the streets of the city; he will be seized where he least expects it...”

Among all, the wife occupies a central place, wise mistress of the house, support of the family. Proverbs:

“A good wife is the crown of her husband”;

“The wisdom of a housewife builds the house”;

“He who finds a wife finds a good thing – and obtains favor from the Lord”;

“House and wealth are inherited from parents, but a prudent wife is from the Lord”.

Sirach is not to be outdone (26:1-4):

“Happy is the husband of a good wife”;

“Blessed is the husband of a good wife;

the number of his days will be doubled.

A loyal wife brings joy to her husband

he will complete his years in peace.

A good wife is a good portion,

she will be granted to the man who fears the Lord.

Whether rich or poor, his heart is glad,

and at all times his face is cheerful.”

3. Women in general

But... one does not know by what sudden second thought, he changes mood and, without a break, bursts out in this grumbling (Sir 26:5ff): “At three things my heart is afraid: and of the fourth I am frightened” (and this is naturally woman!). Indeed: “... heartache and sorrow is a woman jealous of another / and a lash of the tongue makes itself known to all” and he goes straight on, ruminating his ill humor: “An ox-yoke chafing is a bad wife – to take hold of her is like grasping a scorpion”; and so on, listing defects, vices, faults and evil arts of the one who seems suddenly raised to symbol and cause of all the world’s evils.

And it is no wonder if one considers that in the preceding chapter he had not spared the most poisonous barb at the “root” of all evil: “From a woman sin had its beginning, and because of her we all die” (Sir 25:24).

But fortunately it is not a judgment without appeal and still less a universal judgment; perhaps, as a good artist, he wished to accentuate the dark colors so that the image of the bride, envisioned with loving abandon as the finished ideal of beauty and goodness, might stand out the more clearly and purely: “A wife’s charm delights her husband / and her skill puts flesh on his bones. / A silent wife is a gift from the Lord / there is nothing so precious as a disciplined soul. / As the sun rising in the heights of the Lord, / so is the beauty of a good wife in a well-ordered home. / Like the lamp shining on the holy lampstand / so is a beautiful face on a stately figure. / Like golden pillars on a base of silver / so are shapely legs and steadfast feet” (26:13-18).

Not content, he resumes at 36:22-25: “A woman’s beauty lights up the face / and surpasses every human desire; / if kindness and gentleness are on her tongue / her husband is not like other men. / He who acquires a wife gets his best possession, / a helper fit for him and a pillar of support. / Where there is no fence, the property will be plundered / and where there is no wife, a man will wander about and groan...”

A satisfactory judgment, but... never trust completely! Man recommends caution even toward the woman he loves.

And here is a hint of notable psychological subtlety, an intuition that it would be easier to attribute to a woman than to a man: “Do not be jealous of the wife of your bosom, and so teach her an evil lesson to your own harm.” And a warning, perhaps the fruit of bitter experience (9:1-2): “Do not give yourself to a woman so that she gains mastery over your strength.”

But finally we also find a touch of frank objectivity, as a due compensation on the part of the whole male brotherhood in favor of woman, often defenseless and wronged (28:15): “Slander has driven away courageous women, / and deprived them of the fruit of their toil.” An accusation clearly directed at a “talebearer”, at a “double-tongued man”, at the male, in short.

4. Women as daughters

It is a duty of completeness to mention another series of troubles that woman can cause man, the father in particular: “A daughter is a secret anxiety to her father / and worry over her robs him of sleep” (Sir 42:9).

And many are the misfortunes that this daughter (apparently quite incapable of looking after herself) can bring upon her poor father who, dazed by the long list, comes out with a paradoxical assertion: “Better is the wickedness of a man than a woman who does good!” (42:14).

In reality, rather than a paradox, we are faced with an absurdity against which both logic and justice rebel. More acceptable seems the corresponding verse in André Chouraqui’s French version: “Better (preferable) the malice of a man – than that of a woman”: the woman’s reputation is not saved but justice runs fewer risks.

5. In Qoheleth’s vision

The two brief references Qoheleth devotes to woman prove fully integrated in the alternation of his vision of a world made of smoke that disperses and shadows that vanish, but not without ample clearings within which, becoming aware of God’s omnipresent power and of his own limits, he considers the advisability of seeking that measure of “better” that life can offer: small joys, modest, fleeting, but true. For no one “can make straight what (God) has made crooked; in the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider; God has made the one as well as the other” (7:13-14).

And who can oppose God? Perhaps Qoheleth tried it in his obstinate search for wisdom in a human key: “I turned my mind to know and to search out and to seek wisdom and the sum of things...” (7:25), but it seems that he came upon only wickedness and folly. And so he found... “more bitter than death the woman who is a snare, whose heart is a net, and whose hands are fetters”. And, insisting on “adding one thing to another to find the sum...”, he declares: “which my soul is still seeking but I have not found: one man among a thousand I found, but a woman among all these I have not found.”

Thus traditional misogyny reappears; but it should not be taken too seriously. Qoheleth too has his second thoughts and in his mind there makes its way the thought which shuns radical pessimism, leading him to a true profession of faith: “Then I saw all the work of God, that no one can find out what is done under the sun... and I understood that the righteous and the wise and their deeds are in the hand of God” (8:16-17).

Evil is inherent in the human heart; but “as long as one is joined with all the living, there is hope” (9:4).

And therefore, the sage advises, know how to appreciate life: “Go, eat your bread with enjoyment, and drink your wine with a merry heart...”

But man’s heart needs a still more intimate and deeper joy: “Enjoy life with the wife whom you love, all the days of your vain life that are given you under the sun, because that is your portion in life and in your toil at which you toil under the sun” (9:9).

Here is the flash of vivid light which, beyond the disappointing emptiness of the human condition, lets us discover that there is something capable of compensating man for the toil of existing. And, recalling what Qoheleth said earlier (4:9-11), we can believe in his sincerity: “Two are better than one... if they fall, one will lift up the other. But woe to one who is alone and falls and does not have another to help. Again, if two lie together, they keep warm; but how can one keep warm alone?”

What better comfort than a love that “lasts all the days of life”, however fleeting? Perhaps more in need of human and divine warmth was precisely Qoheleth’s disenchanted heart, although not even for him does everything seem dark and cold.

The God “who made everything beautiful in its time” (3:11) had also put into his heart “a sense of eternity”.

6. In the Book of Wisdom

The Book of Wisdom, apart from the radiant female figure who, personifying divine Wisdom, dominates it, has a single passage referring, and only indirectly, to woman; but it is a new and essential concept that deserves careful reflection.

“Blessed is the barren woman who is undefiled, who has not entered into a sinful union – she will have fruit when God examines souls (3:13)... Better is childlessness with virtue, for in the memory of virtue is immortality, because it is known both by God and by mortals” (4:1).

Contrary to the traditional conviction, never until then shaken, of the Hebrews, according to whom sterility was divine punishment and supreme social disgrace while motherhood constituted the only degree of specific dignity attributed to woman, the author redeems the condition of the barren woman as well as that of the eunuch, proclaiming the preeminent value of virtue, for which the righteous are granted “a hope full of immortality” (3:4).

A new vision, a luminous trajectory which, freeing from the narrow perspective of the pallid Sheol, opened the horizons of a true life, a life without end “with the Lord” (5:15).

One certainly cannot relate the biblical concept of sterility, even if “undefiled”, or of the blameless condition of the eunuch to the Gospel ideal of virginity or celibacy for the kingdom of heaven; in some way, however, it anticipates its teaching and opens, from afar but with linear development, the way to the radical experience of the sequela Christi.

A sense of expectation is already in the air, a hope in hearts, everywhere the echo of the prophets’ word. Someone is about to come.

7. In the Book of Proverbs

Deserving separate consideration is what we may call the “portrait of the Hebrew woman” with which the Book of Proverbs closes in chapter 31.

An idealized but very significant figure, in that it gives us an idea of the whole of the qualities a husband could desire in his wife and, more interesting still, of the totality of the initiatives and behaviors that could, at the limit, be permitted and appreciated in a woman belonging to a certain social level.

To her, shrewd and enterprising, the husband, a man intensely engaged in public offices, not only entrusts the total government of the family but also allows full freedom in the management of affairs ordinarily considered a male preserve. “She watches over the affairs of her household.” She rises while it is still night to prepare food for the family and assign tasks to each of the maids; then she devotes herself to personal activities. She works “willingly” with her own hands the raw materials she has had “brought from afar” and sells the manufactured goods to the merchant with considerable economic advantage. And while she works “she considers a field and buys it; with the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard”.

In the prosperity she procures for the family, for which she provides not only “double clothing” against the winter cold but general well-being and security, so much so that “she laughs at the time to come”, she delights in sharing it also with the wretched and the poor. Her intelligent activity brings her strength and dignity and certainly does not make her neglect her own person: “her clothing is purple”.

A true type of woman manager, albeit in relation to the cultural level and custom of the time and setting, in her perfection she might seem arid of feeling as if she thought only of profit. But the author takes care to bring out with effective discretion her moral and affective gifts as well. So that “the heart of her husband” has good reason to trust in her not only for the material security she assures him and the social prestige she brings him “in the gates of the city”, but also because “she does him good and not harm”; from her mouth drips “the teaching of kindness”, fruit and sign of the fear of God that guides her life and informs her works.

And right are the children who “rise up and call her happy”, and her husband who “praises her”.

8. The woman to be praised

It certainly cannot be excluded that a type of woman endowed with such a sum of perfections, and placed at the close of a book that opens with the invitation to Wisdom personified in a female figure, is meant as a further and concluding call to the cult of divine Wisdom, foundation of all virtuous and fruitful industry.

But in the most direct form and the most immediate sense it also indisputably represents an authentic recognition of the worth of the being of whom God said: “I will make him a helper as his partner.”

And another passage of the Old Testament comes to mind, the beautiful prayer that young Tobias addresses to the Lord on the wedding night (Tob 8:5-8):

“Blessed are you, God of our ancestors,

and blessed is your name for all generations...

You made Adam

and you made Eve his wife

as a helper and support.

From the two of them the human race has sprung.

You said: It is not good that the man should be alone; let us make for him a helper like himself...

Be pleased to have mercy on me and on her...

And they said together: Amen, Amen!”

Apart from the accusations and censures, perhaps in places excessive but not groundless, which moreover are widely directed also at the male world; apart from the grumblings, the universal safety valve of male ill-humors about woman of all times; apart, again, from whatever in this modest study we have not managed to see, glimpse, understand and evaluate, it seems we may conclude that the Hebrew woman of the Old Testament, also by virtue of the high moral level proper to the people of the covenant, enjoyed a certain situation of privilege, above all moral, in comparison with the women of other peoples.

In the depth of its spiritual meaning the verse “Her lamp does not go out at night”, which the author dedicates to his ideal “strong woman”, is truly the most beautiful and truthful praise of the Hebrew woman of all times, whose watchful fidelity to the hearth sustained and continued to sustain the edifice of the family, guarding its purity and the religiosity of its life and fidelity to traditions even in the dark and tragic millennia of her people’s diaspora.

Keeper of the Sabbath lamp, her humble but irreplaceable presence, no less than the passionate attachment to the Torah of the Hebrew men, helped keep alive the original spirit of the race and faith in the Promise, making possible the miracle of a people which, reemerged more alive than ever and faithful to itself, presents itself again to the world, after two thousand years, as the mysterious sign of a non-human plan.

CONCLUSION

ANNE, WHO ARE YOU?

1. At the end of the journey

We have now come to the end of the research begun three years ago with the aim of finding a possible answer to the question that – as Daughters of St. Anne, forming a religious family committed to venerating in her with special devotion the mother of the Mother of the Son of God made man and, in this respect, to helping make her known and venerated throughout the world – had always troubled us: who was, truly, St. Anne?

With the passing of time the need became pressing to dispel, since tearing it was not possible, the thick veil of anonymity with which sacred Scripture has wrapped her. Nor were the glimmers of uncertain light coming from the apocryphal writings sufficient, chiefly the Protoevangelium of James, of the second century, which attribute to the mother of the Mother of Jesus the name of Anne.

Until the Spirit who lives in the hearts of believers told us: “Seek his face.”

And we sought it, lingering over the eternal pages of the Bible and questioning one by one the female figures of the Old Testament who people it, in our eagerness to grasp in each of them some of the essential characteristics of the race, its peculiar style of life, the kind of activity entrusted to woman in the sphere of family and society; and above all the breath of the Spirit and the way of relating to the divine, in prayer and in life, of the people to which St. Anne belonged.

It has been a long journey, at times easy and gratifying, at times arid and winding, sometimes disconcerting, in the face of the pitiless honesty with which the writers of the sacred books recount the history – lights and shadows – of their people. A journey which however grew ever more luminous through the appearing of a mysterious presence and a resolute will which, indirectly but decisively, came to clarify the reasons for our faith, our hope, our certainties.

If not the results hoped for, we have gained a clearer vision of the course of human history within the history of the Hebrew people; a course without temporal break, the unfolding of an infallible plan whose meaning will be made known by its Author only on the threshold of eternity.

Indeed, although we limited the research to the figures and concrete data that could be drawn from a history so remote in time and so complex and uncertain in detail, it became clearly apparent to us that the Bible, even if from the literary point of view it reaches peaks of supreme beauty and nobility, providing most precious historical data, is anything but a work or collection of historical or literary works; its supreme purpose is to teach man to sanctify life.

2. “Hear, O Israel!”

“Hear, O Israel! The Lord is our God, the Lord alone!”

“Hear, O Israel!” Every page of the Old Testament vibrates with this call, for the prophets had never tired of summoning the people to listen to the God who, not with audible sounds but with emblematic signs and decisive events, revealed himself to Israel as a direct and privileged interlocutor, unveiling to each new generation part of his mystery.

And Israel learned this language and learned to repeat the eternal Word and to hand it on from century to century, in joyful events and in sad ones; every Israelite says it at the point of death; it was said even on the threshold of the gas chambers invented by modern barbarism, in the Shoah that would have wished to destroy him forever.

Listening to the Word is for the Hebrew an essential condition of fidelity to the covenant, because in listening is included the resolve to adhere to the God who speaks and the commitment to put his command into practice even before knowing its content fully. That is to say that, more even than the fulfillment of the precept, what counts is the recognition of the absolute sovereignty of the One who issues it.

Hence attention to every single norm, with no distinction between the more and the less important or burdensome; to obey, always, because “to obey is better than sacrifice” (1 Sam 15:22); at the limit, better even than prayer. Obedience, in fact, involves the whole person, body, spirit, will, while prayer leaves freedom to express one’s own feelings (whose very wide range finds ample room in the prayer of the Psalms), to the point that the one praying can even come to imagine that God answers him and to answer him in turn by praising him, thanking him and even contesting him. And as there is no distinction of importance in regard to performance, so, at least in theory, there should be no distinction of importance, or even of dignity, between the roles and tasks assigned to man and those assigned to woman.

To man are assigned the tasks inherent in divine worship and the handling of public affairs; but even taking account of the specific characteristics of femininity, one cannot say that woman as such is dispensed from fulfilling the various precepts. In fact, the role of responsibility for the running of the family, committing her continually to the direction or execution of domestic work, takes for her the place of the other precepts, as the Talmud will specify: “While one is engaged in one observance one is dispensed from fulfilling others.”

From the age of the patriarchs there emerge figures of women who are beautiful, lively, shrewd, at times enterprising to the point of unscrupulousness, endowed with a vitality that, at least in part, explains the miracle of the survival of a race which, in spite of the unspeakable adversities suffered over the centuries, passes through them and advances in history; loving and patient women, but not without, when needed, a ready and cutting tongue; tender and proud women, strong in misfortune and exemplarily faithful.

The word of the prophets, the lesson of events, the multiplicity of experiences promoted the gradual maturing of Hebrew spirituality; the attentive reader can in this way sound the maturing of the inner world of the Hebrew woman, so essential in her simplicity, so deep in her irrevocable fidelity to the Covenant, until grasping the authentic meaning of her daily morning prayer: “Lord, I thank you because you have made me as you wanted me.”

The awareness of her radical belonging to God, permeated by the certainty that every manifestation of the divine will is a sign of his infinite love, makes her understand how and why he wanted and made her thus and makes her intuit the universal scope of the divine plan which reflects in woman’s sensibility the tenderness, delicacy, understanding and compassion of his fatherly-motherly heart (Isa 66:13: “As a mother comforts her child, so I will comfort you”).

A fruitful womb offered to welcome every bud of life willed by the Creator, his collaborator in the transmission of life, woman in general, but in particular the Hebrew woman, is essentially mother, deeply in love with the life she receives and gives, so that she cannot do without it except at the price of the deepest unhappiness.

Hannah, wife of Elkanah, is not satisfied with her husband’s love, great as it is (“Am I not more to you than ten sons?”), she wants a son, wants him passionately and makes a gift of him to the Lord; Rachel cries out to Jacob her anguish as a barren woman; Jephthah’s daughter goes to weep on the mountains over her unfulfilled virginity before giving herself up to the executioner; Anna, Tobit’s wife, is vehement in her anger against her husband who has sent away the son whose delay distresses her; Sarah’s wounded and disappointed spirit finds comfort only in Edna’s sorrowing gentleness; Rizpah defies death to defend even only the wretched corpses of her sons and grandsons; and the mother of the seven Maccabean brothers is so much the mother of their souls that she gladly accepts in exchange the torment of their bodies.

The fundamental demand of total self-giving, proper to femininity, is transmitted from generation to generation; in her time Anne, wife of Joachim, will give to the Lord, in her own daughter, the most pure womb that he will need for the accomplishment of his plan of universal salvation.

Wife and mother, the Hebrew woman devotes herself to the sanctification of herself and her family by promoting the holiness of its members in the fulfillment of the norms concerning their spiritual and material well-being. Rearing the children, caring for their first growth with a long period of nursing at the end of which a family banquet celebrates the weaning (cf. Gen 21:8), taking charge of the children’s first education constitute the most important of her tasks. To this are added the exercise of hospitality; the observance of all the duties concerning the good running of the home; the delicate solicitude in promoting and maintaining the balance of relationships, so that throughout the whole environment, through the harmony of things and persons, the presence of the Lord may be clearly perceptible.

Not in the temple nor in the synagogue – we repeat – but in the family does the Hebrew place his vital center; and it is in the family that the domestic queenship of woman comes to the fore, even taking account of the religious duties attributed to her, concerning the celebration of the feasts that recur in the course of the year.

In the house without a wife, the rabbis declare, there is no blessing, nor peace, nor joy. Peace and joy, the living and deep aspiration of the Hebrew soul and its greatest wealth. In spite of the dramatic vicissitudes of its age-old history, the Israelite is a creature of joy; and guardian and guarantor of domestic peace and joy is woman.

3. Who was Anne, then?

We have seen that only the apocryphal writings attribute the name of Anne to the mother of Mary; apart from the uncertain details reported about her and her husband Joachim, we know nothing else. Was she beautiful, rich, of noble family? What singular virtues can be attributed to her? Perhaps Edna’s sweetness, Naomi’s wisdom, Abigail’s shrewdness, Rebekah’s quickness of spirit, Judith’s strength of soul founded on faith. But we cannot go further.

With greater certainty, perhaps, we can think of her as one of the many humble exemplary women who, in the anonymity of prayer and the diligent fulfillment of daily duty, by an inner impulse of the Spirit adhered to that elite spiritual movement which arose after the experience of the exile and spread in the centuries before the birth of Jesus. This movement embodied one of the meanings attributed to the concept of the “remnant” or “small remnant of Israel”, already present in Isaiah (28:5-6) with a more eschatological sense and applied by Jeremiah (24:4ff) to that new people the Lord would form from among the “survivors” of Judah, while Zephaniah (3:12) announced: “I will leave in the midst of you a people humble and lowly. / The remnant of Israel shall seek refuge in the name of the Lord.” And “On whom shall I look?”, the Lord had asked through Isaiah, specifying: “On the humble and contrite in spirit, / who trembles at my word” (Isa 66:2).

The Israel of the humble and the poor answered its God with a fearful but trusting listening, elaborating a spirituality largely new in the recognition of its own nothingness before the divine transcendence and in the consequent sense of radical poverty; in contrition of heart before the inexhaustible, patient fidelity of the Lord, always ready to forgive; in trusting abandonment to divine providence; in total openness, finally, to his will. Anne, mother of Mary, certainly belonged to that “remnant”.

But we had set out on the “search for the face” of Anne. Can we say we have found it?

Through the Christian centuries, hundreds of painters have tried to portray it according to the image each carried carved within; and one may say that each of her countless devotees keeps within an image relating to the relationship he has established with her. But can that suffice?

We had dreamed of catching some more marked line of her face, adhering as closely as possible to the idea we have been able to draw from the Scriptures... And so?

Who knows, the Gospel...

4. On the threshold of new times

Luke (10:38ff) relates: “Jesus entered a certain village, where a woman named Martha welcomed him into her home. She had a sister named Mary, who sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to what he was saying.”

Let not this abrupt transition seem out of place or untimely; the link is easy. Barely a generation has passed from the time of Anne and Joachim to the period of Jesus’ public life; Martha, Mary, Lazarus, the closest, perhaps the most beloved friends of Jesus, are his contemporaries; as genuine Hebrews they live, think, pray, love like the Hebrew Jesus and like Mary, mother of Jesus and daughter of Anne.

Educated certainly in the daily recitation of that formula which constitutes the root of her people’s prayer and its firmest and most explicit profession of faith (“Hear, O Israel!”), Mary of Bethany, seated at Jesus’ feet, is the authentic, unwitting plastic representation of Hebrew spirituality now come to the “fullness of time”.

Not by chance is the Hebrew Jesus ready to defend her from the rebuke of Martha, the sister no less sensitive to the promptings of the Spirit and certainly no less Hebrew than Mary, who, in her busy and loving solicitude, represents the other typical aspect of Hebrew femininity, the sense of cordial and generous hospitality.

The truth emerges from Jesus’ mouth: “Mary has chosen the better part, which will not be taken away from her.”

But even so intensely absorbed in listening, Mary is anything but an inert and passive being; it will be she, in fact, who shortly afterwards will perform, in prophetic function, the sacred gesture of Hebrew hospitality, the anointing of Jesus’ feet (John 12:3), with which she announces and anticipates the Master’s “day of burial”. And it is he who again defends her, this time from Judas’s self-interested criticism, with words that make us understand how close to his heart and sharer of his mystery is this faithful one of listening.

But let us not neglect Martha; the two sisters, the “contemplative” and the “practical”, embody the two complementary aspects of Hebrew femininity; fused in a single person, the meditative attitude may stand out more in one and the activist aspect in the other, but both are always present.

Anne was no less solicitous a mother than Mary when, watching her daughter sleep sweetly, she raised her thought and heart to the Father, nor less contemplative when with diligent love she washed the baby’s diapers.

And indeed, Mary of Nazareth too...

It is again Luke who gives us the interpretive key to the very few words spoken by Mary, when he states: “Mary treasured all these words and pondered them in her heart” (2:19).

The angel’s words... Elizabeth’s words... Simeon’s words... up to that unequivocal answer that must have made her start more than all the other words: “Did you not know that I must be about my Father’s business?” (2:49-51).

Luke does not fail to note that they did not understand, but adds at once that his mother treasured everything in her heart.

Mysterious resonances of the soul which, in the silence of the house of Nazareth, especially after Jesus has left it to begin his mission, gradually acquire meaning; and the mother shows she has understood her son’s heart well when at Cana, beyond the perhaps disconcerting sound of the words, she grasps the true sense of his reply and says confidently to the servants: “Do whatever he tells you.” And she prompts the first miracle.

Gestures of gratuitous love, gestures “of attention that becomes sensitive to grace”, to put it in the words of Pavel Evdokimov, gestures with which Mary of Nazareth and Mary of Bethany reveal how indissoluble are the two basic precepts of Hebrew spirituality that will be the fulcrum of Jesus’ message: faith in the one God and the unity of love of God and neighbor.

5. Anonymity, but in the light

If Mary, in her immaculate purity, reflected the absolute holiness of the Father, she could not but cast a ray of it upon the human root of her existence, upon the mother who with life had given her a receptivity adequate to the Spirit who would overshadow her, to the Grace that would take possession of her.

But the world did not know it.

Anne’s presence on earth is marked by silence. Unknown even to their contemporaries, humble instruments of an event far greater than themselves, the work completed for which the Lord chose them, Anne and Joachim disappear.

In the Protoevangelium of James, the most sensitive and delicate of the apocrypha, the joyful admiration that Mary’s parents express over the fact that “their little daughter had not turned back” as she climbed the temple steps is significant. They had prepared her for this. And they vanish into silence.

But, confined by sacred Scripture to the obscurity of the most absolute anonymity, with the passing of the centuries the figure of Anne is lit with an ever livelier light in the consciousness of the Christian people and rises to a fame of holiness that radiates to every part of the world, inseparable from her daughter both in ecclesial worship and in the prayer of the devout as in the imagination of artists.

The more clearly the greatness of the Mother of Jesus was revealed to the Church’s reflection, the more devotion to St. Anne, mother of Mary, spread throughout the world. Shrines of worldwide renown arose, national and international pilgrimages were organized, associations aimed at spreading her cult were promoted; among the people there took root a particular devotional current which made and still makes converge upon her, privileged mother of the most exalted of daughters, as protector of all the mothers of the world, the prayers and supplications of Christian mothers.

It is perhaps nothing other than a way all her own of coming out, anonymous, from shadow into light.

Therefore, in final conclusion: the face we sought has not emerged, and we knew it could not, almost an identikit, physical too, of Anne; but we trust that, also through the faces of the biblical women whom we have approached, her spiritual face and the dignity of her role in the history of salvation have become somewhat clearer.

FROM THE BACK COVER

The volume aims to discover the face of Anne, the mother of Mary. The Bible is silent about her and the author, instead of following the paths of pious and gratuitous reflection, focuses her research on the fundamental original datum: Anne is mother par excellence, and to understand Anne one must “discover the face of the Mother”.

The author constructs in a biblically irreproachable way a theological profile on the basis of the Old Testament. She has traced the features of the “eternal feminine” present in the Scriptures with unique wisdom, distinguishing each time the ideal aura of the great figures, such as Esther, Judith and Deborah, from the ordinary women of the Bible, no less interesting for the reconstruction of a biblical female face. Both, the great figures and the anonymous ones, are the object of careful examination from which the author draws surprising pictures with a female subject.

Her method is always vigilant and never indulges in moments of devotional or intimist weakness: familiarity with specialist texts on the subject is evident. And yet the reflections are nourished by great passion, first of all for the Jewish people, for whom the author always showed boundless love, because it has suffered perpetually and because it is the people from whom St Anne, the Virgin Mary and Jesus came; and then a passion for the spirituality of her religious congregation.

The volume was born of the specific need of the Institute of the Daughters of St Anne to outline in a renewed way the features of its own spirituality. But it also draws on the long stays and deep impressions of Sepphoris, Haifa and Nazareth, to which the author wished to return “drawn by inexplicable nostalgia” to immerse herself in the light of the word of God.

Natalina Sotgia

Natalina (Annettina) Sotgia, a sister of the Daughters of St Anne, born at Sorgono (NU) in 1912 and a graduate in literature of the Catholic University, taught and served as headmistress in the Institute’s middle schools at Cercola (NA) and Matera. From 1966 to 1978 she was vicar general and in the following ten years (1979-89) directed the communities of Haifa and Nazareth in Israel. She lived that decade intensely, developing an ever deeper attunement with the Jewish people: significant contacts with persons and institutions, affection for the country and service to the poor (the great majority of them Arabs). Back in Italy in 1989, she worked in the congregation’s Study Centre and Historical Archive; much appreciated was her contribution to the Rome group of the Jewish-Christian Friendship, where her memory is still alive. Annie Cagiati expressed in her book Settanta domande sull’ebraismo her gratitude to Sr Natalina, who had collaborated in revising the text. She died on 21 July 2000 in Rome after spending her last two years suffering from a serious illness.
